Chapter 2 Stress and equilibrium

2.12 The largest shear stress and the deviator

In section 2.11 we answered half of the second question from the end of section 2.6.6: among all faces through a point, the normal stress is largest on the face perpendicular to the principal direction with the largest principal stress. The other half of the question is still open. On which face through the point is the shear stress largest, and how large is it? For the bar we found the answer in lemma 2.19 on the largest shear stress in a bar, \(|\sigma|/2\) at the tilt \(45^\circ\), but only among the faces tilted about the axis \(z\). We need the answer for every state of stress and for all faces through the point. For metals, the start of yielding is decided approximately by exactly this largest shear stress, as we said at the end of section 2.4 (BOWER §3.7.3, PDF p. 146).

The route of the section is this. First we write the normal and the shear stress on any face in terms of the principal stresses. We will see that the normal stress is a weighted average of the principal stresses, and that the square of the shear stress measures how far the principal stresses are spread around this average. The theorem on the largest shear stress will follow from this. Then we look at the faces that turn about one axis. Their stresses lie on a circle, which shows all these faces in one picture. Then we split the stress into a part that pulls or pushes equally on all faces and a remainder that carries all the shear. From the remainder we build a single number with which we compare the stress at a point with the yield stress from the tension test. Finally we split the strain in the same way.

The whole section takes place at one point \(P\) inside a body in equilibrium. We will use only results that hold for every body, above all Cauchy's formula (theorem 2.26), the symmetry of stress (theorem 2.41), by which \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zy}}\), and theorem 2.83 on the principal directions of a symmetric matrix with its consequences from section 2.11. For the strain in section 2.12.9 we also make the small deformation assumption (section 1.17.3). We assume nothing about the material, so everything we derive holds for every material. The only exceptions are the two yield criteria in section 2.12.6, for which we need data about the material from tests. We will test the results on three examples from section 2.6.6, the bar, pure shear and the fluid at rest, and on a new example, a thin plate, which we describe when we need it.

2.12.1 Stresses on a face in principal axes

We already know how to compute the shear stress on any face. Cauchy's formula gives the traction vector, the normal stress is its projection onto the normal, and the shear stress follows from \(\tau^2 = |\vek t|^2 - \sigma_{\mathrm{n}}^2\) (item 3 of lemma 2.14 on splitting a vector). The computation becomes transparent if we take the principal directions as the directions along which we measure components.

By theorem 2.83 the symmetric stress matrix at \(P\) has three mutually perpendicular unit eigenvectors, the principal directions, and by definition 2.84 the axes in these directions are the principal axes of the stress. In this section we use the principal axes as a coordinate system with origin at \(P\), so we label them like axes: with the digits \(1\), \(2\) and \(3\) instead of letters, as announced in section 1.5.5, and their unit vectors with \(\vek e_1\), \(\vek e_2\) and \(\vek e_3\), like \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) for the axes \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\). These are the principal directions \(\vek n_1\), \(\vek n_2\) and \(\vek n_3 = \vek n_1\times\vek n_2\) of section 2.11, only with the names of axes. The corresponding principal stresses are, as there, ordered by size, \(\sigma_1 \ge \sigma_2 \ge \sigma_3\). This is not an assumption about the stress, only a choice of names: we call the largest principal stress \(\sigma_1\) and the smallest \(\sigma_3\). CM writes them \(\lambda_1\), \(\lambda_2\) and \(\lambda_3\) (CM, PDF p. 191).

By item 1 of corollary 2.85 the matrix of stress components in principal axes is diagonal. On the face with normal \(\vek e_1\) the traction vector is \(\vek t(\vek e_1) = \sigma_1\,\vek e_1\), which points along the normal and has no shear part. Likewise \(\vek t(\vek e_2) = \sigma_2\,\vek e_2\) and \(\vek t(\vek e_3) = \sigma_3\,\vek e_3\).

Now take any flat face through \(P\) with unit normal \(\vek n\). We denote its components in principal axes by \(n_1\), \(n_2\) and \(n_3\). These are the numbers that we wrote \(\bar n_1\), \(\bar n_2\) and \(\bar n_3\) in corollary 2.85: the projections of the normal onto the principal directions, \(n_1 = \vek n\cdot\vek e_1\), \(n_2 = \vek n\cdot\vek e_2\) and \(n_3 = \vek n\cdot\vek e_3\), and at the same time the numbers of steps along the principal axes that make up the normal:

\[\vek n = n_1\,\vek e_1 + n_2\,\vek e_2 + n_3\,\vek e_3 .\]

In the proof of corollary 2.85 we showed that \(n_1^2 + n_2^2 + n_3^2 = 1\) (step 7) and that the normal stress on the face is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = \sigma_1 n_1^2 + \sigma_2 n_2^2 + \sigma_3 n_3^2\) ((2.81)). For the shear stress we also need the length of the traction vector. We compute scalar products as there, with the rules of lemma 2.12 on the properties of the scalar product and with \(\vek e_{\mathrm{i}}\cdot\vek e_{\mathrm{i}} = 1\) and \(\vek e_{\mathrm{i}}\cdot\vek e_{\mathrm{j}} = 0\) for \(i \neq j\), where the indices \(i\) and \(j\) run over the principal axes \(1\), \(2\), \(3\).

  1. Theorem 2.26 asks of the axes only that they are mutually perpendicular, so Cauchy's formula holds in every rectangular Cartesian coordinate system, so also in principal axes. By (2.25) the traction vector is the sum of three vectors along the axes:
    \[\vek t(\vek n) = n_1\,\vek t(\vek e_1) + n_2\,\vek t(\vek e_2) + n_3\,\vek t(\vek e_3) = n_1\sigma_1\,\vek e_1 + n_2\sigma_2\,\vek e_2 + n_3\sigma_3\,\vek e_3 .\]
  2. The square of the length of the traction vector is \(\vek t(\vek n)\cdot\vek t(\vek n)\). When we expand the product, of the nine terms \(n_{\mathrm{i}}\sigma_{\mathrm{i}}\,n_{\mathrm{j}}\sigma_{\mathrm{j}}\,(\vek e_{\mathrm{i}}\cdot\vek e_{\mathrm{j}})\) only the three with equal indices remain, so \(|\vek t(\vek n)|^2 = \sigma_1^2 n_1^2 + \sigma_2^2 n_2^2 + \sigma_3^2 n_3^2\).
  3. By item 3 of lemma 2.14 on splitting a vector, the square of the shear stress is \(\tau^2 = |\vek t(\vek n)|^2 - \sigma_{\mathrm{n}}^2\). In the figure of the lemma, with \(\vek a = \vek t(\vek n)\) and \(\vek e = \vek n\), the traction vector is the hypotenuse of a right triangle whose legs are the normal part of length \(|\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}|\) and the shear part of length \(\tau\).
  4. We insert step 2 and (2.81):
    \[\begin{aligned} \sigma_{\mathrm{n}} &= \sigma_1 n_1^2 + \sigma_2 n_2^2 + \sigma_3 n_3^2 , \\ \tau^2 &= \sigma_1^2 n_1^2 + \sigma_2^2 n_2^2 + \sigma_3^2 n_3^2 - \big(\sigma_1 n_1^2 + \sigma_2 n_2^2 + \sigma_3 n_3^2\big)^2 . \end{aligned} \tag{2.91}\]

CM writes them in the same way, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\) in the text and \(\tau^2\) as (4.3.18) (PDF p. 191). SADD (3.4.7) (PDF p. 70) writes \(\tau^2 + \sigma_{\mathrm{n}}^2\) in place of \(\tau^2\), which is step 2. Let us test them on the bar pulled by an axial force. Its principal stresses are \(\sigma_1 = \sigma > 0\) along the bar and \(\sigma_2 = \sigma_3 = 0\) across it, and (2.91) gives \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = \sigma\,n_1^2\) and \(\tau^2 = \sigma^2 n_1^2 - \sigma^2 n_1^4 = \sigma^2 n_1^2\,(1 - n_1^2)\). For the oblique cut of section 2.4 the component of the normal along the bar is \(n_1 = \cos\theta\) (figure 2.45), so \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = \sigma\cos^2\theta\) and \(\tau^2 = \sigma^2\cos^2\theta\,\sin^2\theta\). The first is (2.13). The second gives \(\tau = |\sigma\sin\theta\cos\theta|\), since the shear stress, a length, is not negative, and this is (2.14). But the formulas hold for every face, not only for the faces tilted about the axis \(z\).

The formulas (2.91) hide a simple picture. We denote the numbers \(n_1^2\), \(n_2^2\) and \(n_3^2\) by

\[w_1 = n_1^2 , \qquad w_2 = n_2^2 , \qquad w_3 = n_3^2 .\]

Each is a square, so it is not negative, and by step 7 of the proof of corollary 2.85 their sum is \(w_1 + w_2 + w_3 = 1\). The index \(i\) in the sums of this section and the next runs over the principal axes \(1\), \(2\), \(3\). The normal stress is then

\[\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = w_1\sigma_1 + w_2\sigma_2 + w_3\sigma_3 ,\]

a weighted average (tehtano povprečje) of the principal stresses with the weights \(w_1\), \(w_2\) and \(w_3\), as we saw after corollary 2.85. Imagine three weights with masses \(w_1\), \(w_2\) and \(w_3\) placed on the number line at the points \(\sigma_1\), \(\sigma_2\) and \(\sigma_3\) (figure 2.272, top). The line balances if we support it at the point \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\), because the sum of the masses times their signed distances from the support is \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} w_{\mathrm{i}}\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{n}}) = \sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{n}} \cdot 1 = 0\). The normal of the face decides how the mass is shared among the principal stresses. Since the weights are nonnegative, the support lies between the outermost weights, \(\sigma_3 \le \sigma_{\mathrm{n}} \le \sigma_1\). A support to the left of all the weights could not hold the line, since all the weights would turn it the same way, and likewise a support to the right of them. Indeed \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - \sigma_3 = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} w_{\mathrm{i}}\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} - \sigma_3) \ge 0\), because each term is a product of two nonnegative numbers, and likewise \(\sigma_1 - \sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} w_{\mathrm{i}}\,(\sigma_1 - \sigma_{\mathrm{i}}) \ge 0\). This is item 2 of corollary 2.85, that the normal stress on every face lies between the smallest and the largest principal stress. The computation is the same as in steps 8 and 9 of its proof, and the balance of the line shows why it holds.

At the top of the figure is the number line with the principal stresses \(\sigma_3\), \(\sigma_2\) and \(\sigma_1\). Above them stand the blue weights \(w_3\), \(w_2\) and \(w_1\), taller where the weight is larger. The triangle below the line is the support at the point \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\), where the line balances. The grey distances from the support to each principal stress will give the shear stress. At the bottom is the line for the face with the normal \((\vek e_1 + \vek e_3)/\sqrt2\), on which each of the two outer principal stresses carries \(1/2\) and the middle one carries \(0\). The support is then at the midpoint \(c\) of the interval, and the distance from it to each outer stress is \((\sigma_1 - \sigma_3)/2\).

And the shear stress? Let us show that its square is the average of the squares of the distances of the principal stresses from \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\), with the same weights:

\[\tau^2 = w_1\,(\sigma_1 - \sigma_{\mathrm{n}})^2 + w_2\,(\sigma_2 - \sigma_{\mathrm{n}})^2 + w_3\,(\sigma_3 - \sigma_{\mathrm{n}})^2 . \tag{2.92}\]
  1. We write out each square on the right, the square of one of the grey distances, as a product of brackets: \((\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{n}})^2 = \sigma_{\mathrm{i}}^2 - 2\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{n}}^2\).
  2. We multiply by \(w_{\mathrm{i}}\) and add over \(i = 1, 2, 3\). The right side is \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} w_{\mathrm{i}}\sigma_{\mathrm{i}}^2 - 2\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\sum_{\mathrm{i}} w_{\mathrm{i}}\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{n}}^2\sum_{\mathrm{i}} w_{\mathrm{i}}\).
  3. The second sum is \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} w_{\mathrm{i}}\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\), the balance point of the line, and the last one is \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} w_{\mathrm{i}} = 1\), the sum of all three weights. The right side is therefore \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} w_{\mathrm{i}}\sigma_{\mathrm{i}}^2 - 2\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}^2 + \sigma_{\mathrm{n}}^2 = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} w_{\mathrm{i}}\sigma_{\mathrm{i}}^2 - \sigma_{\mathrm{n}}^2\).
  4. With \(w_{\mathrm{i}} = n_{\mathrm{i}}^2\) this is exactly the expression for \(\tau^2\) in (2.91).

In the picture with the weights, \(\tau^2\) is the average of the squares of the grey distances in figure 2.272. So the shear stress on a face is large when the normal shares the mass among principal stresses that are far apart. With half the mass at \(\sigma_3\) and half at \(\sigma_1\) both distances are \((\sigma_1 - \sigma_3)/2\), so

\[\tau^2 = \frac12\Big(\frac{\sigma_1 - \sigma_3}{2}\Big)^2 + \frac12\Big(\frac{\sigma_1 - \sigma_3}{2}\Big)^2 = \Big(\frac{\sigma_1 - \sigma_3}{2}\Big)^2 , \qquad \tau = \frac{\sigma_1 - \sigma_3}{2} .\]

The shear stress is zero exactly when all the mass is at a single point of the line. The terms \(w_{\mathrm{i}}\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{n}})^2\) in (2.92) are not negative, so their sum is zero exactly when every term is zero, that is, when every principal stress with a nonzero weight has the value \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\). Then by step 1 of the derivation of (2.91) the traction vector is \(\vek t(\vek n) = n_1\sigma_1\,\vek e_1 + n_2\sigma_2\,\vek e_2 + n_3\sigma_3\,\vek e_3 = \sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\vek n\), because \(\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\) in every term with \(n_{\mathrm{i}} \neq 0\). The traction vector points along the normal, so \(\vek n\) is a principal direction (definition 2.82), as for the faces of section 2.11.1.

Figure 2.273 shows four cases, each on its own line. On line (a) all the mass is at \(\sigma_1\), \(w_1 = 1\) and \(w_2 = w_3 = 0\). Then \(n_1^2 = 1\) and \(n_2 = n_3 = 0\), so \(\vek n = \pm\vek e_1\), and the face is perpendicular to the principal axis \(1\). The support stands under \(\sigma_1\) and the shear stress is zero, as \(\vek t(\vek e_1) = \sigma_1\,\vek e_1\) from the start of the section already tells. When two principal stresses are equal, the mass may also be shared between them. In the bar pulled by an axial force \(\sigma_2\) and \(\sigma_3\) are the single point \(0\) on line (b). A face with \(w_1 = 0\) has all its mass at this point, however \(w_2\) and \(w_3\) share it, so the support is at \(0\) and there is no shear. A face with \(w_1 = n_1^2 = 0\) has its normal perpendicular to the axis of the bar, so every lengthwise face of the bar is free of shear.

The oblique cut of the same bar with \(\theta = 30^\circ\) on line (c) is a case where the mass is not at one point. By the test above \(n_1 = \cos 30^\circ\), so the weight \(w_1 = \cos^2 30^\circ = 0{,}75\) is at \(\sigma\) and the remaining \(0{,}25\) at \(0\). The support is at \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = 0{,}75\,\sigma\), the grey distances to \(\sigma\) and to \(0\) are \(0{,}25\,\sigma\) and \(0{,}75\,\sigma\), and (2.92) gives

\[\tau^2 = 0{,}75 \cdot (0{,}25\,\sigma)^2 + 0{,}25 \cdot (0{,}75\,\sigma)^2 = 0{,}1875\,\sigma^2 , \qquad \tau = 0{,}433\,\sigma ,\]

which is \(\sigma\sin 30^\circ\cos 30^\circ\) by (2.14). When all three principal stresses are equal, as in a fluid at rest, where \(\sigma_1 = \sigma_2 = \sigma_3 = -p\), all three are the single point \(-p\) on line (d) and all the weights stand at it, however the normal shares them. The support is at \(-p\) and there is no shear stress on any face, as we saw in section 2.6.6.

2.12.2 The maximum shear stress at a point

How large can the spread (2.92) be? All three principal stresses lie in the interval \([\sigma_3, \sigma_1]\) of length \(\sigma_1 - \sigma_3\). None of them is farther than half the length, \((\sigma_1 - \sigma_3)/2\), from its midpoint \(c = (\sigma_1 + \sigma_3)/2\). If we measured the distances in (2.92) from \(c\) instead of from \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\), the average of the squares would therefore be at most \(\big((\sigma_1 - \sigma_3)/2\big)^2\). We will show that the average of the squares of the distances from \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\) is never larger than the average of the squares of the distances from any other point, so in particular from \(c\). Of all points of the line, the balance point is the one around which the weights are least spread.

Theorem 2.93 Maximum shear stress at a point (največja strižna napetost v točki)

Let \(P\) be a point inside a body in equilibrium, let \(\sigma_1 \ge \sigma_2 \ge \sigma_3\) be the principal stresses at \(P\) and \(\vek e_1\), \(\vek e_2\), \(\vek e_3\) mutually perpendicular unit vectors of the corresponding principal directions. Then the shear stress on every flat face through \(P\) is at most

\[\tau_{\max} = \frac{\sigma_1 - \sigma_3}{2} . \tag{2.93}\]

It reaches this value on the faces with the unit normals \((\vek e_1 + \vek e_3)/\sqrt2\) and \((\vek e_1 - \vek e_3)/\sqrt2\), on which the normal stress is \((\sigma_1 + \sigma_3)/2\).

Proof

We must show two things: that the shear stress on no face exceeds \((\sigma_1 - \sigma_3)/2\), and that it reaches this value on the two faces named.

1. Upper bound.

  1. Let \(\vek n\) be the unit normal of the face, \(n_1\), \(n_2\), \(n_3\) its components in principal axes and \(w_{\mathrm{i}} = n_{\mathrm{i}}^2\). The weights are nonnegative with sum \(1\) (step 7 of the proof of corollary 2.85), and by (2.92) \(\tau^2 = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} w_{\mathrm{i}}\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{n}})^2\), where \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} w_{\mathrm{i}}\sigma_{\mathrm{i}}\).
  2. Let \(c = (\sigma_1 + \sigma_3)/2\). We write each difference as a sum of two parts, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = (\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} - c) + (c - \sigma_{\mathrm{n}})\), and square it:
    \[(\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{n}})^2 = (\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} - c)^2 + 2\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} - c)(c - \sigma_{\mathrm{n}}) + (c - \sigma_{\mathrm{n}})^2 .\]
  3. We multiply by \(w_{\mathrm{i}}\) and add over \(i\). The number \(c - \sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\) is the same in all three terms, so we take it out:
    \[\tau^2 = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} w_{\mathrm{i}}\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} - c)^2 + 2\,(c - \sigma_{\mathrm{n}})\sum_{\mathrm{i}} w_{\mathrm{i}}\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} - c) + (c - \sigma_{\mathrm{n}})^2\sum_{\mathrm{i}} w_{\mathrm{i}} .\]
  4. The second sum is \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} w_{\mathrm{i}}\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} - c\sum_{\mathrm{i}} w_{\mathrm{i}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - c\), the last one is \(1\). The second term is therefore \(2\,(c - \sigma_{\mathrm{n}})(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - c) = -2\,(c - \sigma_{\mathrm{n}})^2\), and together with the last term there remains
    \[\tau^2 = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} w_{\mathrm{i}}\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} - c)^2 - (\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - c)^2 .\]
  5. The square \((\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - c)^2\) is not negative, so \(\tau^2 \le \sum_{\mathrm{i}} w_{\mathrm{i}}\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} - c)^2\).
  6. By the choice of names, \(\sigma_3 \le \sigma_{\mathrm{i}} \le \sigma_1\) for every \(i\). We subtract \(c\) from all three sides and use \(\sigma_1 - c = (\sigma_1 - \sigma_3)/2\) and \(\sigma_3 - c = -(\sigma_1 - \sigma_3)/2\). We get \(-(\sigma_1 - \sigma_3)/2 \le \sigma_{\mathrm{i}} - c \le (\sigma_1 - \sigma_3)/2\), so \(|\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} - c| \le (\sigma_1 - \sigma_3)/2\).
  7. Both sides of the last inequality are nonnegative, so by lemma 1.29 that a larger nonnegative number has a larger square, \((\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} - c)^2 \le \big((\sigma_1 - \sigma_3)/2\big)^2\) for every \(i\).
  8. We multiply the inequalities of step 7 by the nonnegative weights \(w_{\mathrm{i}}\) and add. Since \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} w_{\mathrm{i}} = 1\), \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} w_{\mathrm{i}}\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} - c)^2 \le \big((\sigma_1 - \sigma_3)/2\big)^2\).
  9. From steps 5 and 8, \(\tau^2 \le \big((\sigma_1 - \sigma_3)/2\big)^2\). The numbers \(\tau\) and \((\sigma_1 - \sigma_3)/2\) are nonnegative, so by the lemma on the larger square, \(\tau \le (\sigma_1 - \sigma_3)/2\).

2. The two faces with the largest shear stress.

  1. The normal \(\vek n = (\vek e_1 + \vek e_3)/\sqrt2\) has the components \(n_1 = 1/\sqrt2\), \(n_2 = 0\) and \(n_3 = 1/\sqrt2\) in principal axes. It is a unit vector, because \(\tfrac12 + 0 + \tfrac12 = 1\), and its weights are \(w_1 = \tfrac12\), \(w_2 = 0\) and \(w_3 = \tfrac12\).
  2. By (2.91) \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = \tfrac12\,\sigma_1 + \tfrac12\,\sigma_3 = c\).
  3. By (2.92), with weights \(\tfrac12\) at distances \((\sigma_1 - \sigma_3)/2\) from \(c\),
    \[\tau^2 = \tfrac12\,(\sigma_1 - c)^2 + \tfrac12\,(\sigma_3 - c)^2 = \tfrac12\Big(\frac{\sigma_1 - \sigma_3}{2}\Big)^2 + \tfrac12\Big(\frac{\sigma_1 - \sigma_3}{2}\Big)^2 = \Big(\frac{\sigma_1 - \sigma_3}{2}\Big)^2 ,\]
    and since \(\tau \ge 0\), \(\tau = (\sigma_1 - \sigma_3)/2\).
  4. The normal \((\vek e_1 - \vek e_3)/\sqrt2\) has the components \(1/\sqrt2\), \(0\) and \(-1/\sqrt2\). The weights are the squares of the components, so they are the same as in item 1, and steps 2 and 3 give the same normal and shear stress.

Source: CM (4.3.23)-(4.3.25) (PDF pp. 191-192), SADD (3.4.10) and the text after it (PDF pp. 71-72), BOWER §2.2.6 (PDF p. 75). The proof is not from the sources. CM finds the largest value with Lagrange multipliers and states the solutions of the resulting equations without derivation (PDF p. 191). We walk this route, with the solutions derived, at the end of this section (the system (2.96) and theorem 2.94).

In step 4 of the proof we saw that the average of the squares of the distances from any point \(c\) equals the average of the squares of the distances from the balance point \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\), increased by \((\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - c)^2\). The balance point is therefore the point of least spread. Around the midpoint of the interval \([\sigma_3, \sigma_1]\), however, the weights are spread by at most half the length of the interval. We will use the expression (2.92) with weights again for the faces that are equally inclined to all three principal directions.

Figure 2.274 shows on which faces the shear is largest. The normal \((\vek e_1 + \vek e_3)/\sqrt2\) lies halfway between the principal directions \(\vek e_1\) and \(\vek e_3\) and is perpendicular to \(\vek e_2\). The face therefore contains the principal direction \(\vek e_2\) and lies halfway between the faces perpendicular to \(\vek e_1\) and \(\vek e_3\). If all three principal stresses are different, there are exactly two faces with the largest shear, and they are perpendicular to each other, because \((\vek e_1 + \vek e_3)\cdot(\vek e_1 - \vek e_3) = 1 - 1 = 0\). The normal stress on them is in general not zero but \((\sigma_1 + \sigma_3)/2\). The intermediate principal stress \(\sigma_2\) does not appear in \(\tau_{\max}\). There are no other faces with the largest shear. Equality in step 8 of the proof requires \(w_2 = 0\), because \(\sigma_2\) is less than half the length away from \(c\), and equality in step 5 requires \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = c\), which together with \(w_1 + w_3 = 1\) gives \(w_1 = w_3 = \tfrac12\).

On the left is a cube with faces perpendicular to the principal directions. The tensile stresses \(\sigma_1\) pull the faces perpendicular to \(\vek e_1\) and the compressive stresses \(|\sigma_3|\) push the faces perpendicular to \(\vek e_3\). The axes \(\vek e_1\) and \(\vek e_3\) point right and up. The two blue diagonals are the faces with the normals \((\vek e_1 + \vek e_3)/\sqrt2\) and \((\vek e_1 - \vek e_3)/\sqrt2\). On the right is the triangular piece cut off by one of these faces. On its other faces act \(\sigma_1\) and \(|\sigma_3|\). On the oblique face is the traction vector \(\vek t\), the sum of the normal part of size \((\sigma_1 + \sigma_3)/2\) and the shear part of size \((\sigma_1 - \sigma_3)/2\).

Let us test the theorem on the examples.

The bar. In a bar pulled by an axial force with the stress \(\sigma > 0\) in the cross section, the principal stresses are \(\sigma_1 = \sigma\) and \(\sigma_2 = \sigma_3 = 0\). The theorem gives \(\tau_{\max} = \sigma/2\), so for our bar with diameter 10 mm under the force 10 kN, \(127{,}3/2 = 63{,}7\) MPa. This is the value of lemma 2.19 on the largest shear stress in a bar, except that we now know it is the largest among all faces through the point, not only among the faces tilted about the axis \(z\). Since \(\sigma_2\) and \(\sigma_3\) are equal, there are many faces with the largest shear. Every normal with \(n_1^2 = \tfrac12\) gives the weights \(w_1 = \tfrac12\) and \(w_2 + w_3 = \tfrac12\), and how the second half is shared between \(\sigma_2 = 0\) and \(\sigma_3 = 0\) does not matter, because both sit at the same point of the line. All such faces are tilted by \(45^\circ\) from the cross section, in any direction around the axis of the bar (figure 2.275). For a bar that is compressed, \(\sigma < 0\), the principal stresses are \(\sigma_1 = \sigma_2 = 0\) and \(\sigma_3 = \sigma\), and the theorem gives \(\tau_{\max} = (0 - \sigma)/2 = |\sigma|/2\), again as in the lemma.

On the left is the bar from the side, pulled by the stress \(\sigma\) along the axis \(x\). Through the point \(P\) runs a cut tilted by \(45^\circ\) from the cross section. This is the cut of the lemma. Its normal \(\vek n\) makes the angle \(45^\circ\) with the axis, because \(n_1 = \cos 45^\circ = 1/\sqrt2\) and so \(n_1^2 = \tfrac12\). The condition \(n_1^2 = \tfrac12\), however, fixes only the angle between the normal and the axis and does not say to which side of the axis the normal leans. On the right we therefore turn the normal around the axis: the angle \(45^\circ\) stays, and the tip of the normal runs along a circle. Each of the grey normals belongs to another face through \(P\), and on all of them the shear stress is \(\sigma/2\). It must be so, because the stress points along the axis and singles out no direction perpendicular to the axis.

Pure shear. The cube of section 2.6.6 is loaded only by forces along four of its faces, \(\tau_0\) per unit area (figure 2.77). In it \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}} = \tau_0\) and the other components are zero, so the principal stresses are \(\tau_0\) along the diagonal \(AC\), \(0\) along the axis \(y\) and \(-\tau_0\) along the diagonal \(BD\) (section 2.11). Hence \(\vek e_1 = (1, 0, 1)/\sqrt2\), \(\vek e_2 = (0, 1, 0)\) and \(\vek e_3 = (-1, 0, 1)/\sqrt2\), and the theorem gives \(\tau_{\max} = (\tau_0 - (-\tau_0))/2 = \tau_0\). The two faces with the largest shear have the normals

\[\frac{\vek e_1 + \vek e_3}{\sqrt2} = \frac{(0, 0, 2)}{2} = \vek e_{\mathrm{z}} , \qquad \frac{\vek e_1 - \vek e_3}{\sqrt2} = \frac{(2, 0, 0)}{2} = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}} .\]

These are just the faces of the cube, on which the shear force \(\tau_0\) per unit area acts, and the normal stress on them is \((\tau_0 + (-\tau_0))/2 = 0\), as it must be. On no other face through a point of the cube is the shear larger than \(\tau_0\).

The fluid at rest. All three principal stresses are \(-p\), and \(\tau_{\max} = 0\): there is no shear stress on any face.

On the left is the cube of fluid, pushed from all sides by the pressure \(p\). On the right is the number line with the principal stresses. All three equal \(-p\), so the three weights stand on top of each other at the same point. The balance point is right there, the distances from it to all three weights are zero, and by (2.92) \(\tau = 0\) on every face.

A thin plate. Now we need an example in which all three principal stresses are different. Take a thin steel plate lying in the plane of the axes \(x\) and \(y\), with edges parallel to the axes (figure 2.277). On its edges act forces parallel to the plane of the plate and spread evenly along the edge. Per unit area the force on the right edge, whose outward normal is \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), is \((90, 40, 0)\) MPa, on the top edge with outward normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) it is \((40, 30, 0)\) MPa, and on the opposite edges the opposite forces act. The faces of the plate perpendicular to the axis \(z\) are not loaded. We neglect the weight of the plate: in the steel bar 10 m long the weight gave at most \(0{,}765\) MPa (section 2.7.2), so in a plate less than a metre across it gives less than \(0{,}1\) MPa, a little over a thousandth of 90 MPa. As for the bar and for pure shear, we assume that the stress is the same at all points of the plate. The assumption is reasonable here because the forces are spread evenly along each edge and there is no weight: every rectangular piece cut out of the plate then has opposite forces on opposite faces and is in equilibrium. Where the forces along an edge are not even, the assumption does not hold, and the computed stresses are not the true ones there. Then the traction vector on the face with normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) at every point of the plate equals the force per unit area on the right edge, \(\vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}) = (90, 40, 0)\) MPa, and likewise \(\vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}) = (40, 30, 0)\) MPa. By definition 2.27, therefore, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = 90\) MPa, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 40\) MPa, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}} = 40\) MPa and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = 30\) MPa. Since the faces of the plate are not loaded, \(\vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}) = \vek 0\) on them, and since the stress is the same everywhere, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = 0\) in the whole plate. By the symmetry of stress, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}\) are zero too. Such a state, in which the components with the index \(z\) are zero, is called plane stress (ravninsko napetostno stanje). For a plate loaded only in its plane, with a thickness small compared with its length and width, it is a good approximation even when the stress is not the same everywhere, because the components with the index \(z\) cannot change much from the unloaded faces to the middle of the thickness (SADD §7.2, PDF p. 152). How large the error is we do not show here. We chose the numbers so that the computations stay transparent and the steel does not yield, as we will check in section 2.12.6.

On the left is the plate with the axes \(x\) and \(y\). On its edges act the forces per unit area, on the right and top edges along the arrows and on the opposite edges the opposite ones. At its centre is the point \(P\) with a grey square, which on the right is enlarged into the square around the point \(P\). On the face with the normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) act the normal stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and the shear stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\), and on the face with the normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) the normal stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and the shear stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\). On the opposite faces the opposite stresses act. In the square are the principal direction \(\vek e_1\) and the principal direction \(\vek e_2\), which we compute below. Neither is parallel to an edge of the plate.

We get the principal stresses of the plate from the characteristic equation (lemma 2.86). The stress matrix is

\[\ten\sigma = \begin{pmatrix} 90 & 40 & 0 \\ 40 & 30 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\ \text{MPa} .\]

In the six-term formula for the determinant (2.70) of the matrix \(\ten\sigma - \lambda\mat I\) every term contains one entry from each row. In the third row only the entry \(-\lambda\) is nonzero, so only the two terms that contain it remain (we leave out MPa):

\[\begin{aligned} \det(\ten\sigma - \lambda\mat I) &= -\lambda\,\big((90 - \lambda)(30 - \lambda) - 40 \cdot 40\big) \\ &= -\lambda\,(\lambda^2 - 120\,\lambda + 1100) = -\lambda\,(\lambda - 110)(\lambda - 10) . \end{aligned}\]

We check the last equality by multiplying out: \((\lambda - 110)(\lambda - 10) = \lambda^2 - 120\,\lambda + 1100\). The principal stresses are therefore \(\sigma_1 = 110\) MPa, \(\sigma_2 = 10\) MPa and \(\sigma_3 = 0\). We check the principal directions by multiplication:

\[\begin{aligned} \ten\sigma\,(2, 1, 0) &= (220, 110, 0) = 110\,(2, 1, 0) , \\ \ten\sigma\,(-1, 2, 0) &= (-10, 20, 0) = 10\,(-1, 2, 0) , \\ \ten\sigma\,(0, 0, 1) &= \vek 0 . \end{aligned}\]

The vectors \((2, 1, 0)\) and \((-1, 2, 0)\) have length \(\sqrt5\), so the unit vectors of the principal directions are \(\vek e_1 = (2, 1, 0)/\sqrt5\), \(\vek e_2 = (-1, 2, 0)/\sqrt5\) and \(\vek e_3 = \vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\).

Theorem 2.93 gives \(\tau_{\max} = (110 - 0)/2 = 55\) MPa on the faces with the normals

\[\frac{\vek e_1 \pm \vek e_3}{\sqrt2} = \frac{(2, 1, \pm\sqrt5)}{\sqrt{10}} .\]

We check this directly for the plus sign. By Cauchy's formula \(\vek t = \ten\sigma\,\vek n = (220, 110, 0)/\sqrt{10}\), the normal stress is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = \vek t\cdot\vek n = (440 + 110)/10 = 55\) MPa, \(|\vek t|^2 = (48\,400 + 12\,100)/10 = 6050\) MPa², and \(\tau^2 = 6050 - 55^2 = 3025\) MPa², so \(\tau = 55\) MPa. As an additional test we computed with NumPy the shear stress on 200 000 randomly chosen faces. The largest was \(54{,}9996\) MPa, none exceeded 55 MPa. These two faces are not perpendicular to the plate, because their normals have a \(z\) component. They cut the plate obliquely, through its thickness (figure 2.278). Someone who looked only at the faces perpendicular to the plate would not find the largest shear, as we will see in the next section.

On the left is the square around the point \(P\) from above, with the principal direction \(\vek e_1\) and the principal direction \(\vek e_2\). The face with normal \((\vek e_1 + \vek e_3)/\sqrt2\) contains the direction \(\vek e_2\), so it meets the top surface of the plate in a line along \(\vek e_2\). On the right we look along \(\vek e_2\) at a section through the thickness: \(\vek e_1\) points to the right, the axis \(z\) up. The face is tilted by \(45^\circ\) from the surfaces of the plate and cuts a piece off the plate, the rest of the plate is dashed. The left face of the piece, perpendicular to \(\vek e_1\), is pulled by the principal stress \(\sigma_1 = 110\) MPa, and the top and bottom surfaces are not loaded, because \(\sigma_3 = 0\). The stress \(\sigma_2 = 10\) MPa acts on the two faces of the piece that are parallel to the picture. Its forces point perpendicular to the picture and cancel each other, which is why \(\sigma_2\) does not appear in \(\tau_{\max}\). The piece is in equilibrium, so the oblique face alone must balance the force on the left face. Therefore the traction vector \(\vek t\) on it points along \(\vek e_1\), and indeed \((220, 110, 0)/\sqrt{10} = (110/\sqrt2)\,\vek e_1\). Its size is \(110/\sqrt2 = 77{,}8\) MPa and not 110 MPa, because the oblique face is \(\sqrt2\) times larger than the left one and the same force is spread over a larger area. With the normal of the face \(\vek t\) makes the angle \(45^\circ\), so it splits into two parts of equal size, each \(77{,}8/\sqrt2 = 55\) MPa: the normal part and the shear part. The other face, with normal \((\vek e_1 - \vek e_3)/\sqrt2\), is the mirror image of this one across the middle plane of the plate.

A second route: all faces on which the shear has an extremum. Theorem 2.93 says where the shear is largest, but in it we guessed the two faces and then checked them. How would we find them without guessing, and does the shear stress have any other special faces? The second route, the one CM takes (PDF p. 191), answers this. We look at the shear stress as a function of the normal and search for the normals at which it does not change when the face is turned a little. The tool for this are Lagrange multipliers (Lagrangeevi množitelji), which we will prove only in chapter 8 (theorem 8.37). So here this route is not a proof but a calculation that shows the candidates. We will then confirm the candidates with theorem 2.94, which does not need multipliers.

Let us draw all faces through \(P\) at once. Each face is fixed by its unit normal. If we draw all unit normals from the same point, their tips lie on the sphere of radius \(1\), so every point of the sphere is one face. The axes are the principal directions \(\vek e_1\), \(\vek e_2\) and \(\vek e_3\). We have drawn only the eighth of the sphere on which no component of the normal is negative. That is enough, because only the squares \(n_{\mathrm{i}}^2\) appear in (2.91), so changing the sign of any component does not change the stresses. The corners of the eighth are the principal directions themselves. On the faces perpendicular to them the traction vector is parallel to the normal (definition 2.82), so \(\tau = 0\) there. The edges of the eighth are three arcs. On the arc between \(\vek e_1\) and \(\vek e_3\) we have \(n_2 = 0\), these are the normals of the faces that contain the direction \(\vek e_2\). On the arc between \(\vek e_1\) and \(\vek e_2\) we have \(n_3 = 0\), and on the arc between \(\vek e_2\) and \(\vek e_3\) \(n_1 = 0\). In the interior of the eighth, for example at the point \(\vek n\), all three components are positive.

The function whose extrema we seek is the square of the shear stress from (2.91),

\[\tau^2 = \sigma_1^2 n_1^2 + \sigma_2^2 n_2^2 + \sigma_3^2 n_3^2 - \sigma_{\mathrm{n}}^2 , \qquad \sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = \sigma_1 n_1^2 + \sigma_2 n_2^2 + \sigma_3 n_3^2 .\]

We take the square because it has no root in it, and it is largest on the same faces as \(\tau\), since a larger nonnegative number has a larger square (lemma 1.29). We may not change the components \(n_1\), \(n_2\), \(n_3\) freely: the normal must stay a unit vector, \(n_1^2 + n_2^2 + n_3^2 = 1\). Such a condition is called a constraint (vez), and an extremum of a function among the points that satisfy the constraint a constrained extremum (vezani ekstrem). The name says that the point is tied to the sphere and may not leave it.

What holds at a constrained extremum? We stand at the point \(\vek n\) on the sphere and take a small step along the sphere in the direction \(\vek d\), which is perpendicular to \(\vek n\). Let us collect the three partial derivatives of the function \(\tau^2\) into the vector \(\vek g\) with the components \(g_{\mathrm{i}} = \partial(\tau^2)/\partial n_{\mathrm{i}}\). The partial derivative \(g_{\mathrm{i}}\) says by how much \(\tau^2\) changes per unit change of the component \(n_{\mathrm{i}}\) (definition 1.26). In a step of length \(h\) in the direction \(\vek d\) the component \(n_{\mathrm{i}}\) changes by \(h\,d_{\mathrm{i}}\), so to first approximation \(\tau^2\) changes by \(h\,(g_1 d_1 + g_2 d_2 + g_3 d_3) = h\,\vek g\cdot\vek d\). In the figure \(\vek g\) is not perpendicular to \(\vek d\), the number \(\vek g\cdot\vek d\) is positive. A step in the direction \(\vek d\) therefore increases \(\tau^2\), a step in the opposite direction decreases it, and the point \(\vek n\) drawn is neither the largest nor the smallest. At an extremum this must not happen for any direction along the sphere: \(\vek g\) must be perpendicular to every \(\vek d\) that is perpendicular to \(\vek n\). Such a vector has no part along the sphere, so it points along \(\vek n\):

\[g_{\mathrm{i}} = 2\mu\,n_{\mathrm{i}} , \qquad i = 1, 2, 3 . \tag{2.94}\]

The number \(\mu\) is the Lagrange multiplier. We added the factor \(2\) so that it matches the derivative of the constraint. The argument with the words "to first approximation" is only a sketch here. Theorem 8.37 derives it exactly, with our constraint as the function \(f = 1 - n_1^2 - n_2^2 - n_3^2\) with the derivatives \(-2n_{\mathrm{i}}\), which are not all zero on the sphere. The points that satisfy (2.94) and the constraint are called stationary points. Every constrained extremum is a stationary point, but not every stationary point is an extremum, so the solutions are only candidates.

What it means that \(\vek g\) points along \(\vek n\) is shown in figure 2.280. We cut the sphere with the plane in which \(n_3 = 0\). In it lie the axes \(\vek e_1\) and \(\vek e_2\) and the arc of the sphere between them, the same as the edge of the eighth between \(\vek e_1\) and \(\vek e_2\) in figure 2.279. On this arc \(g_3 = 2\,n_3\,(\sigma_3^2 - 2\,\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\sigma_3) = 0\), so \(\vek g\) lies in the plane of the figure. We compute for the plate with \(\sigma_1 = 110\) MPa, \(\sigma_2 = 10\) MPa and \(\sigma_3 = 0\). On the left is the point \(A\) with the normal \(\vek n\), \(n_1^2 = 0{,}1\) and \(n_2^2 = 0{,}9\). There \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = 20\) MPa and \(\vek g = (4870, -569, 0)\) MPa². We split the vector into the part along the normal, \((\vek g\cdot\vek n)\,\vek n\) with \(\vek g\cdot\vek n = 1000\) MPa², and the part along the sphere, of length \(4800\) MPa². The second part is not zero, so a step along the arc in its direction, towards \(B\), increases \(\tau^2\). At \(A\) the shear is \(\tau = 30\) MPa, at \(B\) it is \(50\) MPa, and \(A\) is not a stationary point. On the right is the midpoint \(B\) of the arc with \(n_1 = n_2 = 1/\sqrt2\). There \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = 60\) MPa and \(\vek g = (-1556, -1556, 0)\) MPa² \(= -2200\,\vek n\). The vector points along the normal towards the centre, its part along the sphere is zero. So \(\vek g\cdot\vek d = 0\) for every step \(\vek d\) along the sphere, for the step along the tangent and for the step in the direction \(\vek e_3\) out of the figure. This is the condition (2.94) with \(2\mu = -2200\) MPa², so \(\mu = -1100\) MPa² \(= -\sigma_1\sigma_2\), which the system (2.96) below gives too.

We get the condition (2.94), that \(\vek g\) points along \(\vek n\), and the constraint at once if we multiply the constraint by \(\mu\) and add it to the function. The resulting function of the four variables \(n_1\), \(n_2\), \(n_3\), \(\mu\) is called the Lagrange function:

\[\mathcal F = \tau^2 + \mu\,\big(1 - n_1^2 - n_2^2 - n_3^2\big) \tag{2.95}\]
\[\mathcal F = \tau^2 + \mu\,(1 - n_{\mathrm{i}} n_{\mathrm{i}}) \tag{2.95}\]

Its derivative with respect to \(\mu\) is the bracket \(1 - n_1^2 - n_2^2 - n_3^2\), which is zero exactly when the constraint holds, and its derivatives with respect to \(n_{\mathrm{i}}\) are \(g_{\mathrm{i}} - 2\mu\,n_{\mathrm{i}}\). All four derivatives are zero exactly at the stationary points. This is how CM (4.3.20), (4.3.21) (PDF p. 191) writes the problem, where the multiplier is \(\lambda_{\mathrm{L}}\) and the constraint has the opposite sign. In the lectures the normal of the face is \(\vec m\) with the components \(m_{\mathrm{i}}\), the principal stresses are \(\sigma_{(1)}\), \(\sigma_{(2)}\), \(\sigma_{(3)}\), the shear stress is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{s}}\), and the letter \(\vec n_{(\mathrm{i})}\) there means the principal direction, which is \(\vek e_{\mathrm{i}}\) in the book.

Let us differentiate with respect to \(n_1\), term by term.

  1. The term \(\sigma_1^2 n_1^2\) has the derivative \(2\,\sigma_1^2 n_1\). The terms \(\sigma_2^2 n_2^2\) and \(\sigma_3^2 n_3^2\) do not contain the component \(n_1\), their derivative is zero.
  2. The normal stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\) has the derivative \(\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}/\partial n_1 = 2\,\sigma_1 n_1\).
  3. We differentiate the square \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}^2 = \sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\cdot\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\) by the product rule (lemma 1.82): \(\partial(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}^2)/\partial n_1 = 2\,\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\cdot 2\,\sigma_1 n_1\).
  4. The term \(\mu\,(1 - n_1^2 - n_2^2 - n_3^2)\) has the derivative \(-2\mu\,n_1\).
  5. We add up and factor out \(2 n_1\):
    \[\frac{\partial\mathcal F}{\partial n_1} = 2\,\sigma_1^2 n_1 - 4\,\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\sigma_1 n_1 - 2\mu\,n_1 = 2\,n_1\,\big(\sigma_1^2 - 2\,\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\sigma_1 - \mu\big) .\]

We get the derivatives with respect to \(n_2\) and \(n_3\) by exchanging the index. We set all three equal to zero, divide by \(2\) and add the constraint. The stationary points are the solutions of the system

\[\begin{aligned} n_1\,\big(\sigma_1^2 - 2\,\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\sigma_1 - \mu\big) &= 0 , \\ n_2\,\big(\sigma_2^2 - 2\,\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\sigma_2 - \mu\big) &= 0 , \\ n_3\,\big(\sigma_3^2 - 2\,\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\sigma_3 - \mu\big) &= 0 , \\ n_1^2 + n_2^2 + n_3^2 &= 1 . \end{aligned} \tag{2.96}\]

These are four equations for the four unknowns \(n_1\), \(n_2\), \(n_3\) and \(\mu\). They are not linear, since \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\) contains squares of the unknowns, so we do not solve them by elimination but by separating cases. Each of the first three equations is a product of two factors, and a product is zero only if one of the factors is zero: the component \(n_{\mathrm{i}}\) or the bracket.

Here an assumption enters: let the principal stresses be different, \(\sigma_1 > \sigma_2 > \sigma_3\). We need it because we will divide by the differences \(\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{j}}\). It holds in a general state, for example in our plate with \(110\), \(10\) and \(0\) MPa. It does not hold in the bar, where \(\sigma_2 = \sigma_3 = 0\), nor in a fluid at rest, where all three are equal. What changes then we say after the theorem. We separate the cases by how many components of the normal are zero, and each case is one part of the eighth of the sphere.

  1. No component is zero, the point is in the interior of the eighth. We divide each of the first three equations by its \(n_{\mathrm{i}}\), and what is left is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{i}}^2 - 2\,\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} = \mu\) for \(i = 1, 2, 3\). We subtract equation \(j\) from equation \(i\). The multiplier drops out, we factor the difference of squares, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{i}}^2 - \sigma_{\mathrm{j}}^2 = (\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{j}})(\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{j}})\), and get
    \[(\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{j}})\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{j}} - 2\,\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}) = 0 .\]
    Because \(\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} \ne \sigma_{\mathrm{j}}\), we have \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = (\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{j}})/2\). For the pairs \(1, 2\) and \(1, 3\) we would have \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = (\sigma_1 + \sigma_2)/2\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = (\sigma_1 + \sigma_3)/2\) at the same time, so \(\sigma_2 = \sigma_3\), which contradicts the assumption. There are no stationary points in the interior of the eighth.
  2. Exactly one component is zero, the point is on one of the arcs. Take \(n_1 = 0\), the arc between \(\vek e_2\) and \(\vek e_3\). The first equation is satisfied. We divide the second and the third by \(n_2\) and \(n_3\) and subtract them as in item 1: \((\sigma_2 - \sigma_3)(\sigma_2 + \sigma_3 - 2\,\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}) = 0\). On this arc \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = \sigma_2 n_2^2 + \sigma_3 n_3^2\) and by the constraint \(n_3^2 = 1 - n_2^2\), so
    \[\sigma_2 + \sigma_3 - 2\,\sigma_2 n_2^2 - 2\,\sigma_3\,(1 - n_2^2) = (\sigma_2 - \sigma_3) - 2\,(\sigma_2 - \sigma_3)\,n_2^2 = (\sigma_2 - \sigma_3)\,(1 - 2\,n_2^2) .\]
    The equation is therefore \((\sigma_2 - \sigma_3)^2\,(1 - 2\,n_2^2) = 0\). Because \(\sigma_2 \ne \sigma_3\), what is left is
    \[1 - 2\,n_2^2 = 0 , \qquad n_2 = \pm\frac{1}{\sqrt2} , \qquad n_3 = \pm\frac{1}{\sqrt2} .\]
    This is the midpoint of the arc, \(\vek n = (0, 1, 1)/\sqrt2\), and its images with changed signs. We get the multiplier from the second equation with \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = (\sigma_2 + \sigma_3)/2\): \(\mu = \sigma_2^2 - (\sigma_2 + \sigma_3)\,\sigma_2 = -\sigma_2\sigma_3\). The same calculation with the indices exchanged gives for \(n_2 = 0\) the midpoint of the arc between \(\vek e_1\) and \(\vek e_3\), \(\vek n = (1, 0, 1)/\sqrt2\), and for \(n_3 = 0\) the midpoint of the arc between \(\vek e_1\) and \(\vek e_2\), \(\vek n = (1, 1, 0)/\sqrt2\).
  3. Two components are zero, the point is a corner, \(\vek n = \pm\vek e_{\mathrm{i}}\). The two equations with the zero components are satisfied, in equation \(i\) we have \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{i}}\), and \(\mu = \sigma_{\mathrm{i}}^2 - 2\,\sigma_{\mathrm{i}}^2 = -\sigma_{\mathrm{i}}^2\) satisfies it. So the principal directions are stationary points too. At them \(\tau = 0\), which is the smallest possible value, since \(\tau\) is never negative. In the lectures only case 2 is derived, cases 1 and 3 and the reason for the assumption of different principal stresses are added here. CM states both groups of solutions without derivation, (4.3.22) and (4.3.23) (PDF p. 191).

All three components cannot be zero, because the normal is a unit vector. The system (2.96) therefore has, up to the signs of the components, six solutions: the three corners with \(\tau = 0\) and the three midpoints of the arcs. As a check we solved the system for the plate with \(\sigma_1 = 110\) MPa, \(\sigma_2 = 10\) MPa and \(\sigma_3 = 0\) with SymPy. It returned \(18\) solutions, \(6\) of the form \(\pm\vek e_{\mathrm{i}}\) and \(12\) of the form \((\pm\vek e_{\mathrm{i}} \pm \vek e_{\mathrm{j}})/\sqrt2\), and no others. The normals \(\vek n\) and \(-\vek n\) belong to the same face, so this is \(3 + 6 = 9\) faces. How large the shear stress is on the six faces of the second group, and whether there really is an extremum there, is told by the next theorem, which we prove without multipliers.

Theorem 2.94 Principal shear stresses (glavne strižne napetosti)

Let \(P\), \(\sigma_1 \ge \sigma_2 \ge \sigma_3\) and \(\vek e_1\), \(\vek e_2\), \(\vek e_3\) be as in theorem 2.93. Let \(i < j\) be two of the indices \(1, 2, 3\) and \(k\) the third index. The number

\[\tau_{\mathrm{ij}} = \frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{j}}}{2} \tag{2.97}\]

is called the principal shear stress (glavna strižna napetost) of the pair \(i, j\). Then:

  1. On the faces with the unit normals \((\vek e_{\mathrm{i}} + \vek e_{\mathrm{j}})/\sqrt2\) and \((\vek e_{\mathrm{i}} - \vek e_{\mathrm{j}})/\sqrt2\) the shear stress is \(\tau_{\mathrm{ij}}\) and the normal stress is \((\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{j}})/2\). The normals are perpendicular to each other and both to \(\vek e_{\mathrm{k}}\).
  2. On no face through \(P\) whose normal is perpendicular to \(\vek e_{\mathrm{k}}\) is the shear stress larger than \(\tau_{\mathrm{ij}}\). If \(\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} \ne \sigma_{\mathrm{j}}\), it equals \(\tau_{\mathrm{ij}}\) only on the faces of item 1.
  3. We have \(\tau_{13} = \tau_{12} + \tau_{23}\). The largest of the three principal shear stresses is therefore \(\tau_{13} = \tau_{\max}\) from (2.93).
Proof

We compute with the weights \(w_1 = n_1^2\), \(w_2 = n_2^2\), \(w_3 = n_3^2\) as in the proof of theorem 2.93. Items 1 and 2 speak of the normals on one arc of the eighth of the sphere, where \(w_{\mathrm{k}} = 0\), item 1 of its midpoint. We must show the values at the midpoint, the bound on the whole arc and the sum.

  1. The normal \((\vek e_{\mathrm{i}} + \vek e_{\mathrm{j}})/\sqrt2\) has in the principal axes the components \(n_{\mathrm{i}} = n_{\mathrm{j}} = 1/\sqrt2\) and \(n_{\mathrm{k}} = 0\). It is a unit vector, since \(\tfrac12 + \tfrac12 + 0 = 1\), and its weights are \(w_{\mathrm{i}} = w_{\mathrm{j}} = \tfrac12\) and \(w_{\mathrm{k}} = 0\). The normal \((\vek e_{\mathrm{i}} - \vek e_{\mathrm{j}})/\sqrt2\) has \(n_{\mathrm{j}} = -1/\sqrt2\) and the same weights.
  2. By (2.91), on both faces \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = \tfrac12\,\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} + \tfrac12\,\sigma_{\mathrm{j}} = (\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{j}})/2\).
  3. From this value \(\sigma_{\mathrm{i}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{j}}\) are \((\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{j}})/2\) away, so by (2.92)
    \[\tau^2 = \tfrac12\Big(\frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{j}}}{2}\Big)^2 + \tfrac12\Big(\frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{j}}}{2}\Big)^2 = \Big(\frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{j}}}{2}\Big)^2 .\]
    Because \(i < j\), we have \(\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} \ge \sigma_{\mathrm{j}}\), and because \(\tau \ge 0\), we get \(\tau = (\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{j}})/2 = \tau_{\mathrm{ij}}\).
  4. The scalar product of the normals is \(\tfrac12\,(\vek e_{\mathrm{i}} + \vek e_{\mathrm{j}})\cdot(\vek e_{\mathrm{i}} - \vek e_{\mathrm{j}}) = \tfrac12\,(1 - 0 + 0 - 1) = 0\), because the vectors \(\vek e_{\mathrm{i}}\) are unit vectors and mutually perpendicular. So the normals are perpendicular. Their component \(n_{\mathrm{k}}\) is zero, so they are also perpendicular to \(\vek e_{\mathrm{k}}\). This proves item 1.

For normals perpendicular to \(\vek e_{\mathrm{k}}\) only two weights differ from zero, so we draw them on a line (figure 2.281). At the top is the number line with the principal stresses \(\sigma_{\mathrm{j}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{i}}\), above them the weight \(w\) at \(\sigma_{\mathrm{i}}\) and the weight \(1 - w\) at \(\sigma_{\mathrm{j}}\). The balance point \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\) lies between them, and the stresses are away from it by \((1 - w)(\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{j}})\) and \(w\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{j}})\). In the middle, on the axis \(w\), is the graph of the product \(w\,(1 - w)\), which is largest at \(w = \tfrac12\) with the value \(\tfrac14\) and so does not exceed the horizontal bound \(\tfrac14\). At the bottom, on the number line \(\sigma\), \(\tau_{12}\) is half the distance between \(\sigma_1\) and \(\sigma_2\), \(\tau_{23}\) half the distance between \(\sigma_2\) and \(\sigma_3\), and together they are \(\tau_{13}\), half the whole distance.

  1. Now let \(\vek n\) be any unit normal perpendicular to \(\vek e_{\mathrm{k}}\), that is any point of the arc. Then \(n_{\mathrm{k}} = 0\) and \(w_{\mathrm{k}} = 0\). Write \(w = w_{\mathrm{i}}\). Because the sum of the weights is \(1\), we have \(w_{\mathrm{j}} = 1 - w\), and \(0 \le w \le 1\).
  2. The normal stress is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = w\,\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} + (1 - w)\,\sigma_{\mathrm{j}}\). The principal stresses are away from it by
    \[\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = (1 - w)\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{j}}) , \qquad \sigma_{\mathrm{j}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = -w\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{j}}) .\]
  3. We insert the distances into (2.92) and factor out the common factors:
    \[\tau^2 = w\,(1 - w)^2\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{j}})^2 + (1 - w)\,w^2\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{j}})^2 = w\,(1 - w)\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{j}})^2\,\big((1 - w) + w\big) = w\,(1 - w)\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{j}})^2 .\]
  4. We complete the product \(w\,(1 - w)\) to a square: \(w\,(1 - w) = \tfrac14 - \big(w - \tfrac12\big)^2\). A square is not negative, so \(w\,(1 - w) \le \tfrac14\), with equality only at \(w = \tfrac12\), at the midpoint of the arc. At the corners of the arc, where \(w = 0\) or \(w = 1\), the product is zero.
  5. From steps 7 and 8, \(\tau^2 \le \tfrac14\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{j}})^2 = \tau_{\mathrm{ij}}^2\). The numbers \(\tau\) and \(\tau_{\mathrm{ij}}\) are nonnegative, so by lemma 1.29 on the larger square \(\tau \le \tau_{\mathrm{ij}}\) follows.
  6. If \(\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} \ne \sigma_{\mathrm{j}}\), equality in step 9 holds only at \(w = \tfrac12\), that is at \(n_{\mathrm{i}}^2 = n_{\mathrm{j}}^2 = \tfrac12\). These are the normals \((\pm\vek e_{\mathrm{i}} \pm \vek e_{\mathrm{j}})/\sqrt2\), which fix the two faces of item 1, since \(\vek n\) and \(-\vek n\) belong to the same face. This proves item 2.
  7. The sum is \(\tau_{12} + \tau_{23} = \tfrac12\,(\sigma_1 - \sigma_2) + \tfrac12\,(\sigma_2 - \sigma_3) = \tfrac12\,(\sigma_1 - \sigma_3) = \tau_{13}\). The two terms are not negative, so \(\tau_{13} \ge \tau_{12}\) and \(\tau_{13} \ge \tau_{23}\), and by (2.93) \(\tau_{13} = \tau_{\max}\).

Source: CM (4.3.23), (4.3.24) and (4.3.25) (PDF pp. 191-192) states the normals and the values without derivation and calls them the maximum shear stresses on these planes. The phrase principal shear stress is used by BOWER §6.1.1.1 (PDF p. 409) without a definition. The proof is not from the sources.

The theorem confirms the candidates of the second route. On each arc the midpoint is the most the shear reaches on that arc (item 2), and at the corners the shear is smallest. Of the three midpoints only the blue one is the largest on the whole sphere, by theorem 2.93. The orange and the blackwhite midpoint are largest only along their own arc. When we move from them into the interior of the eighth, the shear grows, so on the whole sphere they are neither largest nor smallest. This is the reason why the solutions of the system (2.96) are only candidates.

Figure 2.282 shows this for the blackwhite midpoint in the plate. On the left is the eighth of the sphere with the principal directions. On the arc between \(\vek e_2\) and \(\vek e_3\) lies its midpoint, the normal \((\vek e_2 + \vek e_3)/\sqrt2\) with the shear \(\tau_{23} = 5\) MPa. From the midpoint we go along two paths. The first stays on the arc and goes towards \(\vek e_3\). The second, the blue path, goes through the interior of the eighth to \(\vek e_1\), along the normals \(\vek n = (\sin\psi, \cos\psi/\sqrt2, \cos\psi/\sqrt2)\) for the angle \(\psi\) from \(0\) to \(90^\circ\). On it the weights are \(w_1 = \sin^2\psi\) and \(w_2 = w_3 = \tfrac12\cos^2\psi\), and (2.92) gives \(\tau^2 = 25 + 11\,000\,\sin^2\psi - 11\,025\,\sin^4\psi\) MPa². On the right is the shear along both paths, with the angle travelled on the sphere from the midpoint on the horizontal axis. Along the arc the shear falls from \(5\) MPa to zero at \(\vek e_3\), as item 2 of the theorem says. Along the blue path, however, the shear grows to \(52{,}6\) MPa at \(\psi = 44{,}9^\circ\) and falls to zero only at \(\vek e_1\). The midpoint of the arc is therefore a top in one direction and a bottom in the other, like the middle of a horse's saddle. At the orange midpoint the picture is the same, only the rise into the interior is small, from \(50\) to \(50{,}8\) MPa.

How do these six faces lie in the body? Let us cut a cube out of the neighbourhood of the point \(P\), with faces perpendicular to the principal directions, and draw it three times. In the first cube are the faces of the pair \(1, 3\). Each passes through two opposite edges of the cube that are parallel to \(\vek e_2\), and the faces meet in the line through the centre along \(\vek e_2\). Their normals \((\vek e_1 + \vek e_3)/\sqrt2\) and \((\vek e_1 - \vek e_3)/\sqrt2\) are perpendicular, a right angle is drawn between them (item 1 of the theorem). On these two faces the shear is \(\tau_{13} = \tau_{\max}\), they are the faces of figure 2.274, which we look at there along \(\vek e_2\). In the second cube are the faces of the pair \(1, 2\) with the normals \((\vek e_1 \pm \vek e_2)/\sqrt2\), which contain the direction \(\vek e_3\), in the third the faces of the pair \(2, 3\) with the normals \((\vek e_2 \pm \vek e_3)/\sqrt2\), which contain the direction \(\vek e_1\).

At what angle do these faces lie? The angle between two faces is the angle between their normals, and a face perpendicular to \(\vek e_{\mathrm{i}}\) has the normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{i}}\). The component of a unit vector along the unit vector \(\vek e_{\mathrm{i}}\) is the cosine of the angle between them (section 2.3). The normal \(\vek n = (\vek e_{\mathrm{i}} + \vek e_{\mathrm{j}})/\sqrt2\) has

\[\vek n\cdot\vek e_{\mathrm{i}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt2} , \qquad \vek n\cdot\vek e_{\mathrm{j}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt2} , \qquad \vek n\cdot\vek e_{\mathrm{k}} = 0 ,\]

and because \(\cos 45^\circ = 1/\sqrt2\) and \(\cos 90^\circ = 0\), it makes the angle \(45^\circ\) with \(\vek e_{\mathrm{i}}\) and \(\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\) and \(90^\circ\) with \(\vek e_{\mathrm{k}}\). Every face of a principal shear stress is therefore tilted by \(45^\circ\) from two faces of the cube and perpendicular to the third pair of faces of the cube. This holds for every state of stress, not only for the bar, where we have already met \(45^\circ\). On these faces the normal stress is in general not zero but \((\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{j}})/2\).

And the angle between faces of two different pairs? Take the normal \((\vek e_1 + \vek e_3)/\sqrt2\) of the pair \(1, 3\) and the normal \((\vek e_2 + \vek e_3)/\sqrt2\) of the pair \(2, 3\) and draw them from the same point. Both have length \(1\). From the tip of one to the tip of the other leads the vector \((\vek e_1 - \vek e_2)/\sqrt2\), which also has length \(1\). The triangle has three equal sides, so the angle between the normals is \(60^\circ\). The scalar product says the same:

\[\frac{\vek e_1 + \vek e_3}{\sqrt2}\cdot\frac{\vek e_2 + \vek e_3}{\sqrt2} = \frac{0 + 0 + 0 + 1}{2} = \frac12 = \cos 60^\circ .\]

Pairs with different third indices always have exactly one index in common, so the scalar product of their normals is always \(\tfrac12\) or \(-\tfrac12\), the angle between the normals \(60^\circ\) or \(120^\circ\), and the angle between the faces \(60^\circ\).

Let us try the theorem on the plate with \(\sigma_1 = 110\) MPa, \(\sigma_2 = 10\) MPa and \(\sigma_3 = 0\). The principal shear stresses are

\[\tau_{13} = \frac{110 - 0}{2} = 55\ \text{MPa} , \qquad \tau_{12} = \frac{110 - 10}{2} = 50\ \text{MPa} , \qquad \tau_{23} = \frac{10 - 0}{2} = 5\ \text{MPa} ,\]

and indeed \(50 + 5 = 55\). We checked the value \(55\) MPa directly above. For the pair \(1, 2\) the normal is \((\vek e_1 + \vek e_2)/\sqrt2 = (1, 3, 0)/\sqrt{10}\) and by Cauchy's formula \(\vek t = \ten\sigma\,\vek n = (210, 130, 0)/\sqrt{10}\) MPa, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = (210 + 390)/10 = 60\) MPa, \(|\vek t|^2 = (44\,100 + 16\,900)/10 = 6100\) MPa², so \(\tau^2 = 6100 - 60^2 = 2500\) MPa² and \(\tau = 50\) MPa. For the pair \(2, 3\) the normal is \((\vek e_2 + \vek e_3)/\sqrt2 = (-1, 2, \sqrt5)/\sqrt{10}\), \(\vek t = (-10, 20, 0)/\sqrt{10}\) MPa, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = (10 + 40)/10 = 5\) MPa, \(|\vek t|^2 = 500/10 = 50\) MPa², so \(\tau^2 = 50 - 5^2 = 25\) MPa² and \(\tau = 5\) MPa. The normal stresses \(60\) and \(5\) MPa are the midpoints \((110 + 10)/2\) and \((10 + 0)/2\), as item 1 says. The normal of the pair \(1, 2\) has no component \(z\): these faces are perpendicular to the plate. By item 2, \(50\) MPa is the most that someone who looks only at faces perpendicular to the plate can find, and the true largest shear of \(55\) MPa escapes him. In the next section we will meet the same three values as the radii of the three Mohr circles: \(55\) MPa, \(50\) MPa and \(5\) MPa.

What remains is the assumption of different principal stresses. Theorem 2.94 does not need it, only the second route needed it, when in cases 1 and 2 we divided by differences of principal stresses. What happens without it is shown in figure 2.284 for the bar in tension, where \(\sigma_1 = \sigma\) and \(\sigma_2 = \sigma_3 = 0\). On the eighth of the sphere two cases change. In case 2 the equation \((\sigma_2 - \sigma_3)^2\,(1 - 2\,n_2^2) = 0\) is satisfied for every \(n_2\). Then every point of the arc between \(\vek e_2\) and \(\vek e_3\) is stationary, and by step 7 of the proof \(\tau = 0\) on the whole arc, as at the corner \(\vek e_1\). In case 1 subtracting the third equation from the second gives \(0 = 0\), so there is no contradiction any more. The pairs \(1, 2\) and \(1, 3\) give the same requirement \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = (\sigma_1 + \sigma_2)/2 = (\sigma_1 + \sigma_3)/2 = \sigma/2\). In the bar \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = \sigma\,n_1^2\), so this is \(n_1^2 = \tfrac12\). All points of the quarter circle with \(n_1 = 1/\sqrt2\) between the midpoint of the arc between \(\vek e_1\) and \(\vek e_2\) and the midpoint of the arc between \(\vek e_1\) and \(\vek e_3\) are therefore stationary, and on the whole quarter circle \(\tau = \sigma/2\). The principal shear stress of the pair \(2, 3\) is zero too, \(\tau_{23} = 0\), and the other two are equal, \(\tau_{12} = \tau_{13} = \sigma/2\). The faces of the pairs \(1, 2\) and \(1, 3\) are then only four of infinitely many faces with the same shear, whose normals lie on a cone around the axis of the bar. If all three principal stresses are equal, as in a fluid at rest, all three principal shear stresses are zero and every point of the sphere is stationary. So whoever used the list of six solutions of the second route without checking the assumption would find for the bar only four faces with the largest shear instead of the whole cone.

2.12.3 Mohr's circle

The theorem says how large the largest shear is, but not how the normal and the shear stress change as we turn the face. For the bar we showed this with the graph in figure 2.46, with one curve for each stress. A nicer picture results if we draw each face as one point in a plane, with the normal stress on the horizontal axis and the shear stress on the vertical one. For faces that turn about one principal direction, these points lie on a circle.

From history

The stress at a point was shown in the mathematical theory of elasticity by a quadric surface drawn by Cauchy (section 2.11, which TIMO on PDF p. 224 calls the ellipsoid of stress), and in plane problems by an ellipse (TIMO, PDF p. 117 and 224). Culmann showed in his book Graphische Statik in 1866 that the stress in a plane system can be represented by a circle, which simplifies the problem greatly (TIMO, PDF p. 224). The normal and the shear stress on each face are the coordinates of one point on a circle whose diameter is the difference of the two principal stresses (TIMO, PDF p. 224 and 225). Mohr did the same for three principal stresses and got three circles. The largest has as its diameter the difference of the largest and the smallest principal stress and belongs to the faces that contain the direction of the middle principal stress. The points of all other faces lie in the region between the circles (TIMO, PDF p. 225). We shall see the proof in lemma 2.97. For a given normal stress the shear is largest exactly on the faces that contain the direction of the middle principal stress (TIMO, PDF p. 225).

With this circle Mohr solved another problem too, strength. Most engineers of the time followed Saint-Venant and took the largest strain as the measure of failure. They determined the dimensions of parts so that the largest strain at the most endangered place under the most unfavourable loading does not exceed the permissible extension in simple tension (TIMO, PDF p. 226). Coulomb had already assumed that failure is triggered by shear (section 1.1, TIMO, PDF p. 226). In Munich, where the first laboratory for testing materials run by an engineering school was founded in 1871, Johann Bauschinger determined with a sensitive gauge the stresses up to which steel returns to its original shape after unloading, in tension, compression and shear (TIMO, PDF p. 218, 219 and 226). These results did not agree with the measure of the largest strain (TIMO, PDF p. 226). In a paper of 1882 Mohr treated Bauschinger's experiments (TIMO, PDF p. 226). The measure with circles, which can be adapted to different states of stress and better matched to experiments, he designed in a paper of 1900 (TIMO, PDF p. 225 and 226). He assumed that among the faces with the same normal stress the one with the largest shear fails first, that is the one on the largest circle, so only the largest circle matters (TIMO, PDF p. 226). He suggested drawing such a circle for every test in which the material fails, and drawing through the circles an envelope, a line that touches all the circles. For a loading that was not tested, failure occurs when the largest circle touches the envelope (TIMO, PDF p. 226). For cast iron, that is iron poured into a mould (figure 2.285), he took as the envelope the two outer tangents of the circles of the tensile and the compressive test. The circle with its centre at the origin that touches the envelope gave the strength in shear, which agreed satisfactorily with experiments (TIMO, PDF p. 226 and 227).

The figure shows the axes \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\) and \(\tau\) with the origin \(O\). Circle I belongs to the tensile test and reaches to the stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{t}}\). Circle II belongs to the compressive test and reaches to \(-\sigma_{\mathrm{c}}\). The envelope is the common tangent of the two circles on each side of the horizontal axis. Circle III with its centre at \(O\) touches the envelope, and the radius to the point of contact is the strength in shear.

For the picture in which each face is one point, we need a sign for the shear stress. The shear stress \(\tau\) is the length of the shear part of the traction vector and so never negative, while the direction of the shear part says in which direction along the face it acts. We consider faces with normal \(\vek n = (n_{\mathrm{x}}, n_{\mathrm{y}}, 0)\), where \(n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 = 1\). These faces contain the direction of the axis \(z\), like the cuts of the bar in section 2.4. In each such face we choose the direction

\[\vek d = (-n_{\mathrm{y}},\ n_{\mathrm{x}},\ 0) ,\]

which is perpendicular to \(\vek n\) and to \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\), like the vector \(\vek d\) in section 2.4, where \(\vek n = (\cos\theta, \sin\theta, 0)\) and \(\vek d = (-\sin\theta, \cos\theta, 0)\). We define the shear component (strižna komponenta) along \(\vek d\) as the projection of the traction vector onto \(\vek d\),

\[\tau_{\mathrm{nd}} = \vek t(\vek n)\cdot\vek d .\]

We will need the condition \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} = 0\). Then by the symmetry of stress also \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zy}} = 0\), the traction vector on the face with normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) is \(\vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}) = (0, 0, \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}})\) and points along the normal, so \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) is a principal direction. The faces that contain the direction of the axis \(z\) therefore turn about a principal direction. The condition holds in the plane stress of a thin plate and in a bar pulled by an axial force, and more generally whenever we lay the axis \(z\) along one of the principal directions.

What the condition gives is shown by a case in which it fails (figure 2.286). On the left we look at the face with normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) from the front, with the axis \(y\) to the right and the axis \(z\) upwards, and the normal points towards us. If the plate with \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = 90\) MPa and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 40\) MPa also had \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = 30\) MPa, the traction vector on this face would be \((90, 40, 30)\) MPa. Its normal part \(90\) MPa points towards us. The shear part \((0, 40, 30)\) MPa lies in the face and has the length \(\sqrt{40^2 + 30^2} = 50\) MPa, while the shear component \(\tau_{\mathrm{nd}}\) along \(\vek d = \vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) would be only \(40\) MPa. The component \(\tau_{\mathrm{nd}}\) then does not capture all of the shear, \(30\) MPa along the axis \(z\) escape it. So a face on which \(\tau_{\mathrm{nd}} = 0\) is in general no longer principal, since it keeps a shear part along the axis \(z\). On the right is the same face at \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = 0\). Its shear part lies wholly along \(\vek d\), so its length is \(\tau = |\tau_{\mathrm{nd}}| = 40\) MPa.

The next lemma says that under this condition the shear part of the traction vector is \(\tau_{\mathrm{nd}}\,\vek d\), so \(\tau = |\tau_{\mathrm{nd}}|\), and the sign tells whether the shear part points along \(\vek d\) or opposite to it. Figure 2.287 shows this on the thin plate of figure 2.277, with the stresses \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = 90\) MPa, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = 30\) MPa and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 40\) MPa.

On the left is the face through the point \(P\), seen along the axis \(z\), with the material behind it grey. We turned the normal from the direction \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) by the angle \(\theta = 60^\circ\) into \(\vek n\), and the direction \(\vek d\) lies in the face, perpendicular to \(\vek n\). We split the traction vector \(\vek t(\vek n)\) into the normal part \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\vek n\) with \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = 79{,}64\) MPa and the shear part \(\tau_{\mathrm{nd}}\,\vek d\) with \(\tau_{\mathrm{nd}} = -45{,}98\) MPa. The shear part points opposite to \(\vek d\), so \(\tau_{\mathrm{nd}}\) is negative. On the right are the axes \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\) and \(\tau_{\mathrm{nd}}\), in which this face is one point \((\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}, \tau_{\mathrm{nd}})\), with the horizontal coordinate \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\) and the vertical coordinate \(\tau_{\mathrm{nd}}\). The lemma below says that this point lies on the circle with centre \(m\) and radius \(R\), here \(m = 60\) MPa and \(R = 50\) MPa. On the same circle is the point of the face with normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), whose radius makes the angle \(\varphi\) with the horizontal axis. The arc \(2\theta\) between the radii of the two points is explained after the lemma.

Lemma 2.95 Mohr's circle (Mohrov krog)

Let the stress components at a point \(P\) be symmetric and let \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} = 0\). For a face through \(P\) with unit normal \(\vek n = (n_{\mathrm{x}}, n_{\mathrm{y}}, 0)\) let \(\vek d\)\( = (-n_{\mathrm{y}}, n_{\mathrm{x}}, 0)\), let \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\) be the normal stress on it and \(\tau_{\mathrm{nd}} = \vek t(\vek n)\cdot\vek d\). Then:

  1. The shear part of the traction vector is \(\vek t(\vek n) - \sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\vek n = \tau_{\mathrm{nd}}\,\vek d\).
  2. The point \((\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}, \tau_{\mathrm{nd}})\) lies on the circle with centre \((m, 0)\) and radius \(R\):
    \[\begin{aligned} (\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - m)^2 + \tau_{\mathrm{nd}}^2 &= R^2 , \\ m &= \frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}}{2} , \\ R &= \sqrt{\Big(\frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}}{2}\Big)^2 + \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}^2} . \end{aligned} \tag{2.98}\]
  3. For every point \((\sigma, \tau)\) of this circle there is a normal \(\vek n = (n_{\mathrm{x}}, n_{\mathrm{y}}, 0)\) with \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = \sigma\) and \(\tau_{\mathrm{nd}} = \tau\).
Proof

We derive all three items from Cauchy's formula and from \(n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 = 1\).

1. The shear part.

  1. By (2.27) with \(n_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} = 0\), the traction vector is
    \[\vek t(\vek n) = (\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} n_{\mathrm{x}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} n_{\mathrm{y}},\ \ \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} n_{\mathrm{x}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} n_{\mathrm{y}},\ \ 0) .\]
  2. The vector \(\vek d\) is a unit vector, because \(n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 = 1\), and perpendicular to \(\vek n\), because \(\vek d\cdot\vek n = -n_{\mathrm{y}} n_{\mathrm{x}} + n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{y}} = 0\).
  3. By item 1 of lemma 2.14 on splitting a vector, the shear part \(\vek v = \vek t(\vek n) - \sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\vek n\), the traction vector without its normal part, is perpendicular to \(\vek n\), so \(v_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{x}} + v_{\mathrm{y}} n_{\mathrm{y}} = 0\). Its \(z\) component is zero, because it is zero for \(\vek t(\vek n)\) and for \(\vek n\).
  4. We compute the vector \((\vek v\cdot\vek d)\,\vek d = (-v_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{y}} + v_{\mathrm{y}} n_{\mathrm{x}})\,(-n_{\mathrm{y}}, n_{\mathrm{x}}, 0)\). Its \(x\) component is \(v_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 - v_{\mathrm{y}} n_{\mathrm{y}} n_{\mathrm{x}}\). By step 3, \(v_{\mathrm{y}} n_{\mathrm{y}} = -v_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{x}}\), so this is \(v_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + v_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 = v_{\mathrm{x}}\). Likewise the \(y\) component is \(-v_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{y}} + v_{\mathrm{y}} n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 = v_{\mathrm{y}} n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + v_{\mathrm{y}} n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 = v_{\mathrm{y}}\). The \(z\) component is zero. Hence the shear part is parallel to \(\vek d\), \(\vek v = (\vek v\cdot\vek d)\,\vek d\).
  5. By the rules of the scalar product, \(\vek v\cdot\vek d = \vek t(\vek n)\cdot\vek d - \sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\,(\vek n\cdot\vek d) = \tau_{\mathrm{nd}} - 0\). The shear part is therefore \(\tau_{\mathrm{nd}}\,\vek d\).

2. The circle.

  1. From step 1 and (2.6) we compute the coordinates of the point
    \[\begin{aligned} \sigma_{\mathrm{n}} &= \vek t(\vek n)\cdot\vek n = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + 2\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{y}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 , \\ \tau_{\mathrm{nd}} &= \vek t(\vek n)\cdot\vek d = -\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{y}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,(n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 - n_{\mathrm{y}}^2) + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{y}} . \end{aligned}\]
    These are the formulas for \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) of (2.60) with \(c = n_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(s = n_{\mathrm{y}}\), since \(\vek n\) is the unit vector of the new axis \(\bar x\) and \(\vek d\) the unit vector of the new axis \(\bar y\).
  2. We introduce the auxiliary numbers \(C = n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 - n_{\mathrm{y}}^2\) and \(S = 2\,n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{y}}\). From \(n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 = 1\) it follows that \(n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 = (1 + C)/2\) and \(n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 = (1 - C)/2\), which we check by adding and subtracting the two equalities.
  3. We insert these into step 6 and write \(a = (\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}})/2\) and \(b = \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\), which are the horizontal and the vertical distance of the point \((\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}})\) from the centre \((m, 0)\):
    \[\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\frac{1 + C}{2} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\,\frac{1 - C}{2} + \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,S = m + a\,C + b\,S , \qquad \tau_{\mathrm{nd}} = -(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}})\,n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{y}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,C = b\,C - a\,S .\]
  4. We have \(C^2 + S^2 = (n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 - n_{\mathrm{y}}^2)^2 + 4n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 = n_{\mathrm{x}}^4 + 2n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + n_{\mathrm{y}}^4 = (n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + n_{\mathrm{y}}^2)^2 = 1\).
  5. When we write out the squares, the terms \(2abCS\) and \(-2abCS\) cancel:
    \[(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - m)^2 + \tau_{\mathrm{nd}}^2 = (aC + bS)^2 + (bC - aS)^2 = (a^2 + b^2)(C^2 + S^2) = a^2 + b^2 = R^2 .\]
    The point \((\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}, \tau_{\mathrm{nd}})\) is therefore at the distance of the radius \(R\) from the centre \((m, 0)\), for every normal \(\vek n\), so it lies on the circle.

3. Every point of the circle belongs to some face.

  1. If \(R = 0\), the circle is the single point \((m, 0)\), and by step 10 every normal gives it. Let \(R > 0\) and let the point \((\sigma, \tau)\) lie on the circle, \((\sigma - m)^2 + \tau^2 = R^2\). We set \(C = \big(a(\sigma - m) + b\tau\big)/R^2\) and \(S = \big(b(\sigma - m) - a\tau\big)/R^2\). Substituting, we check \(aC + bS = (a^2 + b^2)(\sigma - m)/R^2 = \sigma - m\) and \(bC - aS = (a^2 + b^2)\,\tau/R^2 = \tau\), and as in step 10, \(C^2 + S^2 = (a^2 + b^2)\big((\sigma - m)^2 + \tau^2\big)/R^4 = 1\).
  2. Hence \(-1 \le C \le 1\). We look for the normal \(\vek n\). We set \(n_{\mathrm{x}} = \sqrt{(1 + C)/2}\), and \(n_{\mathrm{y}} = \sqrt{(1 - C)/2}\) if \(S \ge 0\) and \(n_{\mathrm{y}} = -\sqrt{(1 - C)/2}\) if \(S < 0\). Then \(n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 = 1\), \(n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 - n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 = C\) and \(2n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{y}} = \pm\sqrt{1 - C^2} = \pm\sqrt{S^2} = S\), where the sign is that of \(S\).
  3. For this normal, by step 8, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = m + aC + bS = \sigma\) and \(\tau_{\mathrm{nd}} = bC - aS = \tau\). The chosen point of the circle is therefore the point of the face with this normal.

Source: The formulas of step 8 are SADD (3.3.4), (3.3.5) (PDF p. 68) and BARBER (1.15), (1.16) (PDF p. 27), who calls them the equations of Mohr's circle. SADD derives Mohr's circles in space and names them after Otto Mohr (SADD (3.4.10), figure 3.7, PDF p. 71). The lemma in this form and the proof are not from the sources.

The lemma says that the points of all faces that contain the direction of the axis \(z\) lie on one circle, Mohr's circle (Mohrov krog).
