Its centre is on the horizontal axis, at the average of the normal stresses \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\), and its radius depends on the difference of these stresses and on \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\). The face with normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) has \(\vek d = \vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\), its point is \((\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}})\). The face with normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) has \(\vek d = -\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), its point is \((\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}, -\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}})\). The midpoint of the segment between these two points is \((m, 0)\), the centre of the circle, so the two points are at the opposite ends of a diameter. Faces that are perpendicular in the body are opposite on the circle. From the circle we read off two things. The normal stress is largest and smallest at the points where the circle meets the horizontal axis, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = m \pm R\). There \(\tau_{\mathrm{nd}} = 0\), so these faces are principal and \(m \pm R\) are principal stresses. The shear stress is largest at the top and at the bottom of the circle, where \(|\tau_{\mathrm{nd}}| = R\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = m\).

Why are perpendicular faces opposite on the circle and not a quarter of the circle apart? Let us write the normal as in section 2.4, \(\vek n = (\cos\theta, \sin\theta, 0)\). Then the auxiliary numbers of the proof are

\[C = \cos^2\theta - \sin^2\theta = \cos 2\theta , \qquad S = 2\sin\theta\cos\theta = \sin 2\theta ,\]

by the double angle formulas for cosine and sine from school trigonometry (KREYSZIG Appendix A3.1, (7), PDF p. 1204). We also write the numbers \(a\) and \(b\) with an angle, \(a = R\cos\varphi\) and \(b = R\sin\varphi\), where \(\varphi\) is the angle between the horizontal axis and the radius to the point \((\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}) = (m + a, b)\). We may do this because \(a^2 + b^2 = R^2\). By step 8 of the proof and by the formulas for the cosine and sine of a difference of angles (KREYSZIG Appendix A3.1, (6), PDF p. 1204),

\[\begin{aligned} \sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - m &= R\,(\cos\varphi\cos 2\theta + \sin\varphi\sin 2\theta) = R\cos(\varphi - 2\theta) , \\ \tau_{\mathrm{nd}} &= R\,(\sin\varphi\cos 2\theta - \cos\varphi\sin 2\theta) = R\sin(\varphi - 2\theta) . \end{aligned}\]

When the normal turns by the angle \(\theta\) from the axis \(x\) toward the axis \(y\), the point on the circle turns by twice the angle, \(2\theta\), in the opposite sense. In figure 2.287, \(\theta = 60^\circ\) and the point has travelled \(120^\circ\) along the circle, from the angle \(\varphi = 53{,}13^\circ\) above the horizontal axis to the angle \(53{,}13^\circ - 120^\circ = -66{,}87^\circ\) below it. A face turned by a quarter turn is half the circle away, and a face turned by half a turn is the same face again, with normal \(-\vek n\), and the same point on the circle.

Let us test the circle on the bar pulled by an axial force. There \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma\) and all other components are zero. The condition of the lemma, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} = 0\), holds, and \(m = \sigma/2\), \(R = \sqrt{(\sigma/2)^2 + 0} = \sigma/2\). The circle passes through the points \((0, 0)\) and \((\sigma, 0)\) (figure 2.288). By step 6 of the proof \(\tau_{\mathrm{nd}} = -\sigma\cos\theta\sin\theta\), which is the shear part \(-\sigma\sin\theta\cos\theta\,\vek d\) of step 4 in section 2.4. For the angle \(30^\circ\) the point is \((0{,}75\,\sigma,\ -0{,}433\,\sigma)\): the normal and the shear stress from the table in section 2.4, the shear one with a negative sign, because the shear part points opposite to \(\vek d\). Exactly, \(\tau_{\mathrm{nd}} = -\sigma\sin 30^\circ\cos 30^\circ = -\tfrac{\sqrt3}{4}\,\sigma\), and the point does lie on the circle: \((0{,}75 - 0{,}5)^2 + \tfrac{3}{16} = 0{,}0625 + 0{,}1875 = 0{,}25 = 0{,}5^2\). All five rows of the table are five points on the lower half of the circle. The faces with tilts between \(90^\circ\) and \(180^\circ\), which are the same as the faces with tilts between \(-90^\circ\) and \(0^\circ\), give the upper half.

The figure shows the axes \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\) and \(\tau_{\mathrm{nd}}\). The circle has its centre at \(\sigma/2\) and radius \(\sigma/2\), and passes through the point \(\sigma\) on the horizontal axis and through the origin. The marks \(\pm\sigma/2\) on the vertical axis show that the largest shear stress is \(\sigma/2\). The points on the circle are the faces with the inclination \(0^\circ\), \(30^\circ\), \(45^\circ\), \(60^\circ\) and \(90^\circ\). The grey radius leads to the point \(30^\circ\), and the arc at the centre shows that the angle between the radius and the horizontal axis is twice the inclination, \(60^\circ = 2\theta\).

Now the thin plate of figure 2.277, with the stresses \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = 90\) MPa, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = 30\) MPa and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 40\) MPa, for the faces perpendicular to the plate. The condition of the lemma holds, because in plane stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}\) are zero. The centre of the circle is \(m = (90 + 30)/2 = 60\) MPa, the radius \(R = \sqrt{30^2 + 40^2} = 50\) MPa (figure 2.289). The face with normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) is the point \((90, 40)\), the face with normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) the point \((30, -40)\). The circle meets the horizontal axis at \(60 + 50 = 110\) MPa and at \(60 - 50 = 10\) MPa, which are the principal stresses \(\sigma_1\) and \(\sigma_2\) that we found above from the characteristic equation. Here \(a = 30 = 50 \cdot 0{,}6\) and \(b = 40 = 50 \cdot 0{,}8\), so \(\cos\varphi = 0{,}6\) and \(\sin\varphi = 0{,}8\). The principal face with \(\sigma_1\) is where \(\varphi - 2\theta = 0\), so \(\cos 2\theta = 0{,}6\) and \(\sin 2\theta = 0{,}8\). From \(C = n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 - n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 = 0{,}6\) and \(n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 = 1\) we get \(n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 = 0{,}8\) and \(n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 = 0{,}2\), and with the positive \(S = 2n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{y}} = 0{,}8\) the normal is \((2, 1, 0)/\sqrt5\), the same as above. The largest shear stress among the faces perpendicular to the plate is the radius, 50 MPa, on the faces with \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = 60\) MPa. These are the faces with the normals \((\vek e_1 + \vek e_2)/\sqrt2 = (1, 3, 0)/\sqrt{10}\) and \((\vek e_1 - \vek e_2)/\sqrt2 = (3, -1, 0)/\sqrt{10}\), halfway between the principal directions \(\vek e_1\) and \(\vek e_2\). We check the first: \(\vek t = \ten\sigma\,\vek n = (210, 130, 0)/\sqrt{10}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = (210 + 390)/10 = 60\) MPa, \(|\vek t|^2 = (44\,100 + 16\,900)/10 = 6100\) MPa², and \(\tau^2 = 6100 - 60^2 = 2500\) MPa², so \(\tau = 50\) MPa.

The figure shows the axes \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\) and \(\tau_{\mathrm{nd}}\). The circle has its centre at \(m = 60\) MPa and the radius \(R = 50\) MPa. The face with the normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) is the point \((\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}) = (90, 40)\) MPa, the face with the normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) the point \((\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}, -\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}) = (30, -40)\) MPa, and the diameter between them is dashed. The circle cuts the horizontal axis at the principal stresses \(\sigma_1 = 110\) MPa and \(\sigma_2 = 10\) MPa. The top and bottom points of the circle are the faces with the largest shear among the faces perpendicular to the plate. The arc \(2\theta\) at the centre leads from the point of the face with the normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) to the principal stress \(\sigma_1\).

Three small squares about the same point. The circle gave two special positions of the faces: the principal faces and the faces with the largest shear among the faces perpendicular to the plate. In a calculation by hand, in exercises and at an exam, we reach them with a few formulas in which the angle of inclination \(\theta\) itself appears. Before we write them down, let us draw both positions in the material, not only on the circle (figure 2.290).

About the point \(P\) of the plate we cut out a small square with faces perpendicular to the axes \(x\) and \(y\). The components we already know act on it: \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = 90\) MPa on the faces with normals \(\pm\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = 30\) MPa on the faces with normals \(\pm\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 40\) MPa along all four faces. The arrows are drawn to scale, so the arrow for \(30\) MPa is three times shorter than the arrow for \(90\) MPa. About the same point we cut out a second square, whose normal is turned from the direction of the axis \(x\) by the angle \(\theta_{\mathrm{p}}\) into the principal direction \(\vek e_1\). Its faces carry no shear arrows, only \(\sigma_1 = 110\) MPa and \(\sigma_2 = 10\) MPa, whose arrow is eleven times shorter and therefore barely visible. The third square has its normal turned by a further \(45^\circ\), into the direction midway between \(\vek e_1\) and \(\vek e_2\). On all four of its faces the normal stress is \(60\) MPa, and along the faces acts the shear of \(50\) MPa, the largest among the faces perpendicular to the plate. The shear arrows point toward the two corners that lie in the direction \(\vek e_1\): the shear pulls the square apart exactly along the direction of the largest tension.

All three squares describe the same stress at the same point. The stress at a point is one, only the faces through \(P\) on which we read it differ, and so the size of the squares does not count either. On the circle of figure 2.289 the blackwhite square is the pair of points \((90, 40)\) and \((30, -40)\), the blue one the pair \(\sigma_1\) and \(\sigma_2\), and the orange one the top and bottom of the circle. A turn of the square by \(45^\circ\) is a quarter of the circle, because the point moves round the circle with the double angle.

What happens between these three positions is shown by a graph of both stresses over the angle of inclination (figure 2.291), like the one we drew for the bar in figure 2.46.

On the horizontal axis we put the angle \(\theta\), on the vertical one the stress in MPa. At \(\theta = 0\) we read on the face with the normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), so the blackwhite curve \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\) starts at \(90\) MPa and the blue curve \(\tau_{\mathrm{nd}}\) at \(40\) MPa (the dots on the vertical axis). As the angle grows, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\) rises to the top of \(110\) MPa at \(\theta_{\mathrm{p}}\), and exactly there the blue curve passes through zero. This is the blue square of figure 2.290. A further \(45^\circ\) on the blue curve is lowest, at \(-50\) MPa, and the blackwhite one is there on the grey line \(m = 60\) MPa. This is the orange square. At \(90^\circ\) from the top the blackwhite curve is lowest, at \(10\) MPa, and the blue one is zero again. Another \(45^\circ\) on, the blue curve reaches \(50\) MPa. The dashed verticals at \(\theta_{\mathrm{p}}\) and \(\theta_{\mathrm{p}} + 90^\circ\) and at \(\theta_{\mathrm{p}} + 45^\circ\) and \(\theta_{\mathrm{p}} + 135^\circ\) show that the special positions follow each other every \(45^\circ\). At \(180^\circ\) both curves are back where they started, because the face with the normal \(-\vek n\) has the same two stresses as the face with the normal \(\vek n\).

Both curves are the formulas of step 8 of the proof of lemma 2.95 on Mohr's circle, written with the angle. Let us collect them, with everything that follows from them, in one statement. In it \(\sigma_{\mathrm{d}}\) is the normal stress on the neighbouring face of the square, the one with the normal \(\vek d\).

Corollary 2.96 Plane double-angle formulas and the angle of the principal directions (ravninski obrazci z dvojnim kotom in kot glavnih smeri)

Let the hypotheses of lemma 2.95 hold: the stress components at the point \(P\) are symmetric and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} = 0\). For an angle \(\theta\) let \(\vek n = (\cos\theta, \sin\theta, 0)\) and \(\vek d = (-\sin\theta, \cos\theta, 0)\). Let \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}(\theta)\) be the normal stress on the face through \(P\) with the normal \(\vek n\), \(\tau_{\mathrm{nd}}(\theta) = \vek t(\vek n)\cdot\vek d\) the shear component on it and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{d}}(\theta)\) the normal stress on the face through \(P\) with the normal \(\vek d\). Let \(m = (\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}})/2\) and \(R\) be the centre and the radius of (2.98). Then:

  1. The stresses on the turned faces are
    \[\begin{aligned} \sigma_{\mathrm{n}}(\theta) &= \frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}}{2} + \frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}}{2}\cos 2\theta + \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\sin 2\theta , \\ \sigma_{\mathrm{d}}(\theta) &= \frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}}{2} - \frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}}{2}\cos 2\theta - \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\sin 2\theta , \\ \tau_{\mathrm{nd}}(\theta) &= -\frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}}{2}\sin 2\theta + \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\cos 2\theta . \end{aligned} \tag{2.99}\]
  2. Conversely, the stresses on the turned faces give the components in the axes \(x\) and \(y\):
    \[\begin{aligned} \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} &= \frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{d}}}{2} + \frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{d}}}{2}\cos 2\theta - \tau_{\mathrm{nd}}\sin 2\theta , \\ \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} &= \frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{d}}}{2} - \frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{d}}}{2}\cos 2\theta + \tau_{\mathrm{nd}}\sin 2\theta , \\ \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} &= \frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{d}}}{2}\sin 2\theta + \tau_{\mathrm{nd}}\cos 2\theta . \end{aligned} \tag{2.100}\]
  3. The shear component \(\tau_{\mathrm{nd}}(\theta)\) is zero exactly when \((\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}})\sin 2\theta = 2\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\cos 2\theta\). When \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} \ne \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\), this holds exactly when
    \[\tan 2\theta = \frac{2\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}} . \tag{2.101}\]
  4. Let \(R > 0\). Among the angles \(0^\circ \le \theta < 180^\circ\) there are exactly two at which \(\tau_{\mathrm{nd}}(\theta) = 0\), the angle \(\theta_{\mathrm{p}}\), at which \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = m + R\), and the angle that is \(90^\circ\) larger or smaller, at which \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = m - R\). These are the largest and the smallest value of \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}(\theta)\). The faces with these normals are principal, and \(m + R\) and \(m - R\) are principal stresses.
  5. Let \(R > 0\). Then \(|\tau_{\mathrm{nd}}(\theta)| \le R\), with equality exactly at the angles that differ from \(\theta_{\mathrm{p}}\) by \(45^\circ\) and a multiple of \(90^\circ\). At these angles \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{d}} = m\).
Proof

We derive all items from the two formulas of step 8 of the proof of lemma 2.95. As there, we write \(a = (\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}})/2\) and \(b = \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\), the horizontal and the vertical distance of the point \((\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}})\) from the centre of the circle.

1. The double angle.

  1. By step 8 of the proof of lemma 2.95, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = m + a\,C + b\,S\) and \(\tau_{\mathrm{nd}} = b\,C - a\,S\), where \(C = n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 - n_{\mathrm{y}}^2\) and \(S = 2\,n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{y}}\). These are the blackwhite and the blue curve.
  2. We put in \(n_{\mathrm{x}} = \cos\theta\) and \(n_{\mathrm{y}} = \sin\theta\). By the double-angle formulas (KREYSZIG appendix A3.1, (7), PDF p. 1204), \(C = \cos^2\theta - \sin^2\theta = \cos 2\theta\) and \(S = 2\sin\theta\cos\theta = \sin 2\theta\). This gives the first and the third line of (2.99).
  3. The neighbouring face of the square has the normal \(\vek d = (\cos(\theta + 90^\circ), \sin(\theta + 90^\circ), 0)\), so \(\sigma_{\mathrm{d}}(\theta) = \sigma_{\mathrm{n}}(\theta + 90^\circ)\). The double angle grows by \(180^\circ\), and the cosine and the sine then change sign: \(\cos(2\theta + 180^\circ) = -\cos 2\theta\) and \(\sin(2\theta + 180^\circ) = -\sin 2\theta\). The first line gives the second.

2. The inverse formulas.

  1. We add and subtract the first two lines of (2.99): \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{d}} = 2m\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{d}} = 2\,(a\,C + b\,S)\). We write \(A = (\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{d}})/2 = a\,C + b\,S\).
  2. We compute \(A\,C - \tau_{\mathrm{nd}}\,S = (aC + bS)\,C - (bC - aS)\,S = a\,(C^2 + S^2) = a\), since the terms \(bSC\) and \(-bCS\) cancel and \(C^2 + S^2 = 1\) by step 9 of the proof of the lemma.
  3. In the same way \(A\,S + \tau_{\mathrm{nd}}\,C = (aC + bS)\,S + (bC - aS)\,C = b\,(S^2 + C^2) = b\).
  4. Since \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = m + a\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = m - a\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = b\), steps 5 and 6 together with \(m = (\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{d}})/2\) are the formulas (2.100).

3. When there is no shear.

  1. By the third line of (2.99), \(\tau_{\mathrm{nd}} = 0\) exactly when \(a\sin 2\theta = b\cos 2\theta\). We multiply by \(2\) and get the first condition. On the graph these are the zeros of the blue curve.
  2. Let \(a \ne 0\) and look for the zeros of the blue curve. If \(\cos 2\theta = 0\) at a solution, then \(\sin 2\theta = \pm 1\) and the condition would give \(\pm a = 0\), which is not true. So \(\cos 2\theta \ne 0\) and we may divide by \(a\cos 2\theta\). The tangent is the quotient of the sine and the cosine, so we get \(\tan 2\theta = b/a\), which is (2.101). Conversely, multiplying (2.101) by \(a\cos 2\theta\) gives the condition back.

4. Two angles and the principal stresses.

  1. Since \(a^2 + b^2 = R^2 > 0\), we may write \(a = R\cos\varphi\) and \(b = R\sin\varphi\), where \(\varphi\) is the angle between the horizontal axis and the radius to the point \((\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}})\). By the formulas for the cosine and the sine of a difference of angles (KREYSZIG appendix A3.1, (6), PDF p. 1204),
    \[\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - m = R\cos(\varphi - 2\theta) , \qquad \tau_{\mathrm{nd}} = R\sin(\varphi - 2\theta) .\]
  2. The sine is zero exactly at the multiples of \(180^\circ\). So \(\tau_{\mathrm{nd}} = 0\) exactly at \(2\theta = \varphi - k \cdot 180^\circ\), that is at \(\theta = \varphi/2 - k \cdot 90^\circ\) with an integer \(k\). These angles follow each other every \(90^\circ\), so a range of \(180^\circ\) holds exactly two of them, which differ by \(90^\circ\).
  3. At these angles \(\cos(\varphi - 2\theta) = \cos(k \cdot 180^\circ)\), which is \(1\) for even and \(-1\) for odd \(k\). At one angle therefore \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = m + R\) (the top of the blackwhite curve), this is the angle \(\theta_{\mathrm{p}}\), at the other \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = m - R\) (the bottom). Since the cosine is nowhere larger than \(1\) and nowhere smaller than \(-1\), these are the largest and the smallest value.
  4. By item 1 of lemma 2.95 the shear part of the stress vector equals \(\tau_{\mathrm{nd}}\,\vek d\). Where \(\tau_{\mathrm{nd}} = 0\), the stress vector points along the normal, so by definition 2.82 the face is principal and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\) is a principal stress. This is the blue square.

5. The largest shear.

  1. By step 10, \(|\tau_{\mathrm{nd}}| = R\,|\sin(\varphi - 2\theta)| \le R\). Equality holds exactly when the sine is \(\pm 1\), that is at \(\varphi - 2\theta = 90^\circ + k \cdot 180^\circ\), so at \(\theta = \varphi/2 - 45^\circ - k \cdot 90^\circ\). These angles differ from the angles of step 11 by \(45^\circ\) (the spacing on the graph).
  2. There \(\cos(\varphi - 2\theta) = 0\), so by step 10 \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = m\), and by step 4 \(\sigma_{\mathrm{d}} = 2m - \sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = m\). This is the orange square.

Source: The first and the third line of (2.99) are SADD (3.3.5) (PDF p. 68). BARBER finds the principal directions in the plane from the condition that the shear component (1.16) is zero, and obtains \(m \pm R\) (BARBER (1.23), PDF p. 30). The inverse formulas, the form with the tangent and the shift by \(45^\circ\) are derived here and checked with SymPy.

The corollary showed three things. The double-angle formulas are only another way of writing the formulas of the proof of the lemma. The inverse formulas are the same formulas used for the turn back, by the angle \(-\theta\): this is why every sine term changes sign. And the special positions follow each other every \(45^\circ\), because the point on the circle turns with the double angle, and from the crossing with the horizontal axis to the top of the circle is a quarter of the circle. Where did we use the condition \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} = 0\)? Only in step 13. The formulas (2.99) hold without it too, but without it a face with \(\tau_{\mathrm{nd}} = 0\) need not be principal, as the example with \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = 30\) MPa before lemma 2.95 showed. There the face with normal \((2, 1, 0)/\sqrt5\) still has \(\tau_{\mathrm{nd}} = 0\), since \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\) does not enter \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\) and \(\tau_{\mathrm{nd}}\), but a shear of \(30 \cdot 2/\sqrt5 = 26{,}83\) MPa in the direction of the axis \(z\) remains on it.

Point 3 requires \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} \ne \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\) because we divide by the difference. When they are equal and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} \ne 0\), the fraction in (2.101) has no value, and the first condition of point 3 gives \(\cos 2\theta = 0\), so \(\theta = 45^\circ\) and \(135^\circ\). Pure shear is such a case: with \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 40\) MPa the principal directions are the diagonals, with principal stresses \(40\) and \(-40\) MPa. Points 4 and 5 require \(R > 0\). For \(R = 0\) we have \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\), for example \(60\), \(60\) and \(0\) MPa. Then by (2.99) \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}(\theta) = 60\) MPa and \(\tau_{\mathrm{nd}}(\theta) = 0\) at every angle: the circle shrinks to a point, every direction in the plane is principal and there is no angle \(\theta_{\mathrm{p}}\).

Computing the angle and the check by substitution. For the plate, (2.101) gives

\[\tan 2\theta = \frac{2 \cdot 40}{90 - 30} = \frac{4}{3} .\]

A calculator returns \(2\theta = 53{,}13^\circ\) for the angle with this tangent, so \(\theta = 26{,}57^\circ\). This is only one of the two angles of item 4. The tangent has the same value at angles that differ by \(180^\circ\), so the equation is also satisfied by \(2\theta = 233{,}13^\circ\), that is \(\theta = 116{,}57^\circ\). The formula does not say at which of the two the normal stress is larger. Substitution into the first line of (2.99) does, with \(m = 60\) MPa, \(a = 30\) MPa and \(b = 40\) MPa:

\[\begin{aligned} \sigma_{\mathrm{n}}(26{,}57^\circ) &= 60 + 30 \cdot 0{,}6 + 40 \cdot 0{,}8 = 110\ \text{MPa} , \\ \sigma_{\mathrm{n}}(116{,}57^\circ) &= 60 + 30 \cdot (-0{,}6) + 40 \cdot (-0{,}8) = 10\ \text{MPa} . \end{aligned}\]

The angle \(26{,}57^\circ\) is therefore \(\theta_{\mathrm{p}}\) at the top of the blackwhite curve, and the angle \(116{,}57^\circ\) is its bottom. Is the substitution really needed, when the calculator returned the right angle? Let us describe the same plate in axes turned by \(90^\circ\), with the new axis \(\bar x\) in the direction of the old axis \(y\). By (2.60) with \(c = 0\) and \(s = 1\) the components are \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = 30\) MPa, \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = 90\) MPa and \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = -40\) MPa. The same formula gives

\[\tan 2\bar\theta = \frac{2 \cdot (-40)}{30 - 90} = \frac{4}{3} ,\]

and the calculator again returns \(\bar\theta = 26{,}57^\circ\), this time measured from the axis \(\bar x\), which is \(116{,}57^\circ\) from the axis \(x\). We substitute: \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = 60 + (-30) \cdot 0{,}6 + (-40) \cdot 0{,}8 = 10\) MPa. The same plate, the same formula and the same calculator have now given the direction of the smaller principal stress \(\sigma_2\). So we never declare the angle returned by the formula with the tangent to be the direction of \(\sigma_1\) until we have substituted it.

Why this happens is shown by the circle (figure 2.292). On Mohr's circle of the plate lies the point of the face with normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \((90, 40)\) MPa. The diameter through this point has the slope \(40/30 = 4/3\): the vertical distance of the point from the centre \(b = 40\) MPa divided by the horizontal one \(a = 30\) MPa. This is exactly the value that formula (2.101) computes, since \(2\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}/(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}) = b/a\). When the normal turns by \(\theta\), the point turns along the circle by \(2\theta\) the other way, and the turn by \(53{,}13^\circ\) takes it to the horizontal axis, to \(\sigma_1 = 110\) MPa. In axes turned by \(90^\circ\) we start on the same circle at the face with normal \(\vek e_{\bar{x}} = \vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\), \((30, -40)\) MPa, at the other end of the same diameter. The slope is again \((-40)/(-30) = 4/3\) and the calculator returns the same angle, but the same turn by \(53{,}13^\circ\) takes this point to \(\sigma_2 = 10\) MPa. The formula with the tangent knows only the diameter, not the end of the diameter at which we started. Only the substitution tells the end.

The faces of the largest shear are \(45^\circ\) further on. At \(\theta = 26{,}57^\circ + 45^\circ = 71{,}57^\circ\) we have \(2\theta = 143{,}13^\circ\), \(\cos 2\theta = -0{,}8\) and \(\sin 2\theta = 0{,}6\), so by (2.99)

\[\begin{aligned} \tau_{\mathrm{nd}} &= -30 \cdot 0{,}6 + 40 \cdot (-0{,}8) = -50\ \text{MPa} , \\ \sigma_{\mathrm{n}} &= 60 + 30 \cdot (-0{,}8) + 40 \cdot 0{,}6 = 60\ \text{MPa} . \end{aligned}\]

These are the shear of \(50\) MPa and the normal stress of \(60\) MPa of the orange square, and the normal is \((\cos 71{,}57^\circ, \sin 71{,}57^\circ, 0) = (1, 3, 0)/\sqrt{10}\), the same as above. The negative sign says that the shear part points opposite to \(\vek d\). In plane stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = 0\), so the first invariant of definition 2.87 is \(I_1 = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and the normal stress on the faces of the largest shear is \(m = I_1/2\), here \(120/2 = 60\) MPa. The inverse formulas (2.100) take us from the blue square back to the blackwhite one: with \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = 110\) MPa, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{d}} = 10\) MPa, \(\tau_{\mathrm{nd}} = 0\) and \(\theta = 26{,}57^\circ\),

\[\begin{aligned} \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} &= 60 + 50 \cdot 0{,}6 - 0 = 90\ \text{MPa} , \\ \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} &= 60 - 50 \cdot 0{,}6 + 0 = 30\ \text{MPa} , \\ \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} &= 50 \cdot 0{,}8 + 0 = 40\ \text{MPa} . \end{aligned}\]

A second route: by the derivative. In the lectures and in most textbooks on strength of materials the angle \(\theta_{\mathrm{p}}\) is found differently: the largest and the smallest value of the function \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}(\theta)\) are sought where its derivative is zero, written as \(\mathrm d\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}/\mathrm d\theta = 0\). The reason is lemma 1.83 on the derivative at an interior extremum: at the top and at the bottom of the curve the tangent is horizontal. This route needs the derivatives of the sine and the cosine, the school formulas \(\sin' = \cos\) and \(\cos' = -\sin\) for an angle in radians, which this book proves only in chapter 8. The proof of the corollary therefore did not use them, but here let us take them as known, to see what this route adds. The derivative of the first line of (2.99) is

\[\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}'(\theta) = -(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}})\sin 2\theta + 2\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\cos 2\theta = 2\,\tau_{\mathrm{nd}}(\theta) ,\]

where the factor \(2\) comes from the double angle. The slope of the blackwhite curve is thus at every point twice the height of the blue one. We check at \(\theta = 0\), at the starting points of both curves: the slope should be \(2 \cdot 40 = 80\) MPa per radian, that is \(80 \cdot \pi/180 = 1{,}396\) MPa per degree, and indeed \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}(1^\circ) - \sigma_{\mathrm{n}}(0^\circ) = 91{,}378 - 90 = 1{,}378\) MPa. The condition \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}'(\theta) = 0\) is therefore the same as \(\tau_{\mathrm{nd}}(\theta) = 0\) and gives the same equation (2.101). That the normal stress is largest or smallest exactly on the faces without shear we saw already on the circle. The route by the derivative adds the reason: twice the shear is the rate at which the normal stress changes with the turn, in MPa per radian. In the same way \(\tau_{\mathrm{nd}}'(\theta) = -2\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}(\theta) - m)\), so the blue curve has a horizontal tangent where the blackwhite one is at the height \(m\), at \(\theta_{\mathrm{p}} + 45^\circ\) and at \(\theta_{\mathrm{p}} + 135^\circ\). This route has the same trap as the tangent: the derivative is zero at the top and at the bottom, so again only substitution tells the two angles apart.

In the lectures the angle of inclination is written \(\alpha\) or \(\varphi\), the shear component \(\tau_{\mathrm{nd}}\) is written \(\sigma_{\mathrm{t}}\), and the angle of the face of the largest shear \(\beta = \alpha_1 + 45^\circ\). The same rules hold for strain. By lemma 2.55 the components of small strain in turned axes change by the same rule as the stress components, so in (2.99) and (2.101) we only change the letter: \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{n}}(\theta) = \tfrac12(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}) + \tfrac12(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}})\cos 2\theta + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\sin 2\theta\) (SADD (2.3.6), PDF p. 48) and \(\tan 2\theta_{\mathrm{p}} = 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}/(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}})\), where \(2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) is the engineering shear strain \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}}\).

Let us return to the largest shear among the faces perpendicular to the plate, the \(50\) MPa on the orange square. Theorem 2.93 gave more, 55 MPa, not 50 MPa. There is no contradiction. The circle in figure 2.289 covers only the faces that contain the direction of the axis \(z\), and the two faces with the largest shear do not contain it. We may also use lemma 2.95 on Mohr's circle in principal axes, for the faces turning about any principal direction, since there all shear components are zero and the condition of the lemma holds. This gives three circles (figure 2.293). The faces that contain the direction \(\vek e_3 = \vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) give the circle through \(\sigma_2 = 10\) and \(\sigma_1 = 110\) MPa, which we have already drawn. The faces that contain the direction \(\vek e_2\) give the circle through \(\sigma_3 = 0\) and \(\sigma_1 = 110\) MPa, with radius \(55\) MPa. The faces that contain the direction \(\vek e_1\) give a small circle through \(0\) and \(10\) MPa, with radius \(5\) MPa. The largest radius belongs to the circle between the largest and the smallest principal stress, and this radius is \(\tau_{\max} = (\sigma_1 - \sigma_3)/2\) of the theorem. The in-plane extreme \(R\) of item 5 of corollary 2.96, half the difference of the two in-plane principal stresses, is therefore the largest shear stress at the point exactly when the third principal stress, the one in the direction of the axis \(z\), does not lie outside the range between them. Here \(\sigma_3 = 0\) lies outside the range from \(10\) MPa to \(110\) MPa, so the largest circle is larger than the in-plane one. If the principal stresses in the plane of the plate were \(110\) and \(-10\) MPa, zero would lie between them and the in-plane circle with the radius \(60\) MPa would be the largest. SADD shows even more: the points of all faces through \(P\), not only of those that contain a principal direction, lie in the region inside the largest circle and outside both smaller ones (SADD (3.4.10), figure 3.7, PDF p. 71). We will prove this below, with the weights of section 2.12.1.

The figure shows the axes and three circles. The largest circle through \(\sigma_3\) and \(\sigma_1\) has the radius \(55\) MPa, the circle through \(\sigma_2\) and \(\sigma_1\), which we drew before, the radius \(50\) MPa, and the small circle through \(\sigma_3\) and \(\sigma_2\) the radius \(5\) MPa. On the horizontal axis are the principal stresses \(\sigma_3\), \(\sigma_2\) and \(\sigma_1\). The top of the largest circle is \(\tau_{\max}\) and the top of the circle through \(\sigma_2\) and \(\sigma_1\) is the point with \(50\) MPa. The light region between the circles is where the points of all other faces lie.

Why exactly this region? Recall how in section 2.12.1 we wrote the stresses on a face with the unit normal \(\vek n\), whose components in the principal axes are \(n_1\), \(n_2\) and \(n_3\). With the weights \(w_{\mathrm{i}} = n_{\mathrm{i}}^2\), which are not negative and have the sum \(1\), the normal stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} w_{\mathrm{i}}\sigma_{\mathrm{i}}\) is the weighted average of the principal stresses, and the square of the shear stress is \(\tau^2 = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} w_{\mathrm{i}}\sigma_{\mathrm{i}}^2 - \sigma_{\mathrm{n}}^2\) ((2.91)). The point \((\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}, \tau)\) has two coordinates, and the weights are three numbers with the sum \(1\), so two of them are free. We therefore expect the points of all faces not to lie on the circles only, but to fill a region of the plane. Where its boundary is, a single computation tells: the expression \(\tau^2 + (\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - \sigma_2)(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - \sigma_3)\) equals the weight \(w_1\) times a number that depends on the principal stresses only.

Where the sign of this number comes from is shown in figure 2.294. On the axis of numbers \(s\) we mark the principal stresses and above it we draw the parabola \((s - \sigma_2)(s - \sigma_3)\). The product is zero when one of the brackets is zero, so the parabola crosses the axis at \(\sigma_2\) and \(\sigma_3\). Between the zeros the brackets have opposite signs and the product is negative, outside them they have the same sign and the product is positive. The number that the weight \(w_1\) multiplies is the value of the parabola at \(\sigma_1\), \((\sigma_1 - \sigma_2)(\sigma_1 - \sigma_3)\). Since \(\sigma_1\) is to the left of neither zero, the brackets are not negative and neither is the value. For the second expression the parabola \((s - \sigma_3)(s - \sigma_1)\) has its zeros at \(\sigma_3\) and \(\sigma_1\). Between them lies \(\sigma_2\), so the value at \(\sigma_2\) is not positive. For the third the parabola \((s - \sigma_1)(s - \sigma_2)\) has its zeros at \(\sigma_1\) and \(\sigma_2\). To the left of both lies \(\sigma_3\), so the value at \(\sigma_3\) is not negative.

Lemma 2.97 Region of Mohr's circles (območje Mohrovih krogov)

Let \(\sigma_1 \ge \sigma_2 \ge \sigma_3\) be the principal stresses at a point \(P\) of a body in equilibrium and \(\vek e_1\), \(\vek e_2\), \(\vek e_3\) mutually perpendicular unit vectors of the corresponding principal directions. Let the unit normal \(\vek n\) of a plane face through \(P\) have the components \(n_1\), \(n_2\) and \(n_3\) in the principal axes, and let \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\) be the normal and \(\tau\) the shear stress on this face. Then:

  1. For the point of a face the equalities and inequalities
    \[\begin{aligned} \tau^2 + (\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - \sigma_2)(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - \sigma_3) &= n_1^2\,(\sigma_1 - \sigma_2)(\sigma_1 - \sigma_3) \ge 0 , \\ \tau^2 + (\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - \sigma_3)(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - \sigma_1) &= n_2^2\,(\sigma_2 - \sigma_3)(\sigma_2 - \sigma_1) \le 0 , \\ \tau^2 + (\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - \sigma_1)(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - \sigma_2) &= n_3^2\,(\sigma_3 - \sigma_1)(\sigma_3 - \sigma_2) \ge 0 . \end{aligned} \tag{2.102}\]
    hold.
  2. For numbers \(a\) and \(b\), let the circle through \(a\) and \(b\) be the circle with centre \(\big((a + b)/2,\ 0\big)\) and radius \(|a - b|/2\) in the plane with the normal stress on the horizontal and the shear stress on the vertical axis. The point \((\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}, \tau)\) lies on or inside the circle through \(\sigma_3\) and \(\sigma_1\), and on or outside the circles through \(\sigma_3\) and \(\sigma_2\) and through \(\sigma_2\) and \(\sigma_1\).
Proof

We must show the three equalities, the signs on the right and the meaning of the inequalities. We write the weights as \(w_{\mathrm{i}} = n_{\mathrm{i}}^2\), and the index \(i\) runs over \(1\), \(2\) and \(3\).

1. Equalities and signs.

  1. The weights are not negative, since they are squares, and by step 7 of the proof of corollary 2.85 on stress in principal axes, \(w_1 + w_2 + w_3 = 1\). By (2.91), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} w_{\mathrm{i}}\sigma_{\mathrm{i}}\) and \(\tau^2 = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} w_{\mathrm{i}}\sigma_{\mathrm{i}}^2 - \sigma_{\mathrm{n}}^2\).
  2. We write the product out as a product of brackets: \((\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - \sigma_2)(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - \sigma_3) = \sigma_{\mathrm{n}}^2 - (\sigma_2 + \sigma_3)\,\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} + \sigma_2\sigma_3\). When we add \(\tau^2\) from step 1, the terms \(-\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}^2\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}^2\) cancel:
    \[\tau^2 + (\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - \sigma_2)(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - \sigma_3) = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} w_{\mathrm{i}}\sigma_{\mathrm{i}}^2 - (\sigma_2 + \sigma_3)\,\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} + \sigma_2\sigma_3 .\]
  3. We insert \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} w_{\mathrm{i}}\sigma_{\mathrm{i}}\) and \(\sigma_2\sigma_3 = \sigma_2\sigma_3\sum_{\mathrm{i}} w_{\mathrm{i}}\), which we may, since the weights have the sum \(1\). We gather all three terms into one sum over \(i\):
    \[\begin{aligned} \tau^2 + (\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - \sigma_2)(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - \sigma_3) &= \sum_{\mathrm{i}} w_{\mathrm{i}}\,\big(\sigma_{\mathrm{i}}^2 - (\sigma_2 + \sigma_3)\,\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} + \sigma_2\sigma_3\big) \\ &= \sum_{\mathrm{i}} w_{\mathrm{i}}\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} - \sigma_2)(\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} - \sigma_3) , \end{aligned}\]
    where the last bracket is the written-out product as in step 2.
  4. For \(i = 2\) the factor \(\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} - \sigma_2\) is zero, for \(i = 3\) the factor \(\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} - \sigma_3\): \(\sigma_2\) and \(\sigma_3\) are the zeros of the parabola \((s - \sigma_2)(s - \sigma_3)\). Only the term with \(i = 1\) remains, the weight \(w_1\) times the value of the parabola at \(\sigma_1\), \(w_1\,(\sigma_1 - \sigma_2)(\sigma_1 - \sigma_3)\). This is the first equality.
  5. We repeat steps 2 to 4 with the pairs \(\sigma_3\), \(\sigma_1\) and \(\sigma_1\), \(\sigma_2\) instead of \(\sigma_2\), \(\sigma_3\). Only the term with \(i = 2\) or with \(i = 3\) remains in the sum, the value of the second parabola at \(\sigma_2\) or of the third at \(\sigma_3\), and we get the second and the third equality.
  6. Signs. The weights are not negative. Since the principal stresses on the axis are ordered so that \(\sigma_1 \ge \sigma_2 \ge \sigma_3\), the numbers \(\sigma_1 - \sigma_2\) and \(\sigma_1 - \sigma_3\) are nonnegative, so the right-hand side of the first equality is not negative (dot above the axis). The number \(\sigma_2 - \sigma_3\) is not negative and \(\sigma_2 - \sigma_1\) is not positive, so the right-hand side of the second equality is not positive (dot below the axis). The numbers \(\sigma_3 - \sigma_1\) and \(\sigma_3 - \sigma_2\) are not positive, and their product is not negative, so the right-hand side of the third equality is not negative (dot above the axis).

2. Meaning of the inequalities.

  1. Let \(a\) and \(b\) be numbers, \(c = (a + b)/2\) and \(d = (a - b)/2\). Then \(a = c + d\) and \(b = c - d\), and by the school formula for the product of a sum and a difference,
    \[(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - a)(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - b) = \big((\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - c) - d\big)\big((\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - c) + d\big) = (\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - c)^2 - d^2 .\]
  2. So \(\tau^2 + (\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - a)(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - b) = (\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - c)^2 + \tau^2 - d^2\). By (1.10), \((\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - c)^2 + \tau^2\) is the square of the distance of the point \((\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}, \tau)\) from the centre \((c, 0)\) of the circle through \(a\) and \(b\), and \(d^2\) is the square of its radius \(|d|\). For one face these three distances are drawn in figure 2.295 after the lemma.
  3. The expression of step 8 is not negative exactly when the square of the distance is not smaller than the square of the radius. Both numbers are nonnegative, so by lemma 1.29, that a larger nonnegative number has a larger square, this happens exactly when the distance is not smaller than the radius, when the point is on or outside the circle. In the same way the expression is not positive exactly when the point is on or inside the circle.
  4. The first and the third inequality of item 1 therefore say that the point \((\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}, \tau)\) is on or outside the circle through \(\sigma_2\) and \(\sigma_3\) and on or outside the circle through \(\sigma_1\) and \(\sigma_2\), and the second says that it is on or inside the circle through \(\sigma_3\) and \(\sigma_1\). All three hold at once exactly in the light region.

Source: SADD (3.4.7)-(3.4.10), figure 3.7 (PDF pp. 70-71). SADD solves the three equations for \(n_1^2\), \(n_2^2\) and \(n_3^2\) and assumes distinct principal stresses for this. The proof with the equalities is not from the source.

The proof showed why the lemma holds. Each of the three expressions is the weighted average of the numbers \((\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{a}})(\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{b}})\) with the weights \(w_{\mathrm{i}}\), and for two of the three principal stresses this number is zero, since they are the zeros of the parabola. A single term remains, whose sign is fixed by the order of the principal stresses alone. We divided by nothing, so the lemma also holds when two principal stresses are equal. Then two circles merge, for instance in the bar pulled by an axial force, with \(\sigma_2 = \sigma_3 = 0\), where the circle through \(\sigma_2\) and \(\sigma_3\) shrinks to a point and the circles through \(\sigma_3\) and \(\sigma_1\) and through \(\sigma_2\) and \(\sigma_1\) are the same circle. The region is then just this circle, the Mohr circle of the bar of figure 2.288. SADD goes another way: when the principal stresses are distinct, it divides the equalities (2.102) by the nonzero numbers on the right and so computes all three weights from the point \((\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}, \tau)\) (SADD (3.4.9), PDF p. 71). Since only \(\tau^2\) appears in the inequalities, they hold in the same way for the point \((\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}, -\tau)\), which is why we drew the region symmetric in figure 2.293.

Let us test the lemma on the thin plate, for which we found \(\sigma_1 = 110\) MPa, \(\sigma_2 = 10\) MPa and \(\sigma_3 = 0\) with the principal directions \(\vek e_1 = (2, 1, 0)/\sqrt5\), \(\vek e_2 = (-1, 2, 0)/\sqrt5\) and \(\vek e_3 = \vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\). Take the face whose normal points in the direction of the fly's flight, \(\vek n = (1, 2, -2)/3\). Its components in the principal axes are the scalar products with the principal directions (lemma 2.45), \(n_1 = 4/(3\sqrt5)\), \(n_2 = 3/(3\sqrt5)\) and \(n_3 = -2/3\), and the weights are \(w_1 = \tfrac{16}{45}\), \(w_2 = \tfrac{9}{45}\) and \(w_3 = \tfrac{20}{45}\), with the sum \(1\). By (2.91), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = (110 \cdot 16 + 10 \cdot 9)/45 = 41{,}11\) MPa and \(\tau^2 = 2632{,}1\) MPa², so \(\tau = 51{,}30\) MPa. The three expressions of (2.102) are, in MPa²,

\[\begin{aligned} 2632{,}1 + 31{,}11 \cdot 41{,}11 &= 3911{,}1 = \tfrac{16}{45} \cdot 100 \cdot 110 , \\ 2632{,}1 + 41{,}11 \cdot (-68{,}89) &= -200{,}0 = \tfrac{9}{45} \cdot 10 \cdot (-100) , \\ 2632{,}1 + (-68{,}89) \cdot 31{,}11 &= 488{,}9 = \tfrac{20}{45} \cdot (-110) \cdot (-10) , \end{aligned}\]

as the lemma says, with the signs \(+\), \(-\), \(+\). The point \(B\) in figure 2.295 is this face. By step 8 of the proof the three expressions are the differences between the square of the distance of the point \(B\) from the centre of a circle and the square of its radius. From the centre of the small circle at \(5\) MPa, \(B\) is \(\sqrt{3911{,}1 + 5^2} = 62{,}74\) MPa away, more than the radius \(5\) MPa. From the centre of the large circle at \(55\) MPa it is \(\sqrt{-200{,}0 + 55^2} = 53{,}15\) MPa away, less than the radius \(55\) MPa. From the centre of the middle circle at \(60\) MPa it is \(\sqrt{488{,}9 + 50^2} = 54{,}67\) MPa away, more than the radius \(50\) MPa. The point \(B\) is therefore outside the small and the middle circle and inside the large one. The same figure shows the face with the normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), which lies on the blue circle, the face with the weights of figure 2.272, the face with the largest shear stress, and 220 randomly chosen faces, whose points we computed with NumPy. No point lies outside the region.

The figure shows the upper half of the region above the axes with the principal stresses \(\sigma_3\), \(\sigma_2\) and \(\sigma_1\). The shaded region is bounded by the large, the middle and the small circle. The points of 220 random faces lie in it. The special faces are \(A\) with the normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(B\) with the normal \((1, 2, -2)/3\), \(C\) with the weights \(0{,}5\), \(0{,}2\) and \(0{,}3\), and \(D\) with the largest shear stress. From the point \(B\) segments lead to the centre of the small, the large and the middle circle. Comparing their lengths with the radii tells that \(B\) is in the region.

Mohr's circle is a tool for faces that turn about one axis. SADD remarks that it can be used for computations in a plane, while for general computations the rule for turning the axes is used (SADD, PDF p. 72), which we derived in section 2.9. The thin plate shows why a circle in one plane is not enough: the circle of the faces perpendicular to the plate gives 50 MPa, while the largest shear is 55 MPa on faces that cut the plate obliquely through its thickness.

2.12.4 Spherical and deviatoric parts of stress

In a fluid at rest the traction vector on every face is \(-p\,\vek n\), all three principal stresses are \(-p\), and there is no shear stress anywhere. What happens if we add such a stress, equal pressure from all sides, to some other stress, for example the stress in the plate? Then the new stress matrix is \(\ten\sigma - p\,\mat I\), where \(\mat I\) is the identity matrix. By Cauchy's formula in components (2.27) the traction vector \(\vek t\) on every face changes by \(-p\,\vek n\), into the new vector \(\vek t - p\,\vek n\) (figure 2.296). The normal stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\) on every face therefore decreases by \(p\), to \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} - p\), because \((-p\,\vek n)\cdot\vek n = -p\), while the shear part \(\vek t - \sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\vek n\) stays the same, because \(\vek t\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\vek n\) change by the same vector \(-p\,\vek n\): the tip of the vector moves along a line parallel to the normal \(\vek n\), so its shadow on the face is the same. The shear on any face does not depend on how much equal pressure or equal tension on all faces the stress contains.

We therefore split the stress into two parts: a part that pulls or pushes equally on all faces, and a remainder. How much equal pull should we take away? The natural choice is the average of the three normal stresses on the faces perpendicular to the axes. This number is the same in all rectangular Cartesian coordinate systems, since it is a third of the first invariant \(I_1 = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\) of definition 2.87, which by lemma 2.88 does not change when the axes turn. In principal axes it is therefore \((\sigma_1 + \sigma_2 + \sigma_3)/3\).

Definition 2.98 Spherical and deviatoric parts of stress (sferični in deviatorni del napetosti)

Let \(\ten\sigma\) be the symmetric matrix of the stress components at a point \(P\) in a chosen rectangular Cartesian coordinate system. The mean stress (srednja napetost) at \(P\) is the number

\[\sigma_{\mathrm{m}} = \frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}}{3} = \frac{I_1}{3} . \tag{2.103}\]

The spherical part (sferični del) of the stress is the matrix \(\sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\,\mat I\). The deviatoric part or deviator (deviatorni del, deviator) of the stress is the matrix

\[\ten s = \ten\sigma - \sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\,\mat I , \tag{2.104}\]

with the components \(s_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\), \(s_{\mathrm{yy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\), \(s_{\mathrm{zz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\) and \(s_{\mathrm{ij}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\) when the indices \(i\) and \(j\) are different. Here the indices \(i\) and \(j\) run over \(x\), \(y\), \(z\). The second deviatoric invariant (druga invarianta deviatorja) is the number

\[J_2 = \frac12\sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} s_{\mathrm{ij}}^2 . \tag{2.105}\]

Source: CM (4.3.14)-(4.3.17) (PDF p. 189), SADD (3.5.1)-(3.5.3) (PDF pp. 72-73), BOWER §2.2.7 (PDF p. 75). CM writes the number \(J_2\) as \(I'_2\), BOWER as \(J_2\) (PDF p. 117).

The matrix \(\ten\sigma - \sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\mat I\) is computed entry by entry, like the sum of matrices in section 1.16: we subtract \(\sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\) from each diagonal entry, and the others stay. The name spherical part says that this part acts equally on all faces, in all directions, like the pressure in a fluid with \(p = -\sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\). CM also calls it the hydrostatic part (hidrostatični del) (CM, PDF p. 189). The name deviator says that this part measures how much the stress deviates from an equal pull in all directions. The books write the deviator differently: CM \(\ten\sigma'\), SADD \(\hat\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\), BOWER \(\sigma'_{\mathrm{ij}}\) (CM (4.3.16), SADD (3.5.2), BOWER, PDF p. 75). We write \(\ten s\), because we keep the prime for derivatives.

For the spherical part every direction is principal. For every unit normal \(\vek n\), \((\sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\mat I)\,\vek n = \sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\vek n\), the traction vector points along the normal, so by definition 2.82 \(\vek n\) is a principal direction with the principal stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\). This is how it is in the fluid at rest in figure 2.79, where all the arrows are perpendicular to the surface of the small body and equally long, however the surface is tilted. There we derived this from the fact that water at rest does not resist shear. The finding that the pressure at a point of a fluid at rest is the same in all directions is called Pascal's law (Pascalov zakon). In the lectures the spherical part is called krogelni del and written \(\ten\sigma^K\), and the deviatoric part is called deviatorični del and written \(\ten\sigma^D\), so that \(\ten\sigma = \ten\sigma^K + \ten\sigma^D\).

Lemma 2.99 Properties of the deviator (lastnosti deviatorja)

Let \(\ten s\) be the deviator of the symmetric stress matrix \(\ten\sigma\) at a point \(P\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\) the mean stress. Then:

  1. \(s_{\mathrm{xx}} + s_{\mathrm{yy}} + s_{\mathrm{zz}} = 0\).
  2. For every unit normal \(\vek n\), \(\vek t(\vek n) = \ten s\,\vek n + \sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\,\vek n\). The normal stress on the face is larger by \(\sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\) than the number \((\ten s\,\vek n)\cdot\vek n\), while the shear part of the traction vector equals \(\ten s\,\vek n - \big((\ten s\,\vek n)\cdot\vek n\big)\,\vek n\) and does not depend on \(\sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\).
  3. If \(\vek e\) is a principal direction of the stress with principal stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{i}}\), then \(\ten s\,\vek e = (\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{m}})\,\vek e\). The deviator has the same principal directions as the stress, and its eigenvalues are \(s_{\mathrm{i}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{i}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\).
Proof

All three items follow from the fact that the deviator differs from the stress only on the diagonal, by \(\sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\).

1. Sum of the diagonal entries.

  1. By definition \(s_{\mathrm{xx}} + s_{\mathrm{yy}} + s_{\mathrm{zz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} - 3\sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\).
  2. By (2.103) \(3\sigma_{\mathrm{m}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\), so the sum is zero.

2. The traction vector.

  1. The stress is symmetric (theorem 2.41), so by (2.54) \(\vek t(\vek n) = \ten\sigma\,\vek n\). The \(x\) component is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} n_{\mathrm{x}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} n_{\mathrm{y}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} n_{\mathrm{z}}\).
  2. We insert \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = s_{\mathrm{xx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = s_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = s_{\mathrm{xz}}\). The \(x\) component is \(s_{\mathrm{xx}} n_{\mathrm{x}} + s_{\mathrm{xy}} n_{\mathrm{y}} + s_{\mathrm{xz}} n_{\mathrm{z}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{m}} n_{\mathrm{x}}\), which is the \(x\) component of the vector \(\ten s\,\vek n\) increased by \(\sigma_{\mathrm{m}} n_{\mathrm{x}}\). Likewise for the \(y\) and \(z\) components. Hence \(\vek t(\vek n) = \ten s\,\vek n + \sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\,\vek n\).
  3. By the rules of the scalar product the normal stress is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = (\ten s\,\vek n)\cdot\vek n + \sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\,(\vek n\cdot\vek n) = (\ten s\,\vek n)\cdot\vek n + \sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\), because \(\vek n\) is a unit vector.
  4. The shear part is \(\vek t(\vek n) - \sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\vek n = \ten s\,\vek n + \sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\vek n - \big((\ten s\,\vek n)\cdot\vek n\big)\,\vek n - \sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\vek n\). The terms with \(\sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\) cancel.

3. Principal directions.

  1. By definition 2.82 \(\ten\sigma\,\vek e = \sigma_{\mathrm{i}}\,\vek e\).
  2. By step 2 of item 2, applied to the normal \(\vek e\), \(\ten s\,\vek e = \ten\sigma\,\vek e - \sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\vek e = (\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{m}})\,\vek e\).
  3. Conversely, let \(\ten s\,\vek v = \mu\,\vek v\) for some nonzero vector \(\vek v\). We compute the components of \(\ten\sigma\,\vek v\) as in step 2 of item 2, only with \(\vek v\) in place of \(\vek n\), so \(\ten\sigma\,\vek v = \ten s\,\vek v + \sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\vek v = (\mu + \sigma_{\mathrm{m}})\,\vek v\).
  4. By lemma 1.98 on the linearity of the product with a matrix also \(\ten\sigma\,(\vek v/|\vek v|) = (\mu + \sigma_{\mathrm{m}})\,\vek v/|\vek v|\), so the unit vector \(\vek v/|\vek v|\) is a principal direction of the stress with the principal stress \(\mu + \sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\). By corollary 2.89 on the principal stresses as the roots of the characteristic equation this is one of the numbers \(\sigma_{\mathrm{i}}\), so \(\mu = \sigma_{\mathrm{i}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\) for some \(i\).

Source: CM (4.3.15), (4.3.16) (PDF p. 189). SADD states that the deviator and the stress have the same principal directions and leaves the proof to exercise 3.15 (SADD, PDF p. 73). The proof is not from the sources.

The lemma says what the two parts mean. The spherical part pulls or pushes equally on every face, by \(\sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\), and has no shear. The deviator carries all the shear, since the shear part on every face depends only on it. Its diagonal entries add up to zero, so on average it neither pulls nor pushes. BOWER puts it in words: the mean stress is a measure of the pressure exerted by the stress, and pressure tends to change the volume of a piece of material, while the deviator is a measure of the shearing, which tends to change the shape of the piece without changing its volume (BOWER §2.2.7, PDF p. 75). How exactly this happens depends on the material, and for a material that behaves the same in all directions we will see it in chapter 3. Why the split matters is shown by experiment: equal pressure from all sides alone, however large, does not make a metal yield (BOWER §3.7.3, PDF p. 146). So we assume that only the deviator decides yielding, also when equal pressure is added to another stress.

This assumption goes further than the experiment. The experiment only says that equal pressure from all sides alone causes no yielding, while the assumption says that, added to another stress, it does not change when the material begins to yield either. For metals BOWER bases the criteria for the onset of yielding, which we meet in section 2.12.6, on this observation (BOWER §3.7.3, PDF p. 146). For soils the assumption does not hold: their yield strength grows strongly with pressure, and equal pressure can make them yield (BOWER, PDF pp. 36 and 183). The yielding of granular materials and of some polymers also changes with the confining pressure (BOWER, PDF p. 36). The assumption removes the mean stress from the criterion for yielding: only the deviator appears in it, the spherical part does not. The example of the thin plate that follows shows what this means in numbers.

Let us split the stress in the thin plate of figure 2.277, with \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = 90\) MPa, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = 30\) MPa and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 40\) MPa, the other components zero. The mean stress is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{m}} = (90 + 30 + 0)/3 = 40\) MPa, and the deviator is

\[\ten s = \begin{pmatrix} 90 - 40 & 40 & 0 \\ 40 & 30 - 40 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 - 40 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 50 & 40 & 0 \\ 40 & -10 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -40 \end{pmatrix}\ \text{MPa} .\]

The diagonal adds up to \(50 - 10 - 40 = 0\), as item 1 of the lemma says. By item 3 the principal values of the deviator are \(110 - 40 = 70\) MPa, \(10 - 40 = -30\) MPa and \(0 - 40 = -40\) MPa, along the same directions as the principal stresses. Figure 2.297 shows the split on a small cube with faces perpendicular to the principal directions.

On the left is the cube with faces perpendicular to the principal directions, with the stresses \(\sigma_1 = 110\) MPa and \(\sigma_2 = 10\) MPa, while \(\sigma_3 = 0\) gives no arrow. The equals sign says that this equals the cube that is pulled equally by \(\sigma_{\mathrm{m}} = 40\) MPa on every face, and, after the sign \(+\), the cube that is pulled or pushed by \(s_1 = 70\) MPa, \(s_2 = -30\) MPa and \(s_3 = -40\) MPa.

By the assumption on yielding above, only the deviator decides the yielding of the plate, and the spherical part \(\sigma_{\mathrm{m}} = 40\) MPa does not. The plate would begin to yield at the same deviator also if we added a pressure of \(100\) MPa from all sides, making the mean stress \(40 - 100 = -60\) MPa.

In each row the stress is on the left, the equals sign comes before the spherical part in the middle, and the sign \(+\) before the deviator on the right. For the bar with the stress \(\sigma\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{m}} = \sigma/3\), and the principal values of the deviator are \(2\sigma/3\), \(-\sigma/3\) and \(-\sigma/3\). So even simple tension has a spherical part, a third of the stress. In pure shear \(\sigma_{\mathrm{m}} = (0 + 0 + 0)/3 = 0\), and the deviator is the whole stress. In a fluid at rest \(\sigma_{\mathrm{m}} = -p\) and the deviator is the zero matrix: the stress is its spherical part alone.

The question remains how to say with one number how much shear the deviator carries. This is what the second deviatoric invariant \(J_2\) of the definition is for. It is half the sum of the squares of all nine components of the deviator, so it is never negative, and it is zero only when the deviator is the zero matrix. The next lemma says that it does not depend on the choice of axes and expresses it by the principal stresses. Before it, let us look at \(J_2\) of the plate in figure 2.299.

On the left are the nine components of the deviator of the plate. Three are diagonal, the remaining six are equal in pairs: \(s_{\mathrm{xy}} = s_{\mathrm{yx}} = 40\) MPa, \(s_{\mathrm{yz}} = s_{\mathrm{zy}} = 0\) and \(s_{\mathrm{zx}} = s_{\mathrm{xz}} = 0\). On the right the number line carries the principal stresses \(\sigma_3 = 0\), \(\sigma_2 = 10\) MPa and \(\sigma_1 = 110\) MPa. The distances between them are \(10\) MPa, \(100\) MPa and \(110\) MPa. From the mean stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{m}} = 40\) MPa the same three points are at the distances given by the principal values of the deviator \(70\), \(-30\) and \(-40\) MPa.

Lemma 2.100 Expressions for the second deviatoric invariant (izrazi za drugo invarianto deviatorja)

Let \(\ten s\) be the deviator of the symmetric stress matrix \(\ten\sigma\) with the principal stresses \(\sigma_1\), \(\sigma_2\) and \(\sigma_3\), and \(I_1\) and \(I_2\) the invariants of the matrix \(\ten\sigma\) of definition 2.87. Then

\[\begin{aligned} J_2 &= \frac12\,(s_{\mathrm{xx}}^2 + s_{\mathrm{yy}}^2 + s_{\mathrm{zz}}^2) + s_{\mathrm{xy}}^2 + s_{\mathrm{yz}}^2 + s_{\mathrm{zx}}^2 \\ &= \frac{I_1^2}{3} - I_2 = \frac16\Big((\sigma_1 - \sigma_2)^2 + (\sigma_2 - \sigma_3)^2 + (\sigma_3 - \sigma_1)^2\Big) , \end{aligned} \tag{2.106}\]

and \(J_2\) has the same value in all rectangular Cartesian coordinate systems. In terms of the stress components in the chosen axes

\[J_2 = \frac16\Big((\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}})^2 + (\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}})^2 + (\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}})^2 + 6\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}^2 + \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}^2 + \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}^2)\Big) , \tag{2.107}\]

and in terms of two differences of the principal stresses

\[J_2 = \frac13\Big((\sigma_1 - \sigma_3)^2 - (\sigma_1 - \sigma_3)(\sigma_2 - \sigma_3) + (\sigma_2 - \sigma_3)^2\Big) . \tag{2.108}\]
Proof

We get the first expression by writing out the sum, the second with the invariants \(I_1\) and \(I_2\), the third in principal axes, and the last two from the second and the third.

  1. The double sum in (2.105) has nine terms. Three are diagonal, \(s_{\mathrm{xx}}^2\), \(s_{\mathrm{yy}}^2\) and \(s_{\mathrm{zz}}^2\). The remaining six are equal in pairs, since \(s_{\mathrm{xy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}} = s_{\mathrm{yx}}\) by the symmetry of stress, and likewise for the other two pairs (\(yz\) and \(zx\)). Half the sum is therefore the first expression in (2.106).
  2. We express the diagonal terms by the stress. We write out \((\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{m}})^2 = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}^2 - 2\sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{m}}^2\), likewise for \(y\) and \(z\), and add. Since \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = 3\sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\), the sum is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}^2 + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}^2 + \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}^2 - 6\sigma_{\mathrm{m}}^2 + 3\sigma_{\mathrm{m}}^2 = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}^2 + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}^2 + \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}^2 - 3\sigma_{\mathrm{m}}^2\).
  3. With \(\sigma_{\mathrm{m}} = I_1/3\), \(3\sigma_{\mathrm{m}}^2 = I_1^2/3\). The off-diagonal entries of \(\ten s\) and \(\ten\sigma\) are equal, so \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} s_{\mathrm{ij}}^2 = \sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}^2 - I_1^2/3\).
  4. The sum of the squares of all nine stress components is the trace (the sum of the diagonal entries) of the matrix \(\ten\sigma\ten\sigma\). By the rule for the matrix product, the diagonal entry is \((\ten\sigma\ten\sigma)_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\sigma_{\mathrm{zx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}^2 + \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}^2 + \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}^2\), because \(\ten\sigma\) is symmetric. Likewise \((\ten\sigma\ten\sigma)_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and \((\ten\sigma\ten\sigma)_{\mathrm{zz}}\) are the sums of the squares of the second and the third row, and the sum of all three is \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}}\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}^2\).
  5. As we showed for definition 2.87, \(I_2 = \tfrac12\big(I_1^2 - \tr(\ten\sigma\ten\sigma)\big)\), so \(\tr(\ten\sigma\ten\sigma) = I_1^2 - 2I_2\).
  6. From steps 3 to 5, \(J_2 = \tfrac12\big(I_1^2 - 2I_2 - I_1^2/3\big) = I_1^2/3 - I_2\).
  7. By lemma 2.88, \(I_1\) and \(I_2\) do not change when the axes turn, so neither does \(J_2\).
  8. In principal axes the stress matrix is diagonal, with \(\sigma_1\), \(\sigma_2\) and \(\sigma_3\) on the diagonal. There \(I_1 = \sigma_1 + \sigma_2 + \sigma_3\) and \(\tr(\ten\sigma\ten\sigma) = \sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2 + \sigma_3^2\), so by step 5 \(I_2 = \tfrac12\big((\sigma_1 + \sigma_2 + \sigma_3)^2 - \sigma_1^2 - \sigma_2^2 - \sigma_3^2\big) = \sigma_1\sigma_2 + \sigma_2\sigma_3 + \sigma_3\sigma_1\).
  9. By step 6, therefore,
    \[J_2 = \frac{\sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2 + \sigma_3^2 + 2(\sigma_1\sigma_2 + \sigma_2\sigma_3 + \sigma_3\sigma_1)}{3} - (\sigma_1\sigma_2 + \sigma_2\sigma_3 + \sigma_3\sigma_1) = \frac{\sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2 + \sigma_3^2 - \sigma_1\sigma_2 - \sigma_2\sigma_3 - \sigma_3\sigma_1}{3} .\]
  10. Writing out the squares of the differences gives \((\sigma_1 - \sigma_2)^2 + (\sigma_2 - \sigma_3)^2 + (\sigma_3 - \sigma_1)^2 = 2(\sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2 + \sigma_3^2) - 2(\sigma_1\sigma_2 + \sigma_2\sigma_3 + \sigma_3\sigma_1)\), which is twice the numerator of step 9. So \(J_2\) is a sixth of this sum.
  11. The expression (2.107). In the second expression, \(J_2 = I_1^2/3 - I_2\), by definition 2.87 \(I_1 = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\) and \(I_2 = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}^2 - \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}^2 - \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}^2\). The part with the normal components is the same computation as in steps 9 and 10, only with \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\) in place of \(\sigma_1\), \(\sigma_2\) and \(\sigma_3\), and it gives a sixth of the sum of the squares of the three differences. The squares of the shear components have the sign plus in \(-I_2\), and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}^2 + \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}^2 + \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}^2\) is a sixth of six times their sum.
  12. The expression (2.108). Write \(a = \sigma_1 - \sigma_3\) and \(b = \sigma_2 - \sigma_3\). The third distance is their difference, \(\sigma_1 - \sigma_2 = a - b\). The sum of the squares in the third expression is therefore \((a - b)^2 + b^2 + a^2 = 2a^2 - 2ab + 2b^2\), and a sixth of it is \((a^2 - ab + b^2)/3\).

Source: The expression of step 3: BOWER (PDF p. 117), where \(J_2 = (\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{kk}}\sigma_{\mathrm{pp}}/3)/2\). The expression with the principal stresses follows from SADD (3.5.4) and (3.5.5) (PDF p. 73). The proof is not from the sources.

The third expression in (2.106) contains only differences of the principal stresses. If we add the same number to all three, all three points on the line move by the same amount, the distances between them stay, and \(J_2\) does not change. This is another way of saying that the spherical part carries no shear. For the plate the principal stresses are \(110\), \(10\) and \(0\) MPa, the differences between them \(100\), \(10\) and \(110\) MPa, and the third expression gives \(J_2 = (100^2 + 10^2 + 110^2)/6 = 22\,200/6 = 3700\) MPa². The first expression with the components of the deviator, the diagonal ones \(50\), \(-10\) and \(-40\) MPa and \(s_{\mathrm{xy}} = 40\) MPa, gives the same, \(\tfrac12\,(50^2 + 10^2 + 40^2) + 40^2 = 2100 + 1600 = 3700\) MPa². So does the second: \(I_1 = 120\) MPa, \(I_2 = 90 \cdot 30 - 40^2 = 1100\) MPa², and \(120^2/3 - 1100 = 3700\) MPa². The expression (2.107) needs only the stress components of the plate, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = 90\) MPa, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = 30\) MPa, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = 0\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 40\) MPa, with no need to compute the deviator: \((60^2 + 30^2 + 90^2 + 6\cdot 40^2)/6 = 22\,200/6 = 3700\) MPa². The expression (2.108) needs only two distances on the line, \(a = 110\) MPa and \(b = 10\) MPa: \((110^2 - 110\cdot 10 + 10^2)/3 = 11\,100/3 = 3700\) MPa². Three times it, \(a^2 - ab + b^2\), will in section 2.12.6 be the square of the number that we compare with the yield stress.

The deviator carries all the shear. Are there axes in which we see it as shear and nothing else, with no normal stresses on the faces of the cube? For pure shear we already know the answer. Its principal stresses are \(\tau_0\), \(0\) and \(-\tau_0\), with the sum zero, so \(\sigma_{\mathrm{m}} = 0\) and the stress is its own deviator. In principal axes we see it as tension \(\tau_0\) in one direction and an equally large pressure in the perpendicular direction, and in axes turned by \(45°\) as shear \(\tau_0\) with no normal stresses. The deviator of the plate has the principal values \(70\), \(-30\) and \(-40\) MPa, also with the sum zero. We will show that for it too, and for every deviator, there are axes in which it is shear alone. The way to them is shown in figure 2.300.

On the left is the cube with faces perpendicular to the principal directions \(\vek e_1\), \(\vek e_2\) and \(\vek e_3\). Its faces carry the principal values of the deviator, the tension \(s_1 = 70\) MPa and the pressures \(s_2 = -30\) MPa and \(s_3 = -40\) MPa, this is the right cube of figure 2.297. At the axes we draw the direction \(\vek n = (\vek e_1 + \vek e_2 + \vek e_3)/\sqrt3\), the diagonal of the cube on the three axes, which is equally inclined to all three of them. In the middle we look at the plane perpendicular to \(\vek n\) from the tip of the vector \(\vek n\), which therefore points toward us. The shadows of the principal axes are \(120°\) apart in this plane. In the plane we choose the perpendicular unit vectors \(\vek a_0\) and \(\vek b_0\) and turn them about \(\vek n\) by the angle \(\theta\) into \(\vek a\) and \(\vek b\). On the right is the cube with faces perpendicular to \(\vek a\), \(\vek b\) and \(\vek n\). We will choose the angle \(\theta\) so that only shear stresses remain on its faces, equal in pairs: \(s_{\mathrm{ab}}\), \(s_{\mathrm{an}}\) and \(s_{\mathrm{bn}}\).

Lemma 2.101 The deviator is shear alone in suitable axes (deviator je v primernih oseh sam strig)

Let \(\ten s\) be the deviator of the symmetric stress matrix \(\ten\sigma\) at a point \(P\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\) the mean stress. Then there are three mutually perpendicular unit vectors \(\vek a\), \(\vek b\) and \(\vek n = \vek a\times\vek b\) for which

\[(\ten s\,\vek a)\cdot\vek a = 0 , \qquad (\ten s\,\vek b)\cdot\vek b = 0 , \qquad (\ten s\,\vek n)\cdot\vek n = 0 . \tag{2.109}\]

In the axes along \(\vek a\), \(\vek b\) and \(\vek n\) all three diagonal entries of the matrix of the deviator are zero, the normal stress on each of the three faces perpendicular to these axes is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\), and

\[J_2 = s_{\mathrm{ab}}^2 + s_{\mathrm{an}}^2 + s_{\mathrm{bn}}^2 , \qquad s_{\mathrm{ab}} = (\ten s\,\vek a)\cdot\vek b , \quad s_{\mathrm{an}} = (\ten s\,\vek a)\cdot\vek n , \quad s_{\mathrm{bn}} = (\ten s\,\vek b)\cdot\vek n . \tag{2.110}\]
Proof

We must show that three such directions exist. We find the first in principal axes and the other two by a turn about it, as in figure 2.300.

  1. By theorem 2.83 the stress has three mutually perpendicular principal directions \(\vek e_1\), \(\vek e_2\) and \(\vek e_3 = \vek e_1\times\vek e_2\) with the principal stresses \(\sigma_1\), \(\sigma_2\) and \(\sigma_3\). Take \(\vek n = (\vek e_1 + \vek e_2 + \vek e_3)/\sqrt3\). Its components in principal axes are all three \(1/\sqrt3\), with the sum of squares \(1\), so it is a unit vector.
  2. By (2.81) the normal stress on the face with the normal \(\vek n\) equals \(\sigma_1/3 + \sigma_2/3 + \sigma_3/3\), each principal stress contributes a third. By (2.90) this is \(I_1/3 = \sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\). By item 2 of lemma 2.99 therefore \((\ten s\,\vek n)\cdot\vek n = \sigma_{\mathrm{m}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{m}} = 0\).
  3. In the plane perpendicular to \(\vek n\) take the unit vectors \(\vek a_0 = (\vek e_1 - \vek e_2)/\sqrt2\) and \(\vek b_0 = (\vek e_1 + \vek e_2 - 2\vek e_3)/\sqrt6\). With the components in principal axes we check that \(\vek a_0\cdot\vek n = (1 - 1)/\sqrt6 = 0\), \(\vek b_0\cdot\vek n = (1 + 1 - 2)/\sqrt{18} = 0\), \(\vek a_0\cdot\vek b_0 = (1 - 1)/\sqrt{12} = 0\) and \(\vek a_0\times\vek b_0 = (2, 2, 2)/\sqrt{12} = \vek n\). Write
    \[A = (\ten s\,\vek a_0)\cdot\vek a_0 , \qquad B = (\ten s\,\vek b_0)\cdot\vek b_0 , \qquad C = (\ten s\,\vek a_0)\cdot\vek b_0 .\]
  4. Let us show that \(B = -A\). The axes along \(\vek a_0\), \(\vek b_0\) and \(\vek n\) are turned rectangular axes. The diagonal entries of the stress matrix in them are by definition 2.27 the normal stresses on the faces with the normals \(\vek a_0\), \(\vek b_0\) and \(\vek n\), and by lemma 2.88 their sum is \(I_1 = 3\sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\). By item 2 of lemma 2.99 each of the numbers \(A\), \(B\) and \((\ten s\,\vek n)\cdot\vek n\) is smaller by \(\sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\) than the corresponding normal stress, so \(A + B + 0 = 3\sigma_{\mathrm{m}} - 3\sigma_{\mathrm{m}} = 0\).
  5. Because \(\ten s\) is symmetric, also \((\ten s\,\vek b_0)\cdot\vek a_0 = C\): both numbers are a double sum of the terms \(s_{\mathrm{ij}}\) multiplied by the component \(i\) of one vector and the component \(j\) of the other, and exchanging the roles of the vectors exchanges \(s_{\mathrm{ij}}\) with \(s_{\mathrm{ji}}\), which equals it.
  6. For numbers \(x\) and \(y\) with \(x^2 + y^2 = 1\) take \(\vek a = x\,\vek a_0 + y\,\vek b_0\) and \(\vek b = -y\,\vek a_0 + x\,\vek b_0\). This is the pair \(\vek a_0\), \(\vek b_0\) turned about \(\vek n\) by the angle \(\theta\) with \(x = \cos\theta\) and \(y = \sin\theta\). By lemma 2.12 \(\vek a\cdot\vek a = x^2 + y^2 = 1\), likewise \(\vek b\cdot\vek b = 1\), \(\vek a\cdot\vek b = -xy + xy = 0\), and both are perpendicular to \(\vek n\), because \(\vek a_0\) and \(\vek b_0\) are.
  7. By lemma 1.98 on the linearity of the product with a matrix \(\ten s\,\vek a = x\,\ten s\,\vek a_0 + y\,\ten s\,\vek b_0\). The scalar product with \(\vek a\) gives by steps 3 to 5
    \[(\ten s\,\vek a)\cdot\vek a = x^2 A + 2xy\,C + y^2 B = A\,(x^2 - y^2) + 2C\,xy .\]

Figure 2.301 shows the expression of step 7 for the plate, for which we compute \(A = 20\) MPa, \(B = -20\) MPa and \(C = 28{,}87\) MPa after the lemma. On the horizontal axis is the angle \(\theta\) from \(-90°\) to \(90°\) by which we turn the pair \(\vek a_0\), \(\vek b_0\). The upper curve is the normal component of the deviator \((\ten s\,\vek a)\cdot\vek a\) on the face with the normal \(\vek a\). At \(\theta = 0\) we have \(\vek a = \vek a_0\) and the curve is at \(A = 20\) MPa. At \(\theta = -90°\) we have \(\vek a = -\vek b_0\), at \(\theta = 90°\) we have \(\vek a = \vek b_0\), both times this is the face with the normal \(\vek b_0\), and the curve is at \(B = -A = -20\) MPa. Since \(A\) and \(B\) have opposite signs, the curve crosses zero between \(-90°\) and \(0\), at \(\theta = -17{,}36°\). Step 8 computes this point. The lower curve is the component \((\ten s\,\vek a)\cdot\vek b\) of the vector \(\ten s\,\vek a\) in the direction \(\vek b\), one of the two shear components on this face, equal to \(C = 28{,}87\) MPa at \(\theta = 0\). By steps 5 and 7

\[(\ten s\,\vek a)\cdot\vek b = -xy\,A + x^2 C - y^2 C + xy\,B = C\,(x^2 - y^2) - 2A\,xy ,\]

since \(B = -A\). The sum of the squares of the two components is therefore

\[(A^2 + C^2)\big((x^2 - y^2)^2 + 4x^2y^2\big) = (A^2 + C^2)\,(x^2 + y^2)^2 = A^2 + C^2 .\]

So both curves stay in the band between \(-R\) and \(R\), where \(R = \sqrt{A^2 + C^2} = 35{,}12\) MPa, and where the upper one is zero, the lower one equals \(R\) or \(-R\). The second zero of the upper curve, \(90°\) further, gives the same pair of directions with the roles exchanged, \(\vek b\) in place of \(\vek a\) and \(-\vek a\) in place of \(\vek b\), so there the lower curve is \(-R\).

  1. Choose \(x\) and \(y\) so that this expression is zero, as at the zero of the upper curve. If \(A = 0\), we take \(x = 1\) and \(y = 0\). Otherwise write \(R = \sqrt{A^2 + C^2}\) and take
    \[t = \frac{C - R}{A} , \qquad x = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + t^2}} , \qquad y = \frac{t}{\sqrt{1 + t^2}} .\]
    Then \(x^2 + y^2 = 1\) and \(A\,(x^2 - y^2) + 2C\,xy = (A - A t^2 + 2C t)/(1 + t^2)\). The numerator is zero: from \(A t = C - R\) it follows that \(A^2 t^2 = C^2 - 2CR + R^2\) and \(2C\,At = 2C^2 - 2CR\), so \(A\,(A t^2 - 2C t - A) = R^2 - C^2 - A^2 = 0\), and because \(A\) is not zero, \(A t^2 - 2Ct - A = 0\). Hence \((\ten s\,\vek a)\cdot\vek a = 0\).
  2. For the axes along \(\vek a\), \(\vek b\) and \(\vek n\) we repeat step 4: \((\ten s\,\vek a)\cdot\vek a + (\ten s\,\vek b)\cdot\vek b + (\ten s\,\vek n)\cdot\vek n = 0\). The first and the third term are zero, so \((\ten s\,\vek b)\cdot\vek b\) is zero too. By step 4 these three numbers are the diagonal entries of the matrix of the deviator in these axes, and the normal stresses on the faces of the new cube are larger by \(\sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\), so all three equal \(\sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\).
  3. The off-diagonal entries of the deviator equal the off-diagonal entries of the stress, in these axes \(s_{\mathrm{ab}}\), \(s_{\mathrm{an}}\) and \(s_{\mathrm{bn}}\). By lemma 2.100 \(J_2\) has the same value in all axes, and the first expression in (2.106), written in these axes, has zero diagonal terms. What remains is (2.110).

Source: The proof is not from the sources.

The lemma says in what sense the deviator carries the shear: in suitable axes the whole deviator is shear, and \(J_2\) is there the sum of the squares of three shear stresses. This is a second view of \(J_2\) besides the distances between the principal stresses in figure 2.299. For the plate, in step 3,

\[A = \frac{70 - 30}{2} = 20\ \text{MPa} , \qquad B = \frac{70 - 30 - 4\cdot 40}{6} = -20\ \text{MPa} , \qquad C = \frac{70 + 30}{\sqrt{12}} = 28{,}87\ \text{MPa} ,\]

and indeed \(B = -A\). Step 8 gives \(R = \sqrt{20^2 + 28{,}87^2} = 35{,}12\) MPa, \(t = (28{,}87 - 35{,}12)/20 = -0{,}3126\), \(x = 0{,}9545\) and \(y = -0{,}2983\). This is a turn by the angle \(\theta = -17{,}36°\): \(\vek a\) is turned from \(\vek a_0\) away from \(\vek b_0\). In principal axes \(\vek a = (0{,}553, -0{,}797, 0{,}244)\) and \(\vek b = (0{,}601, 0{,}179, -0{,}779)\). The shear stresses on the new cube are

\[s_{\mathrm{ab}} = 35{,}12\ \text{MPa} , \qquad s_{\mathrm{an}} = 30{,}53\ \text{MPa} , \qquad s_{\mathrm{bn}} = 39{,}18\ \text{MPa} ,\]

\(s_{\mathrm{ab}}\) acts on the face with the normal \(\vek a\) and on the face with the normal \(\vek b\), and likewise for \(s_{\mathrm{an}}\) and \(s_{\mathrm{bn}}\). The number \(s_{\mathrm{ab}}\) equals \(R\) of step 8, since at the zero of the upper curve the lower curve equals \(R\). The sum of the squares is \(1233{,}3 + 931{,}9 + 1534{,}7 = 3700\) MPa² up to rounding, which is \(J_2\) of the plate. The whole stress of the plate has on the same cube, besides these shear stresses, also the normal stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{m}} = 40\) MPa on every face.

Such axes are not unique. Instead of \(\vek a_0\) and \(\vek b_0\) we could take any pair in the plane, and \(\vek n\) too could be another direction with \((\ten s\,\vek n)\cdot\vek n = 0\). The shear stresses would be different, but the sum of their squares the same. Without the zero sum of the diagonal, however, the lemma does not hold. The stress of the plate has the sum of the diagonal entries \(I_1 = 120\) MPa in all axes, so in no axes are all three zero. Only when we take away the spherical part does a matrix remain that we can see as shear alone.

The deviator is a symmetric matrix, so like the stress it has its own characteristic polynomial, its own principal values and its own three invariants. We write the invariants of the deviator \(J_1\), \(J_2\) and \(J_3\), to tell them from the stress invariants \(I_1\), \(I_2\) and \(I_3\).
