What happens to the characteristic polynomial on the way from the stress to the deviator is shown in figure 2.302 for the plate.

On the horizontal axis we plot the number \(\lambda\) in MPa, on the vertical one the value of the polynomial. The blackwhite curve is the left side of the characteristic equation (2.85) for the stress of the plate, \(\lambda^3 - 120\lambda^2 + 1100\lambda = \lambda\,(\lambda - 10)(\lambda - 110)\). It crosses the axis at the principal stresses \(0\), \(10\) and \(110\) MPa. By item 3 of lemma 2.99 the deviator has the principal values \(s_{\mathrm{i}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{i}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\), so we move each zero by \(\sigma_{\mathrm{m}} = 40\) MPa to the left, to \(-40\), \(-30\) and \(70\) MPa. The orange curve through these three zeros is the characteristic polynomial of the deviator, the same curve as the blackwhite one, only \(40\) MPa further left. Before the move the average of the zeros was at \(\sigma_{\mathrm{m}} = 40\) MPa, after it it is at the origin, since the zeros of the deviator have the sum \(-40 - 30 + 70 = 0\). The coefficient of \(\lambda^2\) is, up to sign, the sum of the zeros, so the polynomial of the deviator has no term with \(\lambda^2\). Where the blackwhite curve crosses the dashed line, and where the orange one crosses the vertical axis, the value of both is \(40\cdot 30\cdot(-70) = -84\,000\) MPa³. This number, with the opposite sign, will be the third invariant of the deviator.

Definition 2.102 Invariants of the deviator (invariante deviatorja)

Let \(\ten s\) be the deviator of the symmetric stress matrix \(\ten\sigma\) at a point \(P\) in a chosen rectangular Cartesian coordinate system. The first deviatoric invariant (prva invarianta deviatorja) is the number

\[J_1 = s_{\mathrm{xx}} + s_{\mathrm{yy}} + s_{\mathrm{zz}} , \tag{2.111}\]

the second is the number \(J_2\) of (2.105), and the third deviatoric invariant (tretja invarianta deviatorja) is the number

\[J_3 = \det\ten s . \tag{2.112}\]

Source: BOWER §3.8.3 (PDF p. 166, crop p166-b2 read), where the third invariant is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{III}} = \det(\mathbf S)\) and which says that the deviator has only two nonzero invariants. The symbols \(J_1\), \(J_2\), \(J_3\): \(J_2\) after BOWER (PDF p. 117).

Lemma 2.103 Invariants of the deviator and its characteristic equation (invariante deviatorja in njegova karakteristična enačba)

Let \(\ten s\) be the deviator of the symmetric stress matrix \(\ten\sigma\) at a point \(P\), \(s_1\), \(s_2\) and \(s_3\) its principal values, and \(I_1\), \(I_2\) and \(I_3\) the stress invariants of definition 2.87. Then:

  1. \(J_1 = 0\), and the numbers \(J_1\), \(J_2\) and \(J_3\) have the same value in all rectangular Cartesian coordinate systems.
  2. For every number \(\lambda\), \(\det(\ten s - \lambda\mat I) = -\lambda^3 + J_2\,\lambda + J_3\). The principal values of the deviator are therefore the solutions of the equation
    \[\lambda^3 - J_2\,\lambda - J_3 = 0 . \tag{2.113}\]
  3. In terms of the principal values of the deviator
    \[J_1 = s_1 + s_2 + s_3 = 0 , \qquad J_2 = -(s_1 s_2 + s_2 s_3 + s_3 s_1) = \frac12\,(s_1^2 + s_2^2 + s_3^2) , \qquad J_3 = s_1 s_2 s_3 . \tag{2.114}\]
  4. In terms of the stress invariants
    \[J_3 = \frac{2}{27}\,I_1^3 - \frac13\,I_1 I_2 + I_3 . \tag{2.115}\]

The sums of products of the components of the deviator are

\[\sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} s_{\mathrm{ij}}\,s_{\mathrm{ji}} = 2J_2 , \qquad \sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}}\sum_{\mathrm{m}} s_{\mathrm{ij}}\,s_{\mathrm{jm}}\,s_{\mathrm{mi}} = 3J_3 . \tag{2.116}\]
\[s_{\mathrm{ij}}\,s_{\mathrm{ji}} = 2J_2 , \qquad s_{\mathrm{ij}}\,s_{\mathrm{jm}}\,s_{\mathrm{mi}} = 3J_3 . \tag{2.116}\]

The first sum is the trace of the matrix \(\ten s\,\ten s\), the second the trace of the matrix \(\ten s\,\ten s\,\ten s\).

Proof

We must show four items and the two formulas for the sums. All follow from the fact that the deviator is the stress with \(\sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\) subtracted on the diagonal, that is, from the characteristic polynomial of the stress, moved as in figure 2.302.

  1. By item 1 of lemma 2.99 \(J_1 = 0\) in any axes. For \(J_2\) this is said by lemma 2.100. For \(J_3\) take turned axes with the stress matrix \(\bar{\ten\sigma}\). By lemma 2.88 \(\bar I_1 = I_1\), so the mean stress is the same in both systems, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\), and the deviator in the turned axes is \(\bar{\ten s} = \bar{\ten\sigma} - \sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\mat I\). The same lemma says that \(\det(\bar{\ten\sigma} - \lambda\mat I) = \det(\ten\sigma - \lambda\mat I)\) for every number \(\lambda\). At \(\lambda = \sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\) this is \(\det\bar{\ten s} = \det\ten s\). In the figure \(-J_3\) is the value of the blackwhite curve at \(\lambda = \sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\), and the curve is the same in all axes.
  2. We apply lemma 2.86 to the matrix \(\ten s\). By its item 2 \(\det(\ten s - \lambda\mat I) = -\lambda^3 + J_1\lambda^2 - K\lambda + J_3\), where by symmetry \(K = s_{\mathrm{xx}}s_{\mathrm{yy}} + s_{\mathrm{yy}}s_{\mathrm{zz}} + s_{\mathrm{zz}}s_{\mathrm{xx}} - s_{\mathrm{xy}}^2 - s_{\mathrm{yz}}^2 - s_{\mathrm{zx}}^2\). The term with \(\lambda^2\) drops out, because \(J_1 = 0\). From \(0 = (s_{\mathrm{xx}} + s_{\mathrm{yy}} + s_{\mathrm{zz}})^2 = s_{\mathrm{xx}}^2 + s_{\mathrm{yy}}^2 + s_{\mathrm{zz}}^2 + 2\,(s_{\mathrm{xx}}s_{\mathrm{yy}} + s_{\mathrm{yy}}s_{\mathrm{zz}} + s_{\mathrm{zz}}s_{\mathrm{xx}})\) it follows that \(s_{\mathrm{xx}}s_{\mathrm{yy}} + s_{\mathrm{yy}}s_{\mathrm{zz}} + s_{\mathrm{zz}}s_{\mathrm{xx}} = -\tfrac12\,(s_{\mathrm{xx}}^2 + s_{\mathrm{yy}}^2 + s_{\mathrm{zz}}^2)\), so by the first expression in (2.106) \(K = -J_2\). Hence \(\det(\ten s - \lambda\mat I) = -\lambda^3 + J_2\lambda + J_3\), which is the orange curve with the opposite sign. By item 1 of the same lemma the eigenvalues of the matrix \(\ten s\) are the solutions of equation (2.113), and by item 3 of lemma 2.99 these are the principal values \(s_1\), \(s_2\) and \(s_3\).
  3. In principal axes the matrix of the deviator is diagonal, with \(s_1\), \(s_2\) and \(s_3\) on the diagonal, since by item 3 of lemma 2.99 \(\ten s\,\vek e_{\mathrm{i}} = s_{\mathrm{i}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{i}}\) for the principal directions \(\vek e_{\mathrm{i}}\). By step 1 we may compute the invariants in these axes. There \(J_1 = s_1 + s_2 + s_3\), by the definition (2.105) \(J_2 = \tfrac12\,(s_1^2 + s_2^2 + s_3^2)\) and \(J_3 = s_1 s_2 s_3\), the determinant of a diagonal matrix, as for \(I_3\) in corollary 2.89. We get the other form of \(J_2\) as in step 2: from \(0 = (s_1 + s_2 + s_3)^2\) it follows that \(s_1 s_2 + s_2 s_3 + s_3 s_1 = -\tfrac12\,(s_1^2 + s_2^2 + s_3^2)\).
  4. By item 2 of lemma 2.86 for the matrix \(\ten\sigma\), \(\det(\ten\sigma - \lambda\mat I) = -\lambda^3 + I_1\lambda^2 - I_2\lambda + I_3\). At \(\lambda = \sigma_{\mathrm{m}} = I_1/3\) the left side is \(\det\ten s = J_3\), and the right side is
    \[-\frac{I_1^3}{27} + \frac{I_1^3}{9} - \frac{I_1 I_2}{3} + I_3 = \frac{2}{27}\,I_1^3 - \frac13\,I_1 I_2 + I_3 ,\]
    since \(-\tfrac1{27} + \tfrac3{27} = \tfrac2{27}\).
  5. The first sum: by symmetry \(s_{\mathrm{ij}}s_{\mathrm{ji}} = s_{\mathrm{ij}}^2\), and by (2.105) the sum of all nine squares is \(2J_2\).
  6. The second sum: the matrix \(\mat T = \ten s\,\ten s\,\ten s\) has the entries \(T_{\mathrm{ik}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}}\sum_{\mathrm{m}} s_{\mathrm{ij}}s_{\mathrm{jm}}s_{\mathrm{mk}}\), so the sum we seek is the sum of its diagonal entries. Let us first show that it is the same in all axes. In turned axes with the rotation matrix \(\mat Q\), by (2.59) \(\bar{\ten\sigma} = \mat Q\ten\sigma\mat Q^\T\), and as in step 2 of the proof of lemma 2.88 \(\sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\mat I = \mat Q\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\mat I)\,\mat Q^\T\), so \(\bar{\ten s} = \mat Q\,\ten s\,\mat Q^\T\). By lemma 2.47 on the orthogonality of the rotation matrix also \(\mat Q^\T\mat Q = \mat I\), so \(\bar{\mat T} = \mat Q\,\ten s\,\mat Q^\T\mat Q\,\ten s\,\mat Q^\T\mat Q\,\ten s\,\mat Q^\T = \mat Q\,\mat T\,\mat Q^\T\). The proof of lemma 2.88 uses of the matrix \(\ten\sigma\) only that it changes into \(\mat Q\ten\sigma\mat Q^\T\) when the axes turn, so it holds for \(\mat T\) too: the sum of its diagonal entries is the same in all axes. In principal axes the matrix of the deviator is diagonal (step 3), so \(\bar{\mat T}\) is diagonal there too, with \(s_1^3\), \(s_2^3\) and \(s_3^3\) on the diagonal, and the sum is \(s_1^3 + s_2^3 + s_3^3\).
  7. Every principal value solves equation (2.113), so \(s_{\mathrm{i}}^3 = J_2\,s_{\mathrm{i}} + J_3\). We add over \(i\): \(s_1^3 + s_2^3 + s_3^3 = J_2\,(s_1 + s_2 + s_3) + 3J_3 = 3J_3\), because the sum of the principal values is zero.

Source: The expression \(J_2 = I_1^2/3 - I_2\) is in lemma 2.100. The proof is not from the sources.

The lemma puts the invariants of the deviator beside the stress invariants. Both are the coefficients of a characteristic polynomial written with its zeros, once with the principal stresses, once with the principal values of the deviator:

\[\begin{aligned} I_1 &= \sigma_1 + \sigma_2 + \sigma_3 , & J_1 &= s_1 + s_2 + s_3 = 0 , \\ I_2 &= \sigma_1\sigma_2 + \sigma_2\sigma_3 + \sigma_3\sigma_1 , & J_2 &= -(s_1 s_2 + s_2 s_3 + s_3 s_1) , \\ I_3 &= \sigma_1\sigma_2\sigma_3 , & J_3 &= s_1 s_2 s_3 . \end{aligned}\]

For the plate \(J_1 = 70 - 30 - 40 = 0\), \(J_2 = -\big(70\cdot(-30) + (-30)\cdot(-40) + (-40)\cdot 70\big) = 2100 - 1200 + 2800 = 3700\) MPa² and \(J_3 = 70\cdot(-30)\cdot(-40) = 84\,000\) MPa³, which is the number in the figure with the opposite sign. With the stress invariants \(I_1 = 120\) MPa, \(I_2 = 1100\) MPa² and \(I_3 = 0\), (2.115) gives the same: \(\tfrac{2}{27}\cdot 120^3 - \tfrac13\cdot 120\cdot 1100 = 128\,000 - 44\,000 = 84\,000\) MPa³. The characteristic equation of the deviator of the plate is \(\lambda^3 - 3700\,\lambda - 84\,000 = 0\). At \(\lambda = 70\) it is \(343\,000 - 259\,000 - 84\,000 = 0\), at \(\lambda = -30\) it is \(-27\,000 + 111\,000 - 84\,000 = 0\) and at \(\lambda = -40\) it is \(-64\,000 + 148\,000 - 84\,000 = 0\). The sum of the cubes is \(343\,000 - 27\,000 - 64\,000 = 252\,000 = 3\cdot 84\,000\) MPa³, as (2.116) says.

In the lectures the characteristic equation of the deviator is written in the form of (2.85), \(\lambda^3 - \sigma^D_{\mathrm{I}}\lambda^2 + \sigma^D_{\mathrm{II}}\lambda - \sigma^D_{\mathrm{III}} = 0\), and next to it stands \(\sigma^D_{\mathrm{II}} = J_2 = \tfrac13\,\sigma_{\mathrm{I}}^2 - \sigma_{\mathrm{II}}\). This equality has the wrong sign. The coefficient of \(\lambda\) in this equation is the coefficient \(K\) of step 2 of the proof, which is \(-J_2\), for the plate \(-3700\) MPa². With \(\sigma^D_{\mathrm{II}} = +3700\) MPa² the equation of the plate would be \(\lambda^3 + 3700\,\lambda - 84\,000 = 0\), which the principal value \(70\) MPa does not solve, since \(70^3 + 3700\cdot 70 - 84\,000 = 518\,000\). The number \(J_2\) is the same in the lectures and here, \(\tfrac13\,I_1^2 - I_2\), and it is never negative, so equation (2.113) has a minus in front of it. Symbols in the lectures: \(\sigma_{\mathrm{I}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{II}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{III}}\) are the stress invariants, here \(I_1\), \(I_2\) and \(I_3\), while the principal stresses are \(\sigma_{(1)}\), \(\sigma_{(2)}\) and \(\sigma_{(3)}\), here \(\sigma_1\), \(\sigma_2\) and \(\sigma_3\).

The invariants have different units, \(J_2\) MPa² and \(J_3\) MPa³, so we cannot compare them with each other or with the stress. A square root and a cube root bring them back to the units of stress.

Definition 2.104 Scaled deviatoric invariants (skalirani invarianti deviatorja)

Let \(\ten s\) be the deviator of the symmetric stress matrix \(\ten\sigma\) at a point \(P\). The scaled deviatoric invariants (skalirani invarianti deviatorja) are the numbers

\[\bar J_2 = \sqrt{\frac23\sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} s_{\mathrm{ij}}^2} , \qquad \bar J_3 = \sqrt[3]{\frac43\sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}}\sum_{\mathrm{m}} s_{\mathrm{ij}}\,s_{\mathrm{jm}}\,s_{\mathrm{mi}}} , \tag{2.117}\]
\[\bar J_2 = \Big(\frac23\,s_{\mathrm{ij}}\,s_{\mathrm{ij}}\Big)^{1/2} , \qquad \bar J_3 = \Big(\frac43\,s_{\mathrm{ij}}\,s_{\mathrm{jm}}\,s_{\mathrm{mi}}\Big)^{1/3} , \tag{2.117}\]

where the cube root of a number \(c\) is the real number whose third power is \(c\). By (2.105) and (2.116) \(\bar J_2 = \sqrt{4J_2/3}\) and \(\bar J_3 = \sqrt[3]{4J_3}\).

In the figure we first mark the number \(c\) on the vertical axis, then follow the horizontal dashed line to the curve of the third power and from there vertically to the \(x\) axis. The cube root stands there. For a negative number \(c\) the root is negative, since the third power of a negative number is negative.

Source: The definition is not from the project's sources. The relations with \(J_2\) and \(J_3\) follow from lemma 2.103.

Why the factors \(\tfrac23\) and \(\tfrac43\)? For the bar with the stress \(\sigma > 0\) the principal values of the deviator are \(2\sigma/3\), \(-\sigma/3\) and \(-\sigma/3\). The sum of the squares is \((4 + 1 + 1)\,\sigma^2/9 = 2\sigma^2/3\), so \(\bar J_2 = \sqrt{4\sigma^2/9} = 2\sigma/3\). The sum of the cubes is \((8 - 1 - 1)\,\sigma^3/27 = 2\sigma^3/9\), so \(\bar J_3 = \sqrt[3]{8\sigma^3/27} = 2\sigma/3\). With these factors both numbers equal the largest principal value of the deviator for the bar. For the plate \(\bar J_2 = \sqrt{4\cdot 3700/3} = 70{,}24\) MPa and \(\bar J_3 = \sqrt[3]{4\cdot 84\,000} = 69{,}52\) MPa, both close to \(s_1 = 70\) MPa. The number \(\bar J_2\) is two thirds of the number \(\sqrt{3J_2}\), which section 2.12.6 introduces as the von Mises equivalent stress, since \(\sqrt{4J_2/3} = \tfrac23\sqrt{3J_2}\).

2.12.5 Derivatives of the invariants with respect to the stress components

We compute the number \(J_2\) from the stress components. How fast does it change if we increase one component a little and leave the others alone? The answer is the derivative of \(J_2\) with respect to that component. Section 2.12.6 will compare \(J_2\) with the yield stress, and then the derivative says which stress component increases \(J_2\) fastest. Let us first see on the plate what such a derivative means (figure 2.304). Its components are \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = 90\) MPa, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = 30\) MPa and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}} = 40\) MPa, the others are zero.

On the left we vary only \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\), which is on the horizontal axis, with \(J_2\) on the vertical one. With \(I_1 = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + 30\) and \(I_2 = 30\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} - 1600\) the second expression in (2.106) gives

\[J_2 = \frac{(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + 30)^2}{3} - 30\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + 1600 = \frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}^2}{3} - 10\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + 1900 ,\]

which is a parabola. The plate is the point at \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = 90\) MPa with \(J_2 = 3700\) MPa². By lemma 1.82 the derivative of this function is \(2\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}/3 - 10\), so at \(90\) MPa it is \(50\) MPa. This is the slope of the tangent, and it is exactly the component \(s_{\mathrm{xx}}\) of the deviator. If we increase \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) by the step \(h = 10\) MPa, the tangent rises by \(s_{\mathrm{xx}}\,h = 500\) MPa², and the curve to \(J_2 = 4233{,}3\) MPa², by \(533{,}3\) MPa². For the step \(h = 1\) MPa the rise of the curve is \(50{,}33\) MPa² and of the tangent \(50\) MPa²: the smaller the step, the more exactly the derivative tells the change.

On the right we vary the shear. On the horizontal axis is the shear stress \(\tau = \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\), both components at once, because the symmetry of the stress ties them. By the first expression in (2.106) \(J_2 = \tfrac12\,(50^2 + 10^2 + 40^2) + \tau^2 = 2100 + \tau^2\), again a parabola, and the plate is the point at \(\tau = 40\) MPa. The tangent has the slope \(2\tau = 80\) MPa, twice \(s_{\mathrm{xy}}\). Over the step \(h = 10\) MPa it rises by \(800\) MPa², and the curve to \(4600\) MPa², by \(900\) MPa². Why twice \(s_{\mathrm{xy}}\)? The shear \(\tau\) stands in the matrix twice, as \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and as \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\). When we increase \(\tau\), we increase both components, and each contributes \(s_{\mathrm{xy}} = 40\) MPa. Before we write the derivative with components, we must therefore say whether we count \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\) as two variables or as one.

Let us look at the nine variables of the definition in a matrix (figure 2.305).

In the matrix are nine components, each one variable. The diagonal carries the three normal stresses, the six fields off it the shear stresses. We differentiate with respect to one, for example \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\), and hold the other eight fixed. At a symmetric stress the mirror fields across the diagonal are equal, but in the definition we count them as two variables.

Definition 2.105 Derivative with respect to a stress component (odvod po komponenti napetosti)

Let \(F\) be a function of the nine variables \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zy}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\), in which \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zy}}\), and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\) are different variables. The derivative \(\partial F/\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{kl}}\) with respect to the component \(\sigma_{\mathrm{kl}}\) is the partial derivative with respect to this variable: we hold the other eight fixed and differentiate \(F\) as a function of the one variable \(\sigma_{\mathrm{kl}}\) by definition 1.9, just as in definition 1.26 for three variables. We take the value of the derivative at a symmetric stress matrix, where \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zy}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\).

The invariants of the deviator are here the functions of nine variables

\[J_2 = \frac12\sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} s_{\mathrm{ij}}^2 , \qquad J_3 = \frac13\sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}}\sum_{\mathrm{m}} s_{\mathrm{ij}}\,s_{\mathrm{jm}}\,s_{\mathrm{mi}} , \tag{2.118}\]
\[J_2 = \frac12\,s_{\mathrm{ij}}\,s_{\mathrm{ij}} , \qquad J_3 = \frac13\,s_{\mathrm{ij}}\,s_{\mathrm{jm}}\,s_{\mathrm{mi}} , \tag{2.118}\]

where \(s_{\mathrm{ij}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\) for different indices and \(s_{\mathrm{ii}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{ii}} - (\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}})/3\) on the diagonal. At a symmetric matrix these are, by (2.105) and (2.116), the numbers \(J_2\) and \(J_3 = \det\ten s\).

Source: The convention is not from the project's sources.

The convention separates \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\), although for a symmetric stress we cannot change each of them by itself. The consequence is that the derivative with respect to \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) tells half of what a change of the shear brings, and the derivative with respect to \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\) the other half. For \(J_2\) of the plate each of them will be \(s_{\mathrm{xy}} = 40\) MPa, and the slope of the right tangent is their sum, \(80\) MPa. The way the function is written is part of the convention. If we wrote \(J_2\) with six variables, as in the first expression of (2.106), where the shear appears once, as \(s_{\mathrm{xy}}^2\), the derivative with respect to \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) would give \(2s_{\mathrm{xy}} = 80\) MPa, twice as much. Both computations are correct, but they answer different questions, so with every derivative with respect to a stress component we say which form we differentiate.

Let us first look at the derivatives the lemma needs on matrices (figure 2.306). At the place \(ij\) of each matrix stands the derivative of one component with respect to a chosen one, in the two left matrices with respect to \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\), in the right one with respect to \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\).

In the left matrix is the derivative of a stress component: the one stands only at the place of the chosen component, everywhere else are zeros, because the other variables are constant. In the middle one is the derivative of a component of the deviator, which has the mean stress subtracted on the diagonal: with respect to the same diagonal component it grows at the rate \(\tfrac23\), with respect to the other two it falls at the rate \(\tfrac13\), the derivative is \(-\tfrac13\). In the right one is the derivative with respect to a shear component: the one is again only at the chosen place, because the mean stress does not contain a shear component.

For \(J_3\) we need the matrix \(\ten s\,\ten s\) and its diagonal (figure 2.307, the numbers of the plate).

The matrix \(\ten s\,\ten s\) has \(4100\), \(1700\) and \(1600\) MPa² on the diagonal, and the sum is \(7400 = 2J_2\). From the diagonal we subtract \(\tfrac23 J_2 = 2466{,}7\) MPa², and we get the difference, which has \(1633{,}3\), \(-766{,}7\) and \(-866{,}7\) MPa² on the diagonal, whose sum is zero. An off-diagonal entry, for example \(1600\) MPa² at the place \(xy\), does not change.

Lemma 2.106 Derivatives of the deviatoric invariants with respect to the stress components (odvodi invariant deviatorja po komponentah napetosti)

Let \(\ten\sigma\) be a symmetric stress matrix at a point \(P\), \(\ten s\) its deviator, and let the derivatives be the derivatives with respect to the stress components of definition 2.105. The indices \(i\), \(j\), \(k\), \(l\) and \(m\) run over \(x\), \(y\), \(z\). The derivative of a stress component with respect to a stress component, the left matrix, is, in the second line with the Kronecker delta of definition 2.58,

\[\frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}}{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{kl}}} = \begin{cases} 1 , & \ix{i} = \ix{k} \ \text{and}\ \ix{j} = \ix{l} , \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} , \end{cases} \tag{2.119}\]
\[\frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}}{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{kl}}} = \delta_{\mathrm{ik}}\,\delta_{\mathrm{jl}} , \tag{2.119}\]

the derivative of a component of the deviator, the middle matrix, is

\[\frac{\partial s_{\mathrm{ij}}}{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{kl}}} = \begin{cases} \frac23 , & \ix{i} = \ix{j} = \ix{k} = \ix{l} , \\ -\frac13 , & \ix{i} = \ix{j} , \ \ix{k} = \ix{l} , \ \ix{i} \ne \ix{k} , \\ 1 , & \ix{i} \ne \ix{j} , \ \ix{i} = \ix{k} , \ \ix{j} = \ix{l} , \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} , \end{cases} \tag{2.120}\]
\[\frac{\partial s_{\mathrm{ij}}}{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{kl}}} = \delta_{\mathrm{ik}}\,\delta_{\mathrm{jl}} - \frac13\,\delta_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\delta_{\mathrm{kl}} , \tag{2.120}\]

and the derivatives of the invariants, the deviator matrix and the difference matrix, are

\[\frac{\partial J_2}{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{kl}}} = s_{\mathrm{kl}} , \qquad \frac{\partial J_3}{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{kl}}} = \Big(\ten s\,\ten s - \frac23\,J_2\,\mat I\Big)_{\mathrm{kl}} . \tag{2.121}\]
\[\frac{\partial J_2}{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{kl}}} = s_{\mathrm{kl}} , \qquad \frac{\partial J_3}{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{kl}}} = s_{\mathrm{km}}\,s_{\mathrm{ml}} - \frac23\,J_2\,\delta_{\mathrm{kl}} . \tag{2.121}\]

The matrix of the derivatives of \(J_2\) is the deviator itself. The matrix of the derivatives of \(J_3\) is \(\ten s\,\ten s - \tfrac23 J_2\,\mat I\), a symmetric matrix whose diagonal entries add up to zero.

Proof

We must show four formulas. We get the first two with the rules of differentiation of lemma 1.82, because the components of the deviator are sums of multiples of the variables. We get the other two with the product rule. The variable with respect to which we differentiate is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{kl}}\) throughout, the other eight are constant.

  1. The component \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\) is one of the nine variables. If it is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{kl}}\) itself, we differentiate the function that assigns to a number the same number, and the derivative is \(1\) (item 4 of lemma 1.82). Otherwise \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\) is one of the constant eight and the derivative is \(0\). This is (2.119).
  2. The mean stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{m}} = (\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}})/3\) contains \(\sigma_{\mathrm{kl}}\) only when \(k = l\), and then in one of the three terms. By step 1 and items 1 and 2 of the same lemma \(\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{m}}/\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{kl}} = \tfrac13\) for \(k = l\) and \(0\) otherwise.
  3. Off the diagonal \(s_{\mathrm{ij}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\), so step 1 holds: the derivative is \(1\) when the two pairs of indices are equal, and \(0\) otherwise. On the diagonal \(s_{\mathrm{ii}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{ii}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\), and steps 1 and 2 give \(1 - \tfrac13 = \tfrac23\) for the derivative with respect to the same diagonal component, \(0 - \tfrac13 = -\tfrac13\) for the derivative with respect to another diagonal component and \(0\) for the derivative with respect to an off-diagonal component. This is (2.120). In the left panel, where \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) grows, \(s_{\mathrm{xx}}\) therefore grows at the rate \(\tfrac23\), while \(s_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and \(s_{\mathrm{zz}}\) fall at the rate \(\tfrac13\).
  4. The derivative of \(J_2\). By the product rule the derivative of the square \(s_{\mathrm{ij}}^2 = s_{\mathrm{ij}}\,s_{\mathrm{ij}}\) equals \(2\,s_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\partial s_{\mathrm{ij}}/\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{kl}}\). Half the sum over all nine terms is
    \[\frac{\partial J_2}{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{kl}}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} s_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\frac{\partial s_{\mathrm{ij}}}{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{kl}}} .\]
  5. For the derivative with respect to a diagonal component, for example \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\), by step 3 only three derivatives differ from zero, and the sum is \(\tfrac23 s_{\mathrm{xx}} - \tfrac13 s_{\mathrm{yy}} - \tfrac13 s_{\mathrm{zz}} = s_{\mathrm{xx}} - \tfrac13\,(s_{\mathrm{xx}} + s_{\mathrm{yy}} + s_{\mathrm{zz}}) = s_{\mathrm{xx}}\), because the diagonal of the deviator adds up to zero (item 1 of lemma 2.99). For the plate this is the slope \(50\) MPa. Likewise for \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\).
  6. For the derivative with respect to an off-diagonal component, for example \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\), a single derivative differs from zero, \(\partial s_{\mathrm{xy}}/\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 1\), and the sum is \(s_{\mathrm{xy}}\). The derivative with respect to \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\) is likewise \(s_{\mathrm{yx}}\), and the sum of the two is the slope \(2s_{\mathrm{xy}}\) of the right panel. With step 5 this is the first formula in (2.121).
  1. The derivative of \(J_3\). The product rule, applied twice, gives for a product of three functions \((fgh)' = f'gh + fg'h + fgh'\). Write \(D_{\mathrm{ij}} = \partial s_{\mathrm{ij}}/\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{kl}}\). The term \(s_{\mathrm{ij}}s_{\mathrm{jm}}s_{\mathrm{mi}}\) is a closed path from \(i\) to \(j\), from \(j\) to \(m\) and back to \(i\), each factor one arrow. Its derivative is \(D_{\mathrm{ij}}\,s_{\mathrm{jm}}s_{\mathrm{mi}} + s_{\mathrm{ij}}\,D_{\mathrm{jm}}\,s_{\mathrm{mi}} + s_{\mathrm{ij}}s_{\mathrm{jm}}\,D_{\mathrm{mi}}\), and each of the three terms has the derivative on its own arrow. When we add over all \(i\), \(j\) and \(m\), the three sums are equal. We get the second from the first by renaming the indices in a cycle, \(j\) to \(i\), \(m\) to \(j\) and \(i\) to \(m\). Then the triangle turns by a third of a full turn and the derivative moves to the first arrow. The sum does not change, because all three indices run over the same values \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\). We get the third sum with two such turns. In the first sum the arrows from \(j\) via \(m\) to \(i\) give the sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{m}} s_{\mathrm{jm}}\,s_{\mathrm{mi}}\), which is the entry \(ji\) of the matrix \(\ten s\,\ten s\). A third of the sum is therefore equal to
    \[\frac{\partial J_3}{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{kl}}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} D_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\Big(\sum_{\mathrm{m}} s_{\mathrm{jm}}\,s_{\mathrm{mi}}\Big) = \sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} D_{\mathrm{ij}}\,(\ten s\,\ten s)_{\mathrm{ji}} .\]
  2. By (2.120) \(D_{\mathrm{ij}}\) is a sum of two parts. The first is \(1\) for \(i = k\), \(j = l\) and \(0\) otherwise, so it picks the term \((\ten s\,\ten s)_{\mathrm{lk}}\) from the sum. The second is \(-\tfrac13\) when \(i = j\) and \(k = l\), and \(0\) otherwise, so for \(k = l\) it contributes \(-\tfrac13\) of the sum of the diagonal entries of the matrix \(\ten s\,\ten s\), and for \(k \ne l\) nothing. Take the values at a symmetric matrix. There \((\ten s\,\ten s)_{\mathrm{lk}} = (\ten s\,\ten s)_{\mathrm{kl}}\), and the sum of the diagonal entries of the matrix \(\ten s\,\ten s\) is \(2J_2\) by (2.116). This gives the difference on the right, the second formula in (2.121).
  3. The sum of the diagonal entries of the matrix \(\ten s\,\ten s - \tfrac23 J_2\,\mat I\) is \(2J_2 - 3\cdot\tfrac23 J_2 = 0\). The matrix is symmetric, because \(\ten s\,\ten s\) (item 3 of lemma 1.102) and \(\mat I\) are symmetric.

Source: The proof is not from the sources.

The lemma says how the stress components move \(J_2\): the matrix of the derivatives is the matrix of the deviator itself. For the plate the largest of the nine derivatives is the one with respect to \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(50\) MPa. The shear, however, can only be increased in both components at once, and then \(J_2\) grows at the rate \(2\cdot 40 = 80\) MPa, like the right tangent, faster still than with \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\). With \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\), on the other hand, \(J_2\) falls at the rate \(40\) MPa, the derivative is \(-40\) MPa: if we increase \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\) from \(0\) to \(1\) MPa, \(J_2\) decreases from \(3700\) to \(3660{,}33\) MPa². The sum of the three diagonal derivatives is \(50 - 10 - 40 = 0\). So if we increase all three normal components by the same step, \(J_2\) does not change, and indeed at \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = 91\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = 31\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = 1\) MPa again \(J_2 = 3700\) MPa². This is a third view of the fact that the spherical part does not count in \(J_2\): on the line of the principal stresses all three points move by the same amount.

For \(J_3\) of the plate we compute the matrix \(\ten s\,\ten s\) and the matrix of the derivatives

\[\ten s\,\ten s = \begin{pmatrix} 4100 & 1600 & 0 \\ 1600 & 1700 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1600 \end{pmatrix}\ \text{MPa}^2 , \qquad \ten s\,\ten s - \frac23\,J_2\,\mat I = \begin{pmatrix} 1633{,}3 & 1600 & 0 \\ 1600 & -766{,}7 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -866{,}7 \end{pmatrix}\ \text{MPa}^2 ,\]

since \(\tfrac23\cdot 3700 = 2466{,}7\) MPa². The diagonal of the right matrix has the sum \(1633{,}3 - 766{,}7 - 866{,}7 = 0\) up to rounding.

That the entry \(xx\) of this matrix is really a slope we test as for \(J_2\) in figure 2.304 (figure 2.309).

On the horizontal axis is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\), on the vertical one \(J_3\). We hold the other components, so \(\sigma_{\mathrm{m}} = (\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + 30)/3\), the deviator has \(s_{\mathrm{xy}} = 40\) MPa and on the diagonal \(s_{\mathrm{xx}} = (2\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} - 30)/3\), \(s_{\mathrm{yy}} = (60 - \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}})/3\) and \(s_{\mathrm{zz}} = -(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + 30)/3\). The row and the column \(z\) have zeros off the diagonal, so

\[J_3 = \det\ten s = s_{\mathrm{zz}}\,\big(s_{\mathrm{xx}}\,s_{\mathrm{yy}} - 40^2\big) = \frac{2\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}^3}{27} - \frac{10\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}^2}{3} + \frac{1300\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}}{3} + 18\,000 ,\]

which is the cubic curve. The plate is the point at \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = 90\) MPa with \(J_3 = 84\,000\) MPa³. The tangent has the slope \(1633{,}3\) MPa², the entry \(xx\) of the matrix of the derivatives. If we increase \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) by the step \(h = 20\) MPa, the tangent rises by \(32\,667\) MPa³, and the curve to \(J_3 = 123\,926\) MPa³, by \(39\,926\) MPa³. For the step \(0{,}1\) MPa \(J_3\) increases from \(84\,000\) to \(84\,163{,}5\) MPa³, and the derivative predicts \(1633{,}3\cdot 0{,}1 = 163{,}3\) MPa³, the difference is only \(0{,}2\) MPa³.

A root does not have a derivative everywhere. Take a bar with the stress \(\sigma\), where \(\bar J_2 = \tfrac23\,|\sigma|\) (figure 2.310).

The axes are \(\sigma\) horizontally and \(\bar J_2\) vertically, and \(\bar J_2\) cannot be negative. The curve is the letter V. The left arm has the slope \(-\tfrac23\), the right one the slope \(\tfrac23\), and at the tip at \(\sigma = 0\) the slopes do not agree, so there is no derivative there.

Derivatives of the scaled invariants. What remains are the derivatives of the numbers \(\bar J_2\) and \(\bar J_3\) of definition 2.104. We do not differentiate the roots directly. We use equalities in which there are no roots, and the move we used for the strain without roots: we write the difference of the squares of two lengths as a rectangle whose one side is the difference of the lengths and the other their sum.

  1. By definition \(\bar J_2\cdot\bar J_2 = \tfrac43 J_2\) and \(\bar J_3\cdot\bar J_3\cdot\bar J_3 = 4J_3\).
  2. Let \(J_2 > 0\). We increase the component \(\sigma_{\mathrm{kl}}\) by \(h \ne 0\) and hold the other eight. We call the value of \(\bar J_2\) before the step \(a\), after it \(b\), and the difference quotient of \(J_2\) over this step \(q\). By (2.121) \(q\) approaches \(s_{\mathrm{kl}}\) as \(h\) goes to \(0\). By step 1 the difference of the squares is \(b^2 - a^2 = \tfrac43\,q\,h\), and as a rectangle it equals \((b - a)(b + a)\). In the figure \(a\) is the length \(L_0\) and \(b\) the length \(L_1\). Since \(a > 0\) and \(b \ge 0\), we have \(a + b \ge a > 0\), so we may divide by \(h\,(a + b)\):
    \[\frac{b - a}{h} = \frac{4\,q}{3\,(a + b)} .\]
    The difference quotient of \(\bar J_2\) has no root any more.
  3. First we show that \(b\) approaches \(a\). From step 2 \(|b - a|\,(a + b) = \tfrac43\,|q\,h|\), and since \(a + b \ge a\), we get \(|b - a| \le \tfrac{4}{3a}\,|q\,h|\). The number \(q\,h\) is the change of \(J_2\) over the step. It goes to \(0\), because \(J_2\) is a differentiable and therefore continuous function of the component \(\sigma_{\mathrm{kl}}\) (lemma 1.80). So \(b - a\) goes to \(0\) as well, and the sum \(a + b\) approaches \(2a\).
  4. Now the quotient. We bring its difference from the number \(2s_{\mathrm{kl}}/(3a)\) to a common denominator:
    \[\frac{4\,q}{3\,(a + b)} - \frac{2\,s_{\mathrm{kl}}}{3a} = \frac{4a\,(q - s_{\mathrm{kl}}) + 2s_{\mathrm{kl}}\,(a - b)}{3a\,(a + b)} .\]
    By the triangle inequality (lemma 1.6) and since \(a + b\) is at least \(a\), the absolute value of this difference is at most
    \[\frac{4}{3a}\,|q - s_{\mathrm{kl}}| + \frac{2\,|s_{\mathrm{kl}}|}{3a^2}\,|b - a| .\]
    Both terms go to \(0\), the first by (2.121), the second by step 3, so by lemma 2.25 their sum does too. A band that brings this sum below a given error brings the difference below it as well, so by the definition of the limit 1.5 the quotient approaches \(2s_{\mathrm{kl}}/(3a)\):
    \[\frac{\partial\bar J_2}{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{kl}}} = \frac{2\,s_{\mathrm{kl}}}{3\,\bar J_2} . \tag{2.122}\]
  5. For \(\bar J_3\) let \(J_3 \ne 0\), let \(a\) and \(b\) be the values of \(\bar J_3\) before and after the step, \(q_3\) the difference quotient of \(J_3\) and \(t = \big(\ten s\,\ten s - \tfrac23 J_2\,\mat I\big)_{\mathrm{kl}}\), which \(q_3\) approaches by (2.121). Instead of the difference of squares we take the difference of cubes, \(b^3 - a^3 = (b - a)(b^2 + ab + a^2)\), which by step 1 equals \(4\,q_3\,h\). The factor \(b^2 + ab + a^2 = (b + a/2)^2 + \tfrac34\,a^2\) is at least \(\tfrac34\,a^2 > 0\). So \((b - a)/h = 4\,q_3/(b^2 + ab + a^2)\), and as in step 3 \(|b - a| \le \tfrac{16}{3a^2}\,|q_3\,h|\), which goes to \(0\). The difference from the number \(4t/(3a^2)\) is
    \[\frac{4\,q_3}{b^2 + ab + a^2} - \frac{4t}{3a^2} = \frac{4\,\big(3a^2\,(q_3 - t) + t\,(a - b)(2a + b)\big)}{3a^2\,(b^2 + ab + a^2)} .\]
    The denominator is at least \(\tfrac94\,a^4\). The numerator goes to \(0\), because \(q_3 - t\) and \(a - b\) go to \(0\), while \(|2a + b|\) stays below \(3|a| + 1\) once \(|b - a| < 1\). As in step 4 therefore
    \[\frac{\partial\bar J_3}{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{kl}}} = \frac{4}{3\,\bar J_3^2}\,\Big(\ten s\,\ten s - \frac23\,J_2\,\mat I\Big)_{\mathrm{kl}} . \tag{2.123}\]
  6. The conditions \(J_2 > 0\) and \(J_3 \ne 0\) entered in steps 2 and 5, where we divided by \(a + b\) and by \(b^2 + ab + a^2\). Where \(J_2 = 0\), the deviator is zero. A step \(h\) in one component there gives \(\bar J_2 = \tfrac23\,|h|\) for a normal and \(\sqrt{2/3}\,|h|\) for a shear component, so there is no derivative. For the bar \(\bar J_2 = \tfrac23\,|\sigma|\), and this function has a kink at \(\sigma = 0\), with the slope \(-\tfrac23\) on the left and \(\tfrac23\) on the right. Where \(J_3 = 0\), formula (2.123) divides by zero. The derivative of \(\bar J_3\) sometimes exists there: for the bar \(J_3 = 2\sigma^3/27\) and \(\bar J_3 = \tfrac23\,\sigma\), a straight line with the slope \(\tfrac23\) also at \(\sigma = 0\). For pure shear with \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}} = \tau = 40\) MPa, however, \(J_3 = 0\). A step \(h\) in \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\) gives \(J_3 = 2h^3/27 - \tfrac23\,\tau^2 h\). The quotient \(\bar J_3/h\) is \(-75{,}3\) at \(h = 0{,}1\) MPa, \(-1622\) at \(0{,}001\) MPa and \(-34\,943\) at \(0{,}00001\) MPa. Its absolute value grows beyond all bounds, so there is no derivative. The graph of the cube root is vertical at zero, because the curve of the third power is horizontal there.

For the plate \(\partial\bar J_2/\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{kl}} = 2s_{\mathrm{kl}}/(3\cdot 70{,}24) = s_{\mathrm{kl}}/105{,}36\), these are the components of the matrix of the deviator divided by \(105{,}36\) MPa, and \(\partial\bar J_3/\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{kl}}\) is the matrix of the derivatives of \(J_3\) multiplied by \(4/(3\cdot 69{,}52^2) = 1/3624{,}8\) MPa⁻²:

\[\frac{\partial\bar J_2}{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{kl}}} : \begin{pmatrix} 0{,}475 & 0{,}380 & 0 \\ 0{,}380 & -0{,}095 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -0{,}380 \end{pmatrix} , \qquad \frac{\partial\bar J_3}{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{kl}}} : \begin{pmatrix} 0{,}451 & 0{,}441 & 0 \\ 0{,}441 & -0{,}212 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -0{,}239 \end{pmatrix} .\]

A test of the quotient of step 2 on the plate: for \(h = 10\) MPa in \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) we have \(a = 70{,}24\) MPa and \(b = 75{,}13\) MPa. The rectangle has the sides \(b - a = 4{,}89\) MPa and \(a + b = 145{,}37\) MPa, and its area \(711{,}1\) MPa² is \(\tfrac43\) of the change of \(J_2\) by \(533{,}3\) MPa². The quotient \((b - a)/h\) is \(0{,}489\), for \(h = 1\) MPa \(0{,}476\) and for \(h = 0{,}1\) MPa \(0{,}4747\), ever closer to \(0{,}4746\), which is rounded to \(0{,}475\) above. The derivatives have no units, because \(\bar J_2\) and \(\bar J_3\) have the units of stress. For the bar with \(\sigma > 0\) (2.122) gives for the derivative with respect to \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) the number \(2\cdot\tfrac23\sigma/(3\cdot\tfrac23\sigma) = \tfrac23\), which agrees with \(\bar J_2 = \tfrac23\sigma\).

2.12.6 The von Mises equivalent stress

In section 2.2 we defined the yield stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}\) with a bar in tension and said that we would treat yielding under loading in several directions later. Now we have the tools at least for the question how to compare the stress at a point with the number \(\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}\). We are looking for one number, computed from the stress at the point, that for a bar in tension equals the stress \(\sigma\) in the cross section. Experiments with metals tell two things (BOWER §3.7.3, PDF p. 146). First, equal pressure from all sides alone does not cause yielding. So we assume that added equal pressure does not change it either, and the number should depend only on the deviator. The assumption holds for metals. It does not hold for soils, where the yield criterion depends on the pressure in addition to the shear stress (BOWER, PDF p. 181). Its effect on the result is that added pressure does not change the number, and pressure alone, however large, gives the number zero (example 4 below). Second, most metals, which are made of many small crystals, behave the same in all directions, so the number should depend only on the sizes of the principal stresses, not on their directions, that is, it should be the same in all coordinate systems. For a metal made of a single crystal this assumption does not hold, since such a crystal yields differently in different directions (BOWER, PDF p. 36). Its effect on the result is that the number does not tell directions in the body apart: the same three numbers give the same number however the principal directions are turned. Both requirements are met by \(J_2\), which depends only on the deviator and by lemma 2.100 is the same in all rectangular Cartesian coordinate systems. But they are also met by the largest shear stress \((\sigma_1 - \sigma_3)/2\) of theorem 2.93. It depends only on the principal stresses, and it does not change when we add the same number to all three. So the requirements do not determine the number, and two yield criteria rest on them, which we write down below (BOWER, PDF p. 146).

On the stress axis the principal stresses are at the top, \(\sigma_1 = 110\), \(\sigma_2 = 10\) and \(\sigma_3 = 0\) MPa. Between them are three differences: \(100\), \(10\) and \(110\) MPa. The largest is \(\sigma_1 - \sigma_3\), and its half is the largest shear stress. At the bottom are the same points, shifted by \(-30\) MPa, because we added an equal pressure of \(30\) MPa. The differences are the same as at the top.

From history

The largest shear stress as a measure is older. Coulomb already thought that failure is triggered by shear (section 1.1, TIMO, PDF p. 226). Tresca studied by experiment how metals flow under great pressure. This was then an entirely new field (TIMO, PDF p. 205 and 206). The experiments encouraged Saint-Venant to be the first to write the fundamental equations of plasticity, that is of permanent change of shape, and to apply them in several practical problems (TIMO, PDF p. 205 and 206). From Tresca's experiments he deduced that the difference between the largest and the smallest principal stress is constant (TP2B, PDF p. 320). By theorem 2.93 this difference is twice the largest shear stress, so this means that the largest shear stress at yielding is everywhere the same. LOVE describes this view as a measure of the tendency to rupture (LOVE, PDF p. 140).

The condition with \(J_2\) was proposed in 1904 by M. T. Huber and independently of him in 1913 by R. von Mises (TIMO, PDF p. 308).

The number that we compare with the yield stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}\) is built from \(J_2\). \(J_2\) measures the size of the deviator: it is half the sum of the squares of its components, just as the square of the length of a vector is the sum of the squares of its components. Why precisely this measure is also the right one physically is shown by the work that the material stores when it changes shape (section 3.6.6).

Let the axes be the principal directions, and on them the components of the deviator \(s_{\mathrm{i}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{i}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\), for the plate with \(\sigma_{\mathrm{m}} = 40\) MPa so \(70\), \(-30\) and \(-40\) MPa. The vector with these components has the length \(\sqrt{s_1^2 + s_2^2 + s_3^2} = \sqrt{2J_2} = 86{,}0\) MPa. The number \(\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}} = \sqrt{3J_2}\), which we define below, is this length multiplied by \(\sqrt{3/2} = 1{,}2247\): \(\sqrt{3/2}\cdot\sqrt{2J_2} = \sqrt{3J_2} = \sqrt{11\,100} = 105{,}4\) MPa.

For a bar in tension the principal stresses are \(\sigma\), \(0\) and \(0\), and by (2.106) \(J_2 = (\sigma^2 + 0 + \sigma^2)/6 = \sigma^2/3\). To get \(\sigma\) we must multiply \(J_2\) by \(3\) and take the square root: \(\sqrt{3 \cdot \sigma^2/3} = |\sigma|\), which in tension, where \(\sigma > 0\), equals \(\sigma\), as the bar's column shows.

Definition 2.107 Von Mises equivalent stress (von Misesova primerjalna napetost)

The von Mises equivalent stress (von Misesova primerjalna napetost) at a point \(P\) is the number

\[\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}} = \sqrt{3 J_2} , \tag{2.124}\]

where \(J_2\) is the second invariant of the deviator of the stress at \(P\).

Source: SADD (3.5.5) (PDF p. 73), BOWER §2.2.7 (PDF p. 75), where \(\sigma_{\mathrm{e}} = \sqrt{\tfrac32\sigma'_{\mathrm{ij}}\sigma'_{\mathrm{ij}}}\).

By lemma 2.100, with the differences between the principal stresses,

\[\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}} = \sqrt{\tfrac12\Big((\sigma_1 - \sigma_2)^2 + (\sigma_2 - \sigma_3)^2 + (\sigma_3 - \sigma_1)^2\Big)} ,\]

and in this form SADD and BOWER write it (SADD, PDF p. 73, BOWER, PDF p. 75). The name equivalent stress says what it is for: it is one number, computed from all the components of the stress at the point, that we compare with the yield stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}\) of the tension test. BOWER describes it as a uniaxial equivalent of a stress in several directions: if a material fails in a tension test at the stress \(\sigma_{\text{crit}}\), it also fails under loading in several directions when \(\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}} = \sigma_{\text{crit}}\) (BOWER, PDF p. 75). The von Mises yield criterion (von Misesov pogoj tečenja) says that the material starts to yield when \(\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}\) (BOWER §3.7.3, PDF p. 145). The Tresca criterion of section 2.4, in turn, compares the largest shear stress with the largest shear stress in a bar in tension at the yield stress, which by theorem 2.93 is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}/2\). By this criterion the material starts to yield when \(\sigma_1 - \sigma_3 = \sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}\) (BOWER, PDF p. 146). So the difference \(\sigma_1 - \sigma_3\) is an equivalent stress too: one number that for a bar in tension equals \(\sigma\) and that we compare with \(\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}\).

Definition 2.108 Tresca equivalent stress (Trescova primerjalna napetost)

Let \(\sigma_1 \ge \sigma_2 \ge \sigma_3\) be the principal stresses at the point \(P\). The Tresca equivalent stress (Trescova primerjalna napetost) at \(P\) is the number

\[\sigma_{\mathrm{T}} = \sigma_1 - \sigma_3 = 2\,\tau_{\max} , \tag{2.125}\]

where \(\tau_{\max}\) is the largest shear stress at \(P\) of theorem 2.93. The Tresca yield criterion (Trescov pogoj tečenja) says that the material starts to yield when \(\sigma_{\mathrm{T}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}\).

Source: BOWER §3.7.3 (PDF p. 146). COOK (3.12-3) (PDF p. 131), where this number is called the stress intensity and written \(S_{\mathrm{I}}\).

For a bar in tension both equivalent stresses equal \(\sigma\), since we calibrated them so: \(\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}}\) by the computation before definition 2.107, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{T}} = \sigma - 0\) from the principal stresses \(\sigma\), \(0\) and \(0\). For other stresses they differ, but never by much: lemma 2.113 below shows that \(\sigma_{\mathrm{T}}\) always lies between \(\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}}\) and \(1{,}155\,\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}}\). BOWER says that tests agree somewhat better with the von Mises criterion than with Tresca's, but that the difference in the fit is very small (BOWER, PDF p. 146).

In this chapter we state the two criteria and the surface in the space of stresses that they define (section 2.12.7). How the material flows on once it reaches the criterion, and how its yield stress changes meanwhile, is described by the flow rule and the hardening law of the theory of plasticity (BOWER §3.7.5 and §3.7.6, PDF pp. 147-153). We do not treat these two here yet.

Let us compute the von Mises stress for our examples, for steel with the yield stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}} = 220\) MPa.

Each example has two bars above the axis in the figure, a blue one for \(\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}}\) and one with a blackwhite outline for \(\sigma_{\mathrm{T}} = \sigma_1 - \sigma_3\). The dashed line is the yield stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}} = 220\) MPa.

  1. The bar with diameter 10 mm under the force 10 kN: the principal stresses are \(127{,}3\) MPa, \(0\) and \(0\), and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}} = \sqrt{\tfrac12\,(127{,}3^2 + 0 + 127{,}3^2)}\), which is \(127{,}3\) MPa. This is how it must be, since we calibrated the number that way. Also \(\sigma_1 - \sigma_3 = 127{,}3\) MPa. Both criteria say that the bar does not yield, since \(127{,}3 < 220\): both bars stay below the line.
  2. Pure shear with \(\tau_0 = 50\) MPa: the principal stresses are \(50\), \(0\) and \(-50\) MPa, and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}} = \sqrt{\tfrac12\,(50^2 + 50^2 + 100^2)} = \sqrt{3}\cdot 50\), which is \(86{,}6\) MPa, while \(\sigma_1 - \sigma_3 = 100\) MPa. In pure shear, steel would start to yield at \(\tau_0 = 220/\sqrt3 = 127{,}0\) MPa by von Mises and at \(\tau_0 = 220/2 = 110\) MPa by Tresca. Here the two criteria differ by about 15 %.
  3. The thin plate: \(\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}} = \sqrt{3 \cdot 3700} = \sqrt{11\,100}\), which is \(105{,}4\) MPa, and \(\sigma_1 - \sigma_3 = 110\) MPa. The criteria differ by about 4 %, and by both the plate does not yield.
  4. The fluid at rest: the deviator is the zero matrix, so \(\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}} = 0\) for every pressure \(p\). All three principal stresses are \(-p\), so also \(\sigma_1 - \sigma_3 = 0\).

The von Mises stress also has a geometric meaning, which SADD gives (SADD, PDF p. 73). In principal axes take the faces whose normals have all three components equal in absolute value.

Definition 2.109 Octahedral plane (oktaedrska ploskev)

Let \(\vek e_1\), \(\vek e_2\) and \(\vek e_3\) be the unit vectors of the principal directions of the stress at a point \(P\). An octahedral plane (oktaedrska ploskev) through \(P\) is a flat face with unit normal

\[\vek n = \frac{\pm\vek e_1 \pm \vek e_2 \pm \vek e_3}{\sqrt3} ,\]

for any choice of signs. The normal and the shear stress on it are called the octahedral normal stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{oct}}\) and the octahedral shear stress \(\tau_{\mathrm{oct}}\) (oktaedrska normalna in strižna napetost).

Source: SADD §3.5 (PDF p. 73).

The normal is a unit vector, since the sum of the squares of its components is \(\tfrac13 + \tfrac13 + \tfrac13 = 1\). The eight choices of signs give eight normals. If we measure equal distances from \(P\) along the principal axes to both sides and join the six points obtained, we get a solid with eight triangular faces, an octahedron (oktaeder), and its faces have exactly these eight normals (figure 2.314). Hence the name.

The edges of the octahedron join the six vertices on the principal axes, which continue outward as \(\vek e_1\), \(\vek e_2\) and \(\vek e_3\). The blue face has the normal \(\vek n\) \((\vek e_1 + \vek e_2 + \vek e_3)/\sqrt3\). On the right is the same face seen from the side. The traction vector \(\vek t\) on it has a part along the normal, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{oct}}\), and a part in the face, \(\tau_{\mathrm{oct}}\), which the next lemma computes.

Let us compute two more things in figure 2.314. First, the normal makes the same angle with each of the three principal directions. Its cosine is the scalar product of unit vectors, \(\vek n\cdot\vek e_3 = 1/\sqrt3\), and the same with \(\vek e_1\) and \(\vek e_2\), so the angle is \(\arccos(1/\sqrt3) = 54{,}74^\circ\). The face is therefore equally inclined to all three principal directions. Second, the stress vector \(\vek t\) on the blue face is, by Cauchy's formula (2.54), \(\vek t = \ten\sigma\,\vek n\). In the principal axes the matrix \(\ten\sigma\) is diagonal, with the principal stresses on the diagonal (corollary 2.85), so it only multiplies each component \(1/\sqrt3\) of the normal by its principal stress:

\[\vek t = \frac{1}{\sqrt3}\,(\sigma_1,\ \sigma_2,\ \sigma_3) . \tag{2.126}\]

For the thin plate with the principal stresses \(110\), \(10\) and \(0\) MPa this is \((63{,}51,\ 5{,}77,\ 0)\) MPa, a vector of length \(63{,}77\) MPa.

Lemma 2.110 Stresses on the octahedral plane (napetosti na oktaedrski ploskvi)

On every octahedral plane through the point \(P\) the normal stress and the shear stress have the values

\[\sigma_{\mathrm{oct}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{m}} , \qquad \tau_{\mathrm{oct}} = \sqrt{\tfrac23\,J_2} = \frac{\sqrt2}{3}\,\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}} . \tag{2.127}\]

With the principal stresses and with the invariants \(I_1\) and \(I_2\),

\[\tau_{\mathrm{oct}} = \frac13\sqrt{(\sigma_1 - \sigma_2)^2 + (\sigma_2 - \sigma_3)^2 + (\sigma_3 - \sigma_1)^2} = \frac{\sqrt2}{3}\sqrt{I_1^2 - 3 I_2} . \tag{2.128}\]
Proof

We show it in two ways. The first uses the expressions with weights of section 2.12.1 and the deviator, the second only the stress vector (2.126) and the two invariants.

First way.

Let us draw the first way for the thin plate. On the number line are its principal stresses \(0\), \(10\) and \(110\) MPa. Above each stands an equal blue weight \(\tfrac13\), because all three components of the octahedral normal have the same absolute value. The triangle is the point where the line with these weights balances, at \(40\) MPa. The grey distances from it to the principal stresses are \(70\), \(-30\) and \(-40\) MPa. At the bottom left their squares are stacked into a column \(4900 + 900 + 1600 = 7400\) MPa². Next to it stands a column a third as high, \(2466{,}7\) MPa², and a column one and a half times as high as the sum, \(11\,100\) MPa². At the bottom right are the square roots of these three columns as lengths to scale: \(49{,}67\) MPa, \(86{,}02\) MPa and \(105{,}4\) MPa. The longest is \(2{,}121\) times the shortest.

  1. All three components of the normal are \(\pm 1/\sqrt3\), so all the weights are \(w_{\mathrm{i}} = n_{\mathrm{i}}^2 = \tfrac13\).
  2. By (2.91) the normal stress is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{oct}} = \tfrac13\,(\sigma_1 + \sigma_2 + \sigma_3)\), the balance point of three equal weights. By (2.90) the sum of the principal stresses is \(I_1\), so \(\sigma_{\mathrm{oct}} = I_1/3 = \sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\).
  3. By (2.92), for the shear stress, \(\tau_{\mathrm{oct}}^2 = \tfrac13\big((\sigma_1 - \sigma_{\mathrm{m}})^2 + (\sigma_2 - \sigma_{\mathrm{m}})^2 + (\sigma_3 - \sigma_{\mathrm{m}})^2\big)\), the average of the squares of the grey distances.
  4. By item 3 of lemma 2.99 the differences \(\sigma_{\mathrm{i}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\) are the principal values \(s_{\mathrm{i}}\) of the deviator. In principal axes the deviator is diagonal, with \(s_1\), \(s_2\) and \(s_3\) on the diagonal, so by (2.105) \(J_2 = \tfrac12\,(s_1^2 + s_2^2 + s_3^2)\), and by lemma 2.100 the value of \(J_2\) in principal axes is the same as in all others. The sum \(s_1^2 + s_2^2 + s_3^2\) is the square of the length of the deviator vector, for the plate the column \(70^2 + 30^2 + 40^2 = 7400\) MPa², so \(J_2 = 3700\) MPa².
  5. From steps 3 and 4, \(\tau_{\mathrm{oct}}^2 = \tfrac13 \cdot 2J_2 = \tfrac23\,J_2\), a third of the column of step 4.
  6. By (2.124) \(J_2 = \sigma_{\mathrm{vM}}^2/3\), so the column \(\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}}^2 = 3J_2\) is one and a half times the column \(2J_2\), and the column \(\tau_{\mathrm{oct}}^2 = \tfrac23\,J_2\) is \(\tfrac29\) of the column \(\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}}^2\). Taking the root: \(\tau_{\mathrm{oct}} = \sqrt{\tfrac29\,\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}}^2} = \tfrac{\sqrt2}{3}\,\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}}\), for the plate \(49{,}67\) and \(105{,}4\) MPa.
  7. By lemma 2.100, (2.106), we have two expressions for \(J_2\):
    \[J_2 = \tfrac16\big((\sigma_1 - \sigma_2)^2 + (\sigma_2 - \sigma_3)^2 + (\sigma_3 - \sigma_1)^2\big) , \qquad J_2 = I_1^2/3 - I_2 .\]
    We put the first into step 5:
    \[\tau_{\mathrm{oct}}^2 = \tfrac23\,J_2 = \tfrac19\big((\sigma_1 - \sigma_2)^2 + (\sigma_2 - \sigma_3)^2 + (\sigma_3 - \sigma_1)^2\big) .\]
    The second gives the same with the invariants:
    \[\tau_{\mathrm{oct}}^2 = \tfrac23\,\Big(\frac{I_1^2}{3} - I_2\Big) = \tfrac29\,(I_1^2 - 3 I_2) .\]
    Taking the root gives (2.128).

Second way.

  1. The stress vector on the octahedral plane is, by (2.126), \(\vek t = (\sigma_1, \sigma_2, \sigma_3)/\sqrt3\), and for the other choices of signs in the normal its components have other signs. The square of its length is in all cases \(|\vek t|^2 = \tfrac13\,(\sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2 + \sigma_3^2)\).
  2. The normal part is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{oct}} = \vek t\cdot\vek n = \tfrac13\,(\sigma_1 + \sigma_2 + \sigma_3) = I_1/3\), since the signs in \(\vek t\) and in \(\vek n\) agree in every component.
  3. The normal and the shear part are perpendicular (lemma 2.14 on splitting a vector), so by Pythagoras' theorem \(\tau_{\mathrm{oct}}^2 = |\vek t|^2 - \sigma_{\mathrm{oct}}^2\).
  4. We expand the square of the sum:
    \[(\sigma_1 + \sigma_2 + \sigma_3)^2 = \sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2 + \sigma_3^2 + 2\,(\sigma_1\sigma_2 + \sigma_2\sigma_3 + \sigma_3\sigma_1) .\]
    By (2.90) this is
    \[I_1^2 = \sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2 + \sigma_3^2 + 2 I_2 ,\]
    hence
    \[\sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2 + \sigma_3^2 = I_1^2 - 2 I_2 .\]
  5. We put this into step 3:
    \[\tau_{\mathrm{oct}}^2 = \tfrac13\,(I_1^2 - 2I_2) - \tfrac19\,I_1^2 .\]
    We collect the terms:
    \[\tau_{\mathrm{oct}}^2 = \tfrac29\,I_1^2 - \tfrac23\,I_2 = \tfrac29\,(I_1^2 - 3 I_2) .\]
  6. By lemma 2.88 the invariants \(I_1\) and \(I_2\) are the same in all rectangular Cartesian coordinate systems. So the expression of step 5 may be computed from the stress components in any axes, by (2.87), without finding the principal stresses.

Source: SADD (3.5.4) (PDF p. 73), where \(\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}} = \tfrac{3}{\sqrt2}\,\tau_{\mathrm{oct}}\) is also written. The proof is not from the sources.

On the octahedral planes the normal stress is the mean stress, and the shear stress is proportional to the von Mises stress. The von Mises stress is therefore, up to the factor \(3/\sqrt2 = 2{,}121\), the shear stress on the faces that are equally inclined to all three principal directions. For the thin plate the octahedral normal is \((\vek e_1 + \vek e_2 + \vek e_3)/\sqrt3 = (0{,}2582,\ 0{,}7746,\ 0{,}5774)\) in the axes \(x\), \(y\), \(z\), and the lemma gives \(\sigma_{\mathrm{oct}} = 40\) MPa and \(\tau_{\mathrm{oct}} = \sqrt{\tfrac23 \cdot 3700}\), which is \(49{,}67\) MPa. We got the same two numbers with NumPy directly from Cauchy's formula for this normal. The second way of the proof gives the same without the principal directions. From the components of the plate \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = 90\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = 30\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 40\) MPa, (2.87) gives \(I_1 = 90 + 30 + 0 = 120\) MPa and \(I_2 = 90 \cdot 30 - 40^2 = 1100\) MPa², so \(\tau_{\mathrm{oct}} = \tfrac{\sqrt2}{3}\sqrt{120^2 - 3 \cdot 1100} = \tfrac{\sqrt2}{3}\sqrt{11\,100}\), which is again \(49{,}67\) MPa. Pythagoras' theorem of step 3 works out too: \(40^2 + \tfrac23 \cdot 3700 = 4066{,}7\), and by step 1 the square of the length of the vector \(\vek t\) is just as much, \(\tfrac13\,(110^2 + 10^2 + 0^2) = 4066{,}7\), which is \(63{,}77^2\).

2.12.7 The yield surface

The two yield criteria have the same form: from the stress at a point we compute one number and compare it with the yield stress. Let us write both with one function and draw which stresses the material carries elastically.

Definition 2.111 Yield function and yield surface (funkcija tečenja in ploskev tečenja)

The yield function (funkcija tečenja) of a material is a function \(f\) that assigns one number to the stress at a point, that is to the six numbers \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}\), such that the material at the point responds elastically when \(f < 0\) and yields when \(f = 0\). The equation \(f = 0\) is the yield criterion (pogoj tečenja), and the set of all stresses that satisfy it is the yield surface (ploskev tečenja). For the von Mises criterion \(f = \sigma_{\mathrm{vM}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}\), for Tresca's \(f = \sigma_{\mathrm{T}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}\). For a material that hardens, \(f\) also depends on the plastic strain so far (through \(\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}\)). The surface that holds before the material has yielded for the first time is the initial yield surface (začetna ploskev tečenja).

Source: BOWER §3.7.3 and §3.7.4 (PDF pp. 145-146).

Why a surface? Six numbers cannot be drawn. For an isotropic material, though, three are enough. Such a material has no preferred directions, so the yield function must not depend on where the principal directions point, only on the values of the principal stresses with their signs (BOWER, PDF p. 146): \(f(\sigma_1, \sigma_2, \sigma_3)\). Three numbers are a point in a space in which we plot the principal stresses on three perpendicular axes (figure 2.317). Every point of this space is one stress at a point of the body, without the information on directions. One equation between three coordinates leaves a surface, just as the equation \(x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 1\) between the coordinates of a point leaves the surface of a ball. Inside the surface \(f < 0\) and the material is elastic, on it the material yields. The stress cannot lie outside it (BOWER, PDF p. 146).

A function of the three principal stresses can also be written with the invariants. The principal stresses are the zeros of the characteristic polynomial \(-\lambda^3 + I_1\lambda^2 - I_2\lambda + I_3\) (lemma 2.86), so the invariants \(I_1\), \(I_2\) and \(I_3\) determine them, though not their order. Since the material has no preferred directions, it does not matter which principal stress we call the first, so \(f\) does not change when the principal stresses are swapped, and it is a function \(f(I_1, I_2, I_3)\). Instead of \(I_2\) and \(I_3\) we may take the invariants of the deviator \(J_2\) and \(J_3\). Indeed, by (2.106) \(I_2 = I_1^2/3 - J_2\). The deviator is \(\ten\sigma - \sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\mat I\), so \(J_3 = \det(\ten\sigma - \sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\mat I)\) is the value of the characteristic polynomial at \(\lambda = \sigma_{\mathrm{m}} = I_1/3\), that is \(J_3 = -I_1^3/27 + I_1^3/9 - I_1 I_2/3 + I_3\), and from this we get \(I_3\). The form \(f(I_1, J_2, J_3)\) is handy because it separates the two experiments of the start of the section. Equal pressure from all sides changes only \(I_1\), so a criterion that such pressure does not change does not contain \(I_1\): what remains is \(f(J_2, J_3)\). The von Mises criterion is the simplest of these, since it contains only \(J_2\):

\[J_2 = k^2 , \qquad k = \frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}}{\sqrt3} . \tag{2.129}\]

This is the same criterion as \(\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}\), because by (2.124) \(\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}}^2 = 3J_2\). The number \(k\) is the yield stress in pure shear. In pure shear with \(\tau_0\) the principal stresses are \(\tau_0\), \(0\) and \(-\tau_0\), so \(J_2 = (\tau_0^2 + \tau_0^2 + 4\tau_0^2)/6 = \tau_0^2\), and the material yields when \(\tau_0 = k\). For our steel \(k = 220/\sqrt3 = 127{,}0\) MPa. The Tresca criterion gives in pure shear \(\sigma_{\mathrm{T}} = 2\tau_0 = \sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}\), that is \(\tau_0 = 110\) MPa. The Tresca stress is therefore not a function of \(J_2\) alone: a bar at the yield stress has \(J_2 = \sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}^2/3\), while pure shear at the Tresca limit has \(J_2 = \sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}^2/4\), although \(\sigma_{\mathrm{T}}\) is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}\) both times.

The yield stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}\) need not stay constant. Experiments show that a metal that was deformed plastically, unloaded and loaded again starts to yield only at a larger stress. This is called strain hardening (utrjevanje) (BOWER §3.7.5, PDF p. 147). On the left of figure 2.316 is such a test with a bar of our steel, with the stress vertical and the strain horizontal. We pull the bar beyond the yield stress \(220\) MPa up to the stress \(260\) MPa, which we chose. Then we unload it: the point of the graph goes along a line parallel to the first one, and at zero stress the bar is permanently longer (BOWER, PDF p. 142). When we load it again, the point goes up along the same line, and the graph bends again only near \(260\) MPa, the largest stress before unloading (BOWER, PDF p. 142). The yield stress has grown by \(40\) MPa. So the yield surface changes with plastic deformation. In the simplest model it grows and keeps its shape (BOWER, PDF p. 147). On the right is the surface seen along the line \(\sigma_1 = \sigma_2 = \sigma_3\), as we shall meet it on the right of figure 2.317: before hardening and after it the circle and the hexagon have the same shape, only \(260/220 = 1{,}18\) times larger. Here we draw only the initial yield surface of definition 2.111, the cylinder and the prism.

We build the figure part by part. On the axes are the principal stresses, here not ordered by size, so that the figure is symmetric. The points with three equal coordinates, \(\sigma_1 = \sigma_2 = \sigma_3\), lie on a line through the origin. These are stresses without shear, as in a fluid at rest (example 4), so the line is called the hydrostatic axis (hidrostatska os). We reach any stress \(S\) from the origin by going first along the axis by \(\xi\) and then perpendicular to it by \(\rho\). What these two distances are is said by a lemma.

Lemma 2.112 Distance of a stress state from the hydrostatic axis (razdalja napetosti od hidrostatske osi)

Let \(\sigma_1\), \(\sigma_2\) and \(\sigma_3\) be the principal stresses at the point \(P\), in any order, \(I_1\) their sum, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{m}} = I_1/3\) the mean stress and \(J_2\) the second invariant of the deviator. In the space with the perpendicular axes \(\sigma_1\), \(\sigma_2\), \(\sigma_3\) the point \((\sigma_1, \sigma_2, \sigma_3)\) has:

  1. its perpendicular projection onto the hydrostatic axis at the point \((\sigma_{\mathrm{m}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{m}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{m}})\), which is at the distance \(\xi = |I_1|/\sqrt3\) from the origin,
  2. the distance from the hydrostatic axis
    \[\rho = \sqrt{2 J_2} = \sqrt{\tfrac23}\,\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}} . \tag{2.130}\]

The stresses with \(\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}\) are therefore exactly the points on the lateral surface of the cylinder of radius \(\sqrt{2/3}\,\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}\) about the hydrostatic axis.

Proof

We split the vector \((\sigma_1, \sigma_2, \sigma_3)\) into a part along the axis and a perpendicular part, by lemma 2.14 on splitting a vector.

  1. The unit vector of the hydrostatic axis is \(\vek a = (1, 1, 1)/\sqrt3\), since all three of its components are equal and its length is \(\sqrt{3 \cdot \tfrac13} = 1\).
  2. The part along the axis is, by lemma 2.14, the scalar product with \(\vek a\) times \(\vek a\). The scalar product is \((\sigma_1 + \sigma_2 + \sigma_3)/\sqrt3 = I_1/\sqrt3\), and the part along the axis is \(\tfrac{I_1}{\sqrt3}\,\vek a = \tfrac{I_1}{3}\,(1, 1, 1) = (\sigma_{\mathrm{m}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{m}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{m}})\). Its length is \(|I_1|/\sqrt3\).
  3. The perpendicular part is the difference \((\sigma_1 - \sigma_{\mathrm{m}},\ \sigma_2 - \sigma_{\mathrm{m}},\ \sigma_3 - \sigma_{\mathrm{m}})\). By point 3 of lemma 2.99 these are the principal values of the deviator \(s_1\), \(s_2\) and \(s_3\).
  4. The square of its length is \(s_1^2 + s_2^2 + s_3^2\). In the principal axes the deviator is diagonal, so by (2.105) \(J_2 = \tfrac12\,(s_1^2 + s_2^2 + s_3^2)\), as in step 4 of the proof of lemma 2.110. Hence \(\rho^2 = 2J_2\).
  5. By (2.124) \(J_2 = \sigma_{\mathrm{vM}}^2/3\), so \(\rho = \sqrt{\tfrac23}\,\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}}\).
  6. By step 5 the criterion \(\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}\) is the same as \(\rho = \sqrt{2/3}\,\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}\). The points at a given distance from a line are the lateral surface of a cylinder about it.

Source: The cylinder about the line \(\sigma_1 = \sigma_2 = \sigma_3\) and the view along the axis: BOWER §3.7.4 (PDF pp. 146-147, figures 3.30 and 3.31). The proof is not from the sources.

The lemma says that the split of the stress into the spherical and the deviatoric part is, in this space, an ordinary perpendicular split: \(\xi\) measures the spherical part, \(\rho\) the size of the deviator. For the steel the radius of the cylinder is \(\sqrt{2/3} \cdot 220\) MPa, which is \(179{,}6\) MPa. The cylinder is unbounded along the axis, and in this we see the assumption of the start of the section: if we add the same number to all three principal stresses, the point moves parallel to the axis, \(\rho\) does not change, and the material is no closer to yielding. For soils, where the assumption does not hold, the surface is not a cylinder.

The Tresca criterion gives a six-sided prism in the same space. The difference of the largest and the smallest principal stress is one of the six differences \(\pm(\sigma_1 - \sigma_2)\), \(\pm(\sigma_2 - \sigma_3)\), \(\pm(\sigma_3 - \sigma_1)\), so the surface \(\sigma_{\mathrm{T}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}\) consists of parts of six planes, for example \(\sigma_1 - \sigma_3 = \sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}\). The differences do not change either if we add the same number to all three stresses, so each of the six planes is parallel to the axis.

Since both surfaces are the same everywhere along the axis, one cross section is enough. The plane through the origin perpendicular to the axis has the equation \(\sigma_1 + \sigma_2 + \sigma_3 = 0\) and contains the stresses without a spherical part. In the figure we mark it \(\pi\). It cuts the cylinder in a circle and the prism in a hexagon. On the right we look along the axis, so that we see the plane \(\pi\) from the front: the three axes show at angles of \(120^\circ\), the cylinder as a circle of radius \(179{,}6\) MPa, the prism as a regular hexagon. The hexagon is regular, because the criterion does not change when the principal stresses are swapped or all three change sign. That it lies inside the circle and touches it only at the vertices is said by lemma 2.113 below. One is uniaxial tension along the first principal axis, with the principal stresses \(220\), \(0\) and \(0\) MPa, where the two criteria are equal because we calibrated both on the tension test. The other five vertices are tension in the other two principal directions and compression in all three. In the middle of the sides the criteria are farthest apart. On the ray of pure shear, with the principal stresses \(\tau_0\), \(0\) and \(-\tau_0\), the lemma gives \(\rho = \sqrt{2J_2} = \sqrt2\,\tau_0\). The Tresca criterion is met at \(\tau_0 = 110\) MPa, which is \(155{,}6\) MPa from the axis, the von Mises criterion at \(\tau_0 = 127{,}0\) MPa, which is \(179{,}6\) MPa from the axis.

Our four examples all lie inside both surfaces. By (2.130) the bar is \(\sqrt{2/3} \cdot 127{,}3 = 104{,}0\) MPa from the axis, pure shear with \(50\) MPa \(\sqrt2 \cdot 50 = 70{,}7\) MPa, the thin plate \(\sqrt{2 \cdot 3700} = 86{,}0\) MPa, and the fluid at rest lies on the axis, at any pressure.

The numbers \(\xi\) and \(\rho\), together with the angle about the axis, are cylindrical coordinates of a point in the space of principal stresses. In the lectures they are called the Haigh-Westergaard coordinates.

We have now met the same number \(J_2\) in several roles, and each says what the von Mises criterion means:

View Quantity With \(J_2\) At the yield stress of the steel
distance from the hydrostatic axis \(\rho\) \(\sqrt{2J_2}\) \(179{,}6\) MPa
shear stress on the octahedral plane \(\tau_{\mathrm{oct}}\) \(\sqrt{2J_2/3}\) \(103{,}7\) MPa
shear stress in pure shear \(k\) \(\sqrt{J_2}\) \(127{,}0\) MPa
equivalent stress, calibrated on tension \(\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}}\) \(\sqrt{3J_2}\) \(220\) MPa

The first view is geometric, the distance \(\rho\). The second is the shear on the face that is equally inclined to all principal directions, \(\tau_{\mathrm{oct}}\) of lemma 2.110. One more view comes with energy: in section 3.6.6 we shall see that the work per unit volume that an elastic isotropic material stores by changing its shape is proportional to \(J_2\). By the von Mises criterion the material therefore yields when this energy reaches the value it has in a bar in tension at the yield stress. TIMO therefore calls the criterion the maximum distortion energy theory (teorija največje energije spremembe oblike) (TIMO, PDF p. 308).

2.12.8 The yield criteria in plane stress

On a free surface of a body one principal stress is zero: the stress vector on a face lying in the surface is zero, so the normal of the surface is a principal direction with the principal stress \(0\). In a thin plate loaded only in its own plane this holds on both faces of the plate, and since the plate is thin, we assume that it holds through the whole thickness (assumption 2 in section 2.8.7, which also says when it does not hold). So it was in our thin plate, where the faces perpendicular to the axis \(z\) are not loaded. Such a state is called plane stress (ravninsko napetostno stanje). Two principal stresses remain, which we denote \(\sigma_{\mathrm{a}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{b}}\), with no agreement on which is larger. Every stress is now a point in the plane with the axes \(\sigma_{\mathrm{a}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{b}}\), and the yield criteria are two curves in it (figure 2.318).

We compute the curves from the two definitions with the principal stresses \(\sigma_{\mathrm{a}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{b}}\) and \(0\).

  1. Von Mises. By the form with differences below definition 2.107, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}}^2 = \tfrac12\big((\sigma_{\mathrm{a}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{b}})^2 + \sigma_{\mathrm{b}}^2 + \sigma_{\mathrm{a}}^2\big) = \sigma_{\mathrm{a}}^2 - \sigma_{\mathrm{a}}\sigma_{\mathrm{b}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{b}}^2\). The yield criterion is
    \[\sigma_{\mathrm{a}}^2 - \sigma_{\mathrm{a}}\sigma_{\mathrm{b}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{b}}^2 = \sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}^2 . \tag{2.131}\]
    This is an ellipse. Indeed, the left side is the sum of squares \((\sigma_{\mathrm{a}} - \tfrac12\sigma_{\mathrm{b}})^2 + \tfrac34\,\sigma_{\mathrm{b}}^2\), so on the curve \(|\sigma_{\mathrm{b}}| \le 2\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}/\sqrt3\), and likewise \(|\sigma_{\mathrm{a}}| \le 2\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}/\sqrt3\). A curve of second degree that does not go off to infinity is an ellipse. The equation does not change when \(\sigma_{\mathrm{a}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{b}}\) are swapped, so its axes are the lines \(\sigma_{\mathrm{b}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{a}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{b}} = -\sigma_{\mathrm{a}}\). On the line \(\sigma_{\mathrm{b}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{a}}\) the equation gives \(\sigma_{\mathrm{a}}^2 = \sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}^2\), on the line \(\sigma_{\mathrm{b}} = -\sigma_{\mathrm{a}}\) it gives \(3\sigma_{\mathrm{a}}^2 = \sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}^2\). The ellipse is therefore \(\sqrt3\) times longer along the first line than along the second.
  2. Tresca. The equivalent stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{T}}\) is the difference of the largest and the smallest of the numbers \(\sigma_{\mathrm{a}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{b}}\) and \(0\). When \(\sigma_{\mathrm{a}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{b}}\) are both positive, the smallest number is \(0\), and the criterion is that the larger of the two equals \(\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}\): these are the vertical and the horizontal side of the hexagon at the top right. When they have opposite signs, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{T}} = |\sigma_{\mathrm{a}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{b}}|\), and the criterion \(\sigma_{\mathrm{a}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{b}} = \pm\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}\) gives the two oblique sides. When both are negative, the largest number is \(0\), and we get the two sides at the bottom left.

Where do the curves agree and where not?

  • In uniaxial stress, at the point \((220, 0)\), they agree, because both equivalent stresses are calibrated on the tension test.
  • In equal biaxial stress, at the point \((220, 220)\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}} = \sqrt{220^2 - 220 \cdot 220 + 220^2} = 220\) MPa and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{T}} = 220 - 0 = 220\) MPa. The cause is that a stress with the principal values \(\sigma\), \(\sigma\) and \(0\) is the sum of equal tension \(\sigma\) from all sides and uniaxial compression \(-\sigma\) in the third direction. Equal tension from all sides changes neither number, what remains is uniaxial compression, for which both equal \(\sigma\).
  • In pure shear, on the line \(\sigma_{\mathrm{b}} = -\sigma_{\mathrm{a}}\), the ratio is largest: the Tresca criterion is met at the point \((110, -110)\), the von Mises criterion at the point \(\sigma_{\mathrm{a}} = 127{,}0\) MPa, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{b}} = -127{,}0\) MPa. The ratio is \(127{,}0/110 = 2/\sqrt3 = 1{,}155\). The curves have the same ratio at the middle of the vertical and horizontal sides of the hexagon, on the lines \(\sigma_{\mathrm{a}} = 2\sigma_{\mathrm{b}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{b}} = 2\sigma_{\mathrm{a}}\): there the Tresca criterion is met at \((220, 110)\) and the von Mises criterion at \(\sigma_{\mathrm{a}} = 254{,}0\) MPa and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{b}} = 127{,}0\) MPa. There too the middle principal stress is halfway between the extreme ones (\(220\), \(110\), \(0\)), and the stress is pure shear of \(110\) MPa with an equal tension of \(110\) MPa added from all sides.

The hexagon lies wholly in the ellipse and touches it at its six vertices. That this is no accident of this figure, and that the ratio is nowhere larger than in pure shear, is said by a lemma. Before we state it, let us see on the thin plate what the ratio depends on (figure 2.319).

On the number line are \(\sigma_3 = 0\) and \(\sigma_1 = 110\) MPa, with \(\sigma_2 = 10\) MPa between them. Both equivalent stresses depend only on the differences of the principal stresses, so we write them with the distances of neighbours, \(a = 100\) and \(b = 10\) MPa. The Tresca stress is their sum, \(110\) MPa. Now imagine that we hold \(\sigma_3\) and \(\sigma_1\) fixed and move \(\sigma_2\) from \(\sigma_3\) to \(\sigma_1\). The Tresca stress does not change, so its square, \(12\,100\) MPa², is a horizontal line in the graph below. The square of the von Mises stress changes, it is the blue parabola. At both ends, where \(\sigma_2\) coincides with \(\sigma_3\) or with \(\sigma_1\), the parabola touches the line. It is lowest in the middle, at \(\sigma_2 = 55\) MPa, and there it is three quarters of \(12\,100\), that is \(9075\) MPa². The plate is the point at \(\sigma_2 = 10\) MPa, with \(\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}}^2 = 11\,100\) MPa², \(1000\) MPa² below the line and \(2025\) MPa² above the lowest value. The lemma says that this is so for every stress, and the proof says what these two differences are.

Lemma 2.113 Comparison of the Tresca and von Mises stresses (primerjava Trescove in von Misesove napetosti)

Let \(\sigma_1 \ge \sigma_2 \ge \sigma_3\) be the principal stresses at the point \(P\). Then

\[\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}} \le \sigma_{\mathrm{T}} \le \frac{2}{\sqrt3}\,\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}} . \tag{2.132}\]

The left equality holds exactly when two principal stresses are equal, the right one exactly when \(\sigma_2\) is midway between \(\sigma_1\) and \(\sigma_3\).

Proof

We express both numbers with the differences of neighbouring principal stresses, \(a = \sigma_1 - \sigma_2 \ge 0\) and \(b = \sigma_2 - \sigma_3 \ge 0\).

  1. By (2.125) \(\sigma_{\mathrm{T}} = \sigma_1 - \sigma_3 = a + b\).
  2. By the form with differences below definition 2.107, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}}^2\) \(= \tfrac12\big(a^2 + b^2 + (a + b)^2\big) = a^2 + ab + b^2\).
  3. The difference of the squares, the distance of the parabola below the blackwhite line, is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{T}}^2 - \sigma_{\mathrm{vM}}^2 = (a + b)^2 - (a^2 + ab + b^2) = ab \ge 0\). It is zero exactly when \(a = 0\) or \(b = 0\), that is when two principal stresses are equal, at the ends.
