Since both numbers are nonnegative, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{T}}^2 \ge \sigma_{\mathrm{vM}}^2\) gives \(\sigma_{\mathrm{T}} \ge \sigma_{\mathrm{vM}}\).
  4. For the second inequality we compute the distance of the parabola above the dashed line, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}}^2 - \tfrac34\,\sigma_{\mathrm{T}}^2 = a^2 + ab + b^2 - \tfrac34\,(a^2 + 2ab + b^2) = \tfrac14\,(a - b)^2 \ge 0\). It is zero exactly when \(a = b\), that is when \(\sigma_2\) is midway. From \(\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}}^2 \ge \tfrac34\,\sigma_{\mathrm{T}}^2\) follows \(\sigma_{\mathrm{T}} \le \tfrac{2}{\sqrt3}\,\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}}\).

Source: The proof is not from the sources. That the difference between the criteria is small is said by BOWER (PDF p. 146).

The lemma says that the Tresca stress is never smaller than the von Mises stress and exceeds it by at most \(2/\sqrt3 - 1 = 15{,}5\,\%\). By the Tresca criterion the material therefore yields earlier or at the same time, never later: the hexagon is inscribed in the ellipse. Our examples confirm it. The bar is at the point with \(\sigma_{\mathrm{a}} = 127{,}3\) MPa and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{b}} = 0\), with two equal principal stresses, and both numbers are \(127{,}3\) MPa. Pure shear is at the point \((50, -50)\), with \(\sigma_2 = 0\) midway, and the ratio is \(100/86{,}6 = 1{,}155\). The thin plate is at the point \((110, 10)\), and the ratio \(110/105{,}4 = 1{,}04\) is in between. All three points are inside the hexagon, so the steel yields by neither criterion.

Before we use the criteria, let us collect what they assume, why, when it holds and what it does to the result.

  • The material yields before it breaks, and so it has a yield stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}\). Such materials are called ductile (žilavi), and they are mostly metals. SADD says that it is for them that inelastic yielding is described by such stresses (SADD, PDF p. 73). When it does not hold: for brittle materials such as sandstone not even Mohr's theory, of which the maximum shear criterion is a special case, agrees with the tests (TIMO, PDF p. 308).
  • The material is isotropic, so the criterion contains only the principal stresses and not the directions (BOWER, PDF p. 146). Effect: the same curve in figure 2.318 holds however the principal directions are turned relative to the body.
  • Equal pressure from all sides does not cause yielding (BOWER, PDF p. 146). Effect: both yield surfaces are unbounded along the hydrostatic axis. For soils this does not hold (start of section 2.12.6).
  • The choice between the criteria changes the computed limit by at most \(15{,}5\,\%\) (lemma 2.113), in pure shear from \(110\) to \(127{,}0\) MPa.

Where is each one used? The von Mises stress agrees somewhat better with tests (BOWER, PDF p. 146) and is computed straight from the components, without the principal stresses. Finite element programs usually plot just this stress, because one number tells how near to yielding the point is, whichever stress component dominates there (SADD, PDF p. 73, COOK, PDF p. 131). The Tresca criterion consists of straight lines only, so it sometimes simplifies a calculation by hand (BOWER, PDF p. 146), and by lemma 2.113 it is on the safe side relative to von Mises.

Example: tension with torsion. Our bar of diameter 10 mm under the force 10 kN, in which \(\sigma = 127{,}3\) MPa, is in addition twisted about its axis, so that the shear stress on its surface is \(\tau = 60\) MPa. How the shear stress is computed from the moment, and why it is largest at the surface, comes in chapter 16, here we take it as given. On the surface of the bar we imagine a small square with sides along the bar, in the direction \(x\), and around the circumference, in the direction \(y\) (figure 2.320). On its sides perpendicular to the axis of the bar acts the normal stress \(\sigma\), and on all four the shear stress \(\tau\). The surface of the bar carries no load, so the components with the index of the direction normal to the surface are zero, and this is plane stress. The bar is not stressed around its circumference, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0\) (chapter 16), so only \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}} = \tau\) remain.

  1. Only \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \tau\) are different from zero. The mean stress is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{m}} = \sigma/3\), so the deviator has the components \(s_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma - \sigma/3 = 2\sigma/3\), \(s_{\mathrm{yy}} = s_{\mathrm{zz}} = -\sigma/3\) and \(s_{\mathrm{xy}} = \tau\).
  2. By the first line of (2.106) \(J_2 = \tfrac12\big(\tfrac49\sigma^2 + \tfrac19\sigma^2 + \tfrac19\sigma^2\big) + \tau^2 = \tfrac13\,\sigma^2 + \tau^2\).
  3. By (2.124) \(\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}} = \sqrt{3J_2} = \sqrt{\sigma^2 + 3\tau^2}\), and the von Mises criterion is
    \[\sigma^2 + 3\tau^2 = \sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}^2 . \tag{2.133}\]
  4. For the Tresca criterion we need the principal stresses. One is \(0\), in the direction perpendicular to the surface. The other two are the eigenvalues of the matrix with the first row \(\sigma\), \(\tau\) and the second \(\tau\), \(0\), that is the zeros of the equation \((\sigma - \lambda)(0 - \lambda) - \tau^2 = \lambda^2 - \sigma\lambda - \tau^2 = 0\), in figure 2.321 the intersections of Mohr's circle with the horizontal axis:
    \[\lambda = \frac{\sigma}{2} \pm \frac12\sqrt{\sigma^2 + 4\tau^2} .\]
  5. For \(\tau \ne 0\) the root is larger than \(|\sigma|\), so one zero is positive and the other negative: the circle encloses the origin. In order they are \(\sigma_1 = \tfrac{\sigma}{2} + \tfrac12\sqrt{\sigma^2 + 4\tau^2}\), \(\sigma_2 = 0\) and \(\sigma_3 = \tfrac{\sigma}{2} - \tfrac12\sqrt{\sigma^2 + 4\tau^2}\). By (2.125) \(\sigma_{\mathrm{T}} = \sigma_1 - \sigma_3 = \sqrt{\sigma^2 + 4\tau^2}\), the diameter of the circle, and the Tresca criterion is \(\sigma^2 + 4\tau^2 = \sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}^2\).

We see steps 4 and 5 on Mohr's circle (lemma 2.95), which figure 2.321 shows for our bar. The lemma holds, because the components with the index of the direction normal to the surface are zero. On the axes are the normal and the shear stress on the faces perpendicular to the surface. The cross section, the face with the normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), is the point with \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = 127{,}3\) MPa and \(\tau_{\mathrm{nd}} = 60\) MPa, the face with the normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) the point with \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = 0\) and \(\tau_{\mathrm{nd}} = -60\) MPa. The two points are at opposite ends of a diameter. The centre is at \(m = 127{,}3/2 = 63{,}65\) MPa, the radius is \(R = \sqrt{63{,}65^2 + 60^2} = 87{,}47\) MPa, which is \(\tfrac12\sqrt{\sigma^2 + 4\tau^2}\) of step 4. The circle cuts the horizontal axis at \(\sigma_1 = 63{,}65 + 87{,}47 = 151{,}1\) MPa and at \(\sigma_3 = 63{,}65 - 87{,}47 = -23{,}8\) MPa. The radius is larger than the distance of the centre from the origin, so the circle encloses the origin, and the third principal stress, \(\sigma_2 = 0\), lies between the two. This is the reason of step 5. The diameter of the circle is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{T}} = 2R = 174{,}9\) MPa.

In the plane with the axes \(\sigma\) and \(\tau\) both criteria are ellipses with the same semi-axis \(\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}} = 220\) MPa along the axis \(\sigma\), at the point of pure tension. Along the axis \(\tau\) the von Mises ellipse has the semi-axis \(\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}/\sqrt3 = 127{,}0\) MPa, the Tresca ellipse \(\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}/2 = 110\) MPa. These are the yield stresses in pure shear of section 2.12.7, and from them come the factors \(3\) and \(4\) at \(\tau^2\). For our bar \(J_2 = 127{,}3^2/3 + 60^2 = 9002\) MPa², so \(\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}} = \sqrt{127{,}3^2 + 3 \cdot 60^2} = 164{,}3\) MPa. The Tresca stress is the diameter of Mohr's circle, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{T}} = \sqrt{127{,}3^2 + 4 \cdot 60^2} = 174{,}9\) MPa. Both numbers are below \(220\) MPa: the point of the bar lies inside both ellipses. If we twist the bar harder at the same force, the point moves up along the vertical at \(127{,}3\) MPa. It reaches the Tresca ellipse at \(\tau = \sqrt{(220^2 - 127{,}3^2)/4} = 89{,}7\) MPa, the von Mises ellipse at \(\tau = \sqrt{(220^2 - 127{,}3^2)/3} = 103{,}6\) MPa.

We shall meet the same two components, the normal stress \(\sigma\) on the cross section and the shear stress \(\tau\), in a shaft that is twisted and at the same time pulled by an axial force (chapter 16) and in a beam that bends under a transverse force (chapter 5). Equation (2.133) holds at every point where only these two components are different from zero.

2.12.9 Spherical and deviatoric parts of strain

The strain at a point is described by the small strain tensor \(\ten\varepsilon\), a symmetric matrix with the components \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and so on (section 1.17). It too can be split into a part that is the same in all directions and a remainder. The meaning of the two parts is even more vivid here than for stress, since strain describes the shape of a piece of material.

Definition 2.114 Volumetric, spherical and deviatoric strain (prostorninska, sferična in deviatorna deformacija)

Let \(\ten\varepsilon\) be the small strain tensor at a point \(P\), written with components in a chosen rectangular Cartesian coordinate system. The volumetric strain (prostorninska deformacija) at \(P\), which measures the change of volume of the small piece around \(P\), is the number

\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} .\]

The spherical strain (sferični del deformacije) is the matrix \(\tfrac13\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\,\mat I\), and the deviatoric part of the strain or deviatoric strain (deviatorna deformacija) is the matrix

\[\ten e = \ten\varepsilon - \tfrac13\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\,\mat I , \tag{2.134}\]

with the components \(e_{\mathrm{xx}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}/3\), \(e_{\mathrm{yy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}/3\), \(e_{\mathrm{zz}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}/3\) and \(e_{\mathrm{ij}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) for different indices.

Source: SADD (2.5.1)-(2.5.3) (PDF p. 49), BOWER §2.1.9 (PDF p. 51).

The components \(e_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(e_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and the like have two indices and are not bold, so we do not confuse them with the unit vectors of the axes \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\). SADD calls the volumetric strain the cubical dilatation and writes it \(\vartheta\), and the deviatoric strain \(\hat e_{\mathrm{ij}}\) (SADD, PDF p. 49). In the lectures the volumetric strain is called the dilatation (dilatacija) and written \(e\). In this book \(\ten e\) is the deviatoric strain, so for the volumetric strain we stay with \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\). The next lemma says what the two parts mean.

Lemma 2.115 Meaning of the spherical and deviatoric strain (pomen sferičnega in deviatornega dela deformacije)

Let the small deformation assumption hold at the point \(P\) (section 1.17.3): all partial derivatives of the displacements are small in absolute value compared with \(1\), so the piece around \(P\) changes only a little. Then:

  1. If the strain at \(P\) equals its spherical part, every short fibre through \(P\), whatever its direction, has to first order the strain \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}/3\) (on the middle piece both edges lengthen by the same fraction), and the right angle between two short fibres in perpendicular directions changes only by terms that are products of two derivatives of the displacements.
  2. The deviatoric strain has zero volumetric strain: \(e_{\mathrm{xx}} + e_{\mathrm{yy}} + e_{\mathrm{zz}} = 0\). In the figure the lengthening along the rod is balanced by the thinning in the transverse directions.
  3. If after loading we simplify a small piece around \(P\) to the parallelepiped spanned by the vectors of its edges multiplied by the deformation gradient \(\mat F\) at \(P\) (section 2.10.5), the relative change of its volume (the orange piece against the blackwhite cube) differs from \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\) by at most \(6g^2 + 6g^3\), where \(g\) is the largest absolute value of the partial derivatives of the displacements at \(P\).
Proof

We use the strain of a fibre (1.61) and the change of volume of lemma 2.77. The first we apply to the edges of the middle piece, the second to the orange piece.

1. The spherical part.

  1. The matrix \(\tfrac13\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\,\mat I\) has \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}/3\) on the diagonal and zeros elsewhere. On the middle piece this diagonal means equal lengthenings along \(x\) and across, and the zeros outside it mean no shear.
  2. By (1.61) a fibre in the direction of the unit vector \(\vek n\) has the strain \(\tfrac13\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\,(n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + n_{\mathrm{z}}^2) = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}/3\), because the terms with two different indices are zero and the sum of the squares of the components of a unit vector is \(1\). In figure 2.322 this is the middle piece: the edge along the axis \(x\) and the edge along the axis \(y\) lengthen by the same amount \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} h/3\).
  3. By section 2.9.6 the cosine of the angle between two short fibres in perpendicular directions \(\vek m\) and \(\vek n\) after loading is, to first order, \(2\,\vek m^\T\ten\varepsilon\,\vek n\), and the angle stays right to first order when this number is zero. For \(\ten\varepsilon = \tfrac13\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\,\mat I\) we have \(\vek m^\T\ten\varepsilon\,\vek n = \tfrac13\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\,(\vek m\cdot\vek n) = 0\), because \(\vek m\) and \(\vek n\) are perpendicular. So the middle piece still has right angles after loading.

2. The deviatoric strain.

  1. By definition \(e_{\mathrm{xx}} + e_{\mathrm{yy}} + e_{\mathrm{zz}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} - 3 \cdot \varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}/3 = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} = 0\).

3. The change of volume.

  1. By section 2.10.5 the loading maps a small piece at \(P\) (the blackwhite cube) onto a body that differs from the parallelepiped (the orange piece) spanned by the vectors of its edges multiplied by the deformation gradient \(\mat F\) only by remainders that are small compared with the length of the edges. We drop the remainders, as the assumption of point 3 says. For the hanging bar and an edge of 1 mm this changes the ratio of volumes by \(1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-10}\), for a shorter edge by even less (figure 2.232). By item 1 of lemma 2.77 on the change of volume the ratio of the volume of the parallelepiped to the volume of the piece is \(|\det\mat F|\).
  2. By item 2 of the same lemma the ratio of volumes of the orange piece and the blackwhite cube, \(\det\mat F\), differs from \(1 + H_{\mathrm{xx}} + H_{\mathrm{yy}} + H_{\mathrm{zz}}\) by at most \(6g^2 + 6g^3\), where \(H_{\mathrm{ij}}\) are the entries of the displacement gradient \(\mat H = \mat F - \mat I\), the partial derivatives of the displacements at \(P\), and \(g\) is the largest of their absolute values. The ratio of this difference to \(g\) is at most \(6g + 6g^2\), so for \(g = 0{,}001\) it is \(0{,}006006\), about \(0{,}6\,\%\). For \(g\) near \(1/6\) or more the difference is not small, so the assumption of small strains requires \(g\) much smaller than that. Since \(|H_{\mathrm{xx}} + H_{\mathrm{yy}} + H_{\mathrm{zz}}| \le 3g\), we have \(\det\mat F \ge 1 - 3g - 6g^2 - 6g^3\), which for \(g = 0{,}001\) is more than \(0{,}996\). So the determinant is positive, and \(|\det\mat F| = \det\mat F\).
  3. By (1.59) \(H_{\mathrm{xx}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(H_{\mathrm{yy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and \(H_{\mathrm{zz}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\), so the ratio of the volumes is approximately \(1 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = 1 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\). In the figure these are the lengthening of the edge along the rod and the shortening of the transverse edges.
  4. The relative change of volume is this ratio minus \(1\), so \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\) up to the error \(6g^2 + 6g^3\) of step 2. In figure 2.322 it is the difference between the volume of the orange piece and that of the blackwhite cube, divided by the volume of the blackwhite cube.

Source: SADD, PDF p. 49, BOWER §2.1.9 (PDF pp. 51-52), where \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{kk}} \approx J - 1\). The proof is not from the sources.

So the spherical part stretches or shrinks the piece equally in all directions to first order, so that it stays similar to itself: a cube stays a cube, only larger or smaller. The deviatoric part has zero volumetric strain, so by item 3 of the lemma, applied to it, it does not change the volume to first order, but it changes the shape. SADD says this too: the spherical strain represents only the change of volume, the deviatoric strain the changes of shape (SADD, PDF p. 49).

Two examples from chapter 1. The steel cube with edge 10 mm of section 1.6.2 is glued to a table with its bottom face, and its top face is pushed by 10 µm in the direction \(x\). Its displacement field is \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = 0{,}001\,z\) and \(u_{\mathrm{y}} = u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\), where \(0{,}001\) is the shift of 10 µm divided by the height of 10 mm. The only nonzero strain components are \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zx}} = \tfrac12\,(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial z + \partial u_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial x) = \tfrac12\,(0{,}001 + 0) = 5 \cdot 10^{-4}\), and the diagonal components are zero, since \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) does not depend on \(x\) and \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\) are zero. So \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} = 0\), and the strain is purely deviatoric: the cube changes its shape but not its volume. For this cube we found this in section 1.6.2 with the area of a parallelogram, and now the numbers show that the volume does not change to first order. That it does not change exactly, only the computation with the area shows.

The steel hanging bar of length 10 m of section 1.7.1 stretches under its own weight. Only the centre \(O\) of its top end is fixed, and the weight is carried by a force spread evenly over the top face, which is the idealization of that section. The axis \(x\) points vertically down from \(O\). At the point \(P = (5\ \text{m}, 4\ \text{mm}, 0)\) we think of a small cube of material with edge \(h\). There the bar has the strain along the bar \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = 2a\,(L - x) = 2 \cdot 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{-1} \cdot 5\ \text{m} = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6}\), where \(a = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-7}\) m⁻¹ is the constant of section 1.2 and \(L - x = 10\ \text{m} - 5\ \text{m}\), and the transverse strains \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = -0{,}3\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = -5{,}856 \cdot 10^{-7}\), where \(0{,}3\) is the ratio of thinning to stretching of steel from section 1.6. The shear components are zero. The volumetric strain is

\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\,(1 - 2 \cdot 0{,}3) = 0{,}4\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = 7{,}808 \cdot 10^{-7} .\]

The factor \(0{,}4\) is \(1\) for the stretch along the bar, reduced by twice \(0{,}3\) for the thinning in the two transverse directions. So a small piece of material around \(P\) grows by \(0{,}78\) millionths of its volume, because it lengthens more than it thins in the two transverse directions together. The spherical part stretches every fibre by \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}/3 = 2{,}603 \cdot 10^{-7}\) of its length. The deviatoric strain has the components

\[\begin{aligned} e_{\mathrm{xx}} &= 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6} - 2{,}603 \cdot 10^{-7} = 1{,}692 \cdot 10^{-6} , \\ e_{\mathrm{yy}} = e_{\mathrm{zz}} &= -5{,}856 \cdot 10^{-7} - 2{,}603 \cdot 10^{-7} = -8{,}459 \cdot 10^{-7} , \end{aligned}\]

with the sum \(1{,}692 \cdot 10^{-6} - 2 \cdot 8{,}459 \cdot 10^{-7} = 2 \cdot 10^{-10}\). This remainder is only rounding in the last digit: with the unrounded numbers the sum is exactly \(0\), as point 2 of the lemma says. With the deviatoric part the piece lengthens along the bar and thins by half as much in each of the two transverse directions, so that its volume does not change to first order. Figure 2.322 shows all three pieces together.

The axis \(x\) points down along the bar, the axis \(y\) to the right and the axis \(z\) into the depth. The blackwhite cubes are the piece before loading, with the edge \(h\). The changes of the edges are millionths of an edge, so we draw them exaggerated 300 000 times. We draw the top left front corner of every piece in place, so that the whole change of an edge shows at its other end, as a blue distance. On the left is the orange piece after the whole strain: the edge along the bar is longer by \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}h\), the transverse edge shorter by \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}h\). In the middle is the piece after the spherical part, which lengthens every edge by the same amount, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} h/3\) downwards and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} h/3\) across. On the right is the piece after the deviatoric part, which lengthens it by \(e_{\mathrm{xx}}h\) and thins it by \(e_{\mathrm{yy}}h\). The equals sign and the sign \(+\) say that the change of every edge of the left piece is the sum of the changes in the middle and the right one: along the bar \(1{,}952 = 0{,}260 + 1{,}692\), across it \(-0{,}586 = 0{,}260 - 0{,}846\), both in millionths of the edge. We may add them because the components of \(\ten\varepsilon\) enter the strain of a fibre (1.61) only to the first power, and \(\ten\varepsilon\) is the sum of the spherical and the deviatoric part.

Point 3 of lemma 2.115 can also be seen without the determinant, on the left piece of figure 2.322. The shear components of the strain of the bar are zero, so the axes \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\) are principal directions of strain (definition 2.91), with the principal strains \(\varepsilon_1 = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and \(\varepsilon_2 = \varepsilon_3 = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\). There is no shear strain between principal directions (corollary 2.92), so the edges of the cube along them stay perpendicular to first order. Only their lengths change, from \(h\) to \(h\,(1 + \varepsilon_1)\) along the bar and to \(h\,(1 + \varepsilon_2)\) and \(h\,(1 + \varepsilon_3)\) across it: the cube becomes a cuboid. The ratio of the volume \(V'\) of the cuboid and the volume \(V = h^3\) of the cube is

\[\frac{V'}{V} = (1 + \varepsilon_1)(1 + \varepsilon_2)(1 + \varepsilon_3) = 1 + (\varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2 + \varepsilon_3) + (\varepsilon_1\varepsilon_2 + \varepsilon_2\varepsilon_3 + \varepsilon_3\varepsilon_1) + \varepsilon_1\varepsilon_2\varepsilon_3 .\]

The first bracket holds the strains themselves, the second their products in pairs, the last term is the product of three. For the bar the first bracket is \(1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6} - 2 \cdot 5{,}856 \cdot 10^{-7} = 7{,}808 \cdot 10^{-7}\), the second \(-1{,}94 \cdot 10^{-12}\), two and a half millionths of the first. Since we know the lengths of the edges and the right angles only to first order, we keep only the first bracket: the relative change of volume is, to first order, the sum of the principal strains. That this sum is the same number as \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\), computed in any axes, is said by a lemma.

Lemma 2.116 The volumetric strain is an invariant (prostorninska deformacija je invarianta)

Let \(\ten\varepsilon\) be the matrix of small strains at the point \(P\) in a chosen rectangular Cartesian coordinate system and \(\bar{\ten\varepsilon}\) the matrix of small strains at \(P\) in the system turned by the rotation matrix \(\mat Q\). The piece around \(P\) is the same, only the axes change, so we expect the relative change of its volume not to change. Then

\[\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + \bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} . \tag{2.135}\]

In particular \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} = \varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2 + \varepsilon_3\), where \(\varepsilon_1\), \(\varepsilon_2\) and \(\varepsilon_3\) are the principal strains at \(P\).

Proof

We express the sum of the diagonal elements in the turned axes with the old components.

  1. By lemma 2.55 \(\bar{\ten\varepsilon} = \mat Q\,\ten\varepsilon\,\mat Q^\T\), so a diagonal element is \(\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{kk}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} Q_{\mathrm{ki}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,Q_{\mathrm{kj}}\).
  2. We sum over \(k\) and change the order of summation: \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} \bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{kk}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\sum_{\mathrm{k}} Q_{\mathrm{ki}}Q_{\mathrm{kj}}\).
  3. The inner sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} Q_{\mathrm{ki}}Q_{\mathrm{kj}}\) is the element of the product \(\mat Q^\T\mat Q\) in row \(i\) and column \(j\). By lemma 2.47 on the orthogonality of the rotation matrix \(\mat Q^\T\mat Q = \mat I\), so the sum is \(1\) for \(i = j\) and \(0\) otherwise.
  4. Of the double sum only the terms with \(i = j\) remain: \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} \bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{kk}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\).
  5. For the turned system we take the axes along the principal directions of strain (we reverse one principal direction if needed so that the system is right-handed, which does not change the principal strains). By point 1 of corollary 2.92 the diagonal elements there are \(\varepsilon_1\), \(\varepsilon_2\) and \(\varepsilon_3\), as for the cube with edges along the bar and across it. By step 4 their sum equals \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\).

Source: SADD gives the volumetric strain as the first invariant of strain (SADD, PDF p. 49). The proof is not from the sources.

What the lemma means we see on the hanging bar at the point \(P\) if we turn the axes about the \(z\) axis (figure 2.323).

On the left is the piece around \(P\), seen along the \(z\) axis, with the \(x\) axis pointing down and the \(y\) axis to the right, as in figure 2.322. We draw the deformation magnified 100 000 times. The square with edges along the axes becomes a rectangle: the edge along \(x\) lengthens by \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}h\), the edge along \(y\) shortens by \(|\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}|h\). On the right are the axes \(\bar x\) and \(\bar y\), turned by \(45^\circ\) about the \(z\) axis, while the third axis stays the \(z\) axis. The square with edges along them is made of the same material, but it becomes a rhombus. A fibre in the direction \(\bar x\), with the unit vector \((\vek e_{\mathrm{x}} + \vek e_{\mathrm{y}})/\sqrt2\), has by (1.61) the strain

\[\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \tfrac12\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \tfrac12\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \tfrac12\,(1{,}952 - 0{,}5856) \cdot 10^{-6} = 0{,}6832 \cdot 10^{-6} ,\]

because \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\). The same holds for a fibre in the direction \(\bar y\), with the unit vector \((-\vek e_{\mathrm{x}} + \vek e_{\mathrm{y}})/\sqrt2\), so both edges of the rhombus lengthen by the same amount \(\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}h\). For these two vectors \(\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = \tfrac12\,(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}) = -1{,}269 \cdot 10^{-6}\). By section 2.9.6 the cosine of the angle between the edges of the rhombus after loading is \(2\,\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = -2{,}538 \cdot 10^{-6}\), so the right angle grows by \(2{,}538 \cdot 10^{-6}\) radians. In the turned axes, part of the stretching along the axes has become shear.

Below are the diagonal elements of both systems as arrows to scale, placed one after another, in millionths. The upper row is \(1{,}952 - 0{,}5856 - 0{,}5856\), the lower one \(0{,}6832 + 0{,}6832 - 0{,}5856\). The last two arrows are equal, because the \(z\) axis does not turn. Both rows end at the same dashed line, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} = 0{,}7808 \cdot 10^{-6}\). The individual diagonal elements differ in the turned axes, but their sum is the same, as the lemma says.

For the stress we measured the size of the deviatoric part by one number, the octahedral shear stress \(\tau_{\mathrm{oct}}\) (lemma 2.110). A similar number exists for the strain. Take a short fibre from \(P\) in the direction \(\vek n\) that is equally inclined to all three principal directions of strain, and the plane through \(P\) perpendicular to it. We ask how much the fibre stretches and by how much the right angle between it and the fibres in this plane decreases (figure 2.324).

On the left we look at the plane through \(P\) from the side, so that the direction \(\vek n\) is vertical. Drawn is the vector \(\ten\varepsilon\,\vek n\), the product of the strain matrix with the direction of the fibre. Its part along \(\vek n\) is \(\vek n^\T\ten\varepsilon\,\vek n\), the strain of the fibre by (1.61). Its part in the plane defines a direction that we denote \(\vek m\). On the right are the fibres in the directions \(\vek n\) and \(\vek m\) before loading, at a right angle, and after it.

Lemma 2.117 Octahedral shear strain (oktaedrska strižna deformacija)

Let \(\ten\varepsilon\) be the matrix of small strains at the point \(P\), \(\varepsilon_1\), \(\varepsilon_2\) and \(\varepsilon_3\) the principal strains, \(\vek n_1\), \(\vek n_2\) and \(\vek n_3\) the corresponding mutually perpendicular principal directions of strain and \(\vek n = (\pm\vek n_1 \pm \vek n_2 \pm \vek n_3)/\sqrt3\) for any choice of signs. The direction \(\vek n\) and the plane perpendicular to it are in the figure, and the vector \(\ten\varepsilon\,\vek n\) has a part along \(\vek n\) and a part in the plane. Then:

  1. \(\vek n^\T\ten\varepsilon\,\vek n = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}/3\). This is the length of the part of the vector \(\ten\varepsilon\,\vek n\) along \(\vek n\).
  2. The part of the vector \(\ten\varepsilon\,\vek n\) perpendicular to \(\vek n\) has the length
    \[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{oct}} = \frac13\sqrt{(\varepsilon_1 - \varepsilon_2)^2 + (\varepsilon_2 - \varepsilon_3)^2 + (\varepsilon_3 - \varepsilon_1)^2} . \tag{2.136}\]
  3. For every unit vector \(\vek m\) perpendicular to \(\vek n\) (like \(\vek m\) in the figure), \(|\vek m^\T\ten\varepsilon\,\vek n| \le \varepsilon_{\mathrm{oct}}\). For \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{oct}} > 0\) equality holds exactly when \(\vek m\) points in the direction of the perpendicular part of point 2 or opposite to it. For \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{oct}} = 0\) it holds for every \(\vek m\).

The number \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{oct}}\) is called the octahedral shear strain (oktaedrska strižna deformacija), and the number \(\gamma_{\mathrm{oct}} = 2\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{oct}}\) the engineering octahedral shear strain.

Proof

The computation is the same as in the second way of the proof of lemma 2.110, with the principal strains in place of the principal stresses.

  1. In the axes along \(\vek n_1\), \(\vek n_2\) and \(\vek n_3\) the matrix \(\ten\varepsilon\) is diagonal by point 1 of corollary 2.92, and the direction \(\vek n\) has the components \(\pm 1/\sqrt3\). The vector \(\ten\varepsilon\,\vek n\) therefore has the components \(\pm\varepsilon_1/\sqrt3\), \(\pm\varepsilon_2/\sqrt3\) and \(\pm\varepsilon_3/\sqrt3\), with the same signs as \(\vek n\).
  2. The part along \(\vek n\) is the scalar product \(\vek n\cdot(\ten\varepsilon\,\vek n) = \tfrac13\,(\varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2 + \varepsilon_3)\), which by lemma 2.116 equals \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}/3\). This is point 1.
  3. By lemma 2.14 on splitting a vector and Pythagoras' theorem, the square of the length of the perpendicular part is \(|\ten\varepsilon\,\vek n|^2 - (\vek n^\T\ten\varepsilon\,\vek n)^2 = \tfrac13\,(\varepsilon_1^2 + \varepsilon_2^2 + \varepsilon_3^2) - \tfrac19\,(\varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2 + \varepsilon_3)^2\).
  4. We multiply by \(9\) and write out the square of the sum: \(3\,(\varepsilon_1^2 + \varepsilon_2^2 + \varepsilon_3^2) - (\varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2 + \varepsilon_3)^2 = 2\,(\varepsilon_1^2 + \varepsilon_2^2 + \varepsilon_3^2) - 2\,(\varepsilon_1\varepsilon_2 + \varepsilon_2\varepsilon_3 + \varepsilon_3\varepsilon_1)\). This is the sum \((\varepsilon_1 - \varepsilon_2)^2 + (\varepsilon_2 - \varepsilon_3)^2 + (\varepsilon_3 - \varepsilon_1)^2\), since each of the three squared differences contributes two squares and one double product. We divide by \(9\) and take the root, which is the length of the perpendicular part: this is point 2.
  5. We denote the perpendicular part by \(\vek p\), so that \(\ten\varepsilon\,\vek n = \tfrac13\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\,\vek n + \vek p\). For a unit \(\vek m\) perpendicular to \(\vek n\), \(\vek m^\T\ten\varepsilon\,\vek n = \tfrac13\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\,(\vek m\cdot\vek n) + \vek m\cdot\vek p = \vek m\cdot\vek p\).
  6. By the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality (corollary 2.15) for \(\vek m\) and \(\vek p\) \(|\vek m\cdot\vek p| \le |\vek m|\,|\vek p| = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{oct}}\). For \(\vek p \ne \vek 0\) and \(\vek m = \pm\vek p/|\vek p|\) we get \(\vek m\cdot\vek p = \pm|\vek p|\), which is equality. For any other \(\vek m\) there is no equality. Indeed, by item 3 of lemma 2.14, for the unit vector \(\vek e = \vek p/|\vek p|\) we have \(1 = |\vek m|^2 = (\vek m\cdot\vek e)^2 + |\vek r|^2\) with \(\vek r = \vek m - (\vek m\cdot\vek e)\,\vek e\). Equality \(|\vek m\cdot\vek p| = |\vek p|\) means \((\vek m\cdot\vek e)^2 = 1\), hence \(\vek r = \vek 0\) and \(\vek m = \pm\vek e\). For \(\vek p = \vek 0\) we have \(\vek m\cdot\vek p = 0 = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{oct}}\) for every \(\vek m\). This is point 3.

Source: The proof is not from the sources. The octahedral plane and the stresses on it are in SADD §3.5 (PDF p. 73).

We see point 3 of the lemma if we look at the plane along the direction \(\vek n\) (figure 2.325).

The direction \(\vek n\) points toward us, the plane is the sheet of paper. In it lies the perpendicular part \(\vek p\) of the vector \(\ten\varepsilon\,\vek n\) from point 2, for the hanging bar of length \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{oct}} = 1{,}196 \cdot 10^{-6}\). A fibre in the plane has a direction, a unit vector \(\vek m\). We draw three such directions: \(\vek m_1\) along \(\vek p\), \(\vek m_2\) at \(60^\circ\) to \(\vek p\) and \(\vek m_3\) perpendicular to \(\vek p\). By step 5 of the proof \(\vek m^\T\ten\varepsilon\,\vek n = \vek m\cdot\vek p\), and this is the projection of \(\vek p\) onto the line of direction \(\vek m\), from \(P\) to the foot of the perpendicular from the tip of \(\vek p\). The length of the projection, \(|\vek m\cdot\vek p|\), is a leg of a right triangle with hypotenuse \(\vek p\), so it is not longer than \(|\vek p|\), like the leg and the hypotenuse in figure 2.33. This is the inequality of point 3.

The foot for the direction \(\vek m\) is the point \((\vek m\cdot\vek p)\,\vek m\). Its distance from the midpoint \(\vek p/2\) is \(|\vek p|/2\) for every \(\vek m\), since \(|(\vek m\cdot\vek p)\,\vek m - \vek p/2|^2 = (\vek m\cdot\vek p)^2 - (\vek m\cdot\vek p)^2 + |\vek p|^2/4\). So all the feet lie on the circle with diameter \(\vek p\), and the projections are chords of this circle from \(P\). The longest is the diameter, the projection onto \(\vek m_1\), \(1{,}196 \cdot 10^{-6}\). The projection onto \(\vek m_2\) is \(1{,}196 \cdot 10^{-6} \cdot \cos 60^\circ = 0{,}598 \cdot 10^{-6}\), and the projection onto \(\vek m_3\) is zero, its foot is \(P\) itself.

What does the lemma say about fibres? By section 2.9.6 the cosine of the angle between two short fibres in perpendicular directions \(\vek m\) and \(\vek n\) after loading is, to first order, \(2\,\vek m^\T\ten\varepsilon\,\vek n\), and by that many radians the right angle between them decreases. Among all fibres in the plane perpendicular to \(\vek n\), the right angle therefore decreases most for the fibre in the direction \(\vek m\) of the perpendicular part, the direction \(\vek m_1\) in figure 2.325, namely by \(\gamma_{\mathrm{oct}} = 2\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{oct}}\). For the bar this is \(2{,}392 \cdot 10^{-6}\) radians, for the direction \(\vek m_2\) \(2 \cdot 0{,}598 \cdot 10^{-6} = 1{,}196 \cdot 10^{-6}\) radians, and for the direction \(\vek m_3\) the right angle stays right to first order. The number \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{oct}}\) is a tensor component, like \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\), and it is half the engineering angle \(\gamma_{\mathrm{oct}}\), just as \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) is half of \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}}\). When the piece as a whole does not turn, the two halves show separately: the fibre in the direction \(\vek m\) turns toward \(\vek n\) by \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{oct}}\) and the fibre in the direction \(\vek n\) toward \(\vek m\) by \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{oct}}\). The assumption is that of small strains of section 2.9.6: the terms left out are products of two derivatives of the displacements, so for derivatives below \(0{,}001\) they are below a few millionths. For large strains, as in the rubber band, the relation between \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{oct}}\) and the angle does not hold.

For the hanging bar at the point \(P\) the principal strains are \(1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6}\) and twice \(-5{,}856 \cdot 10^{-7}\), their differences are \(2{,}538 \cdot 10^{-6}\) (twice) and \(0\). By (2.136) \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{oct}} = \tfrac13\sqrt{2 \cdot 2{,}538^2} \cdot 10^{-6}\), which is \(1{,}196 \cdot 10^{-6}\), and \(\gamma_{\mathrm{oct}} = 2{,}392 \cdot 10^{-6}\) radians. The fibre in the direction \(\vek n\) has the strain \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}/3 = 2{,}603 \cdot 10^{-7}\), the same number as for the spherical part above. The spherical part contributes nothing in point 2 of the lemma. The deviatoric part has the same principal directions, since \(\ten e\,\vek n_{\mathrm{i}} = \ten\varepsilon\,\vek n_{\mathrm{i}} - \tfrac13\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\,\vek n_{\mathrm{i}} = (\varepsilon_{\mathrm{i}} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}/3)\,\vek n_{\mathrm{i}}\). So its principal strains are \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{i}} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}/3\), and subtracting the same number does not change their differences. For the bar the difference of the deviatoric principal strains is \(1{,}692 \cdot 10^{-6} + 8{,}459 \cdot 10^{-7} = 2{,}538 \cdot 10^{-6}\), the same as above. So \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{oct}}\) is a measure of the deviatoric part alone: it measures the change of shape, just as \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\) measures the change of volume. In section 3.6.6 we shall see that for an isotropic elastic material the octahedral shear stress is proportional to the octahedral shear strain.

We have split stress and strain in the same way, into a part that is the same in all directions and a deviatoric part. Whether the parts are related, the mean stress to the volumetric strain and the stress deviator to the deviatoric strain, depends on the material. For a material that behaves the same in all directions we will see it in chapter 3.

All the stresses of this chapter are forces per unit area of faces in the loaded body (definition 2.20). As long as a steel bar does not yield, its strain along the bar is below about \(0{,}0011\) (section 2.2), and the transverse strain is \(0{,}3\) times as large with the opposite sign. How the areas of two faces change we see on the left piece of figure 2.322. The face across the bar has both edges transverse. Each shortens by \(0{,}3 \cdot 0{,}0011\) of its length, so its area decreases by about \(2 \cdot 0{,}3 \cdot 0{,}0011 = 0{,}066\,\%\). The face along the bar has one edge along the bar, which lengthens by \(0{,}0011\) of its length, and one transverse edge, which shortens by \(0{,}3 \cdot 0{,}0011\). Its area therefore increases by about \(0{,}0011 - 0{,}00033 = 0{,}077\,\%\). The dropped product of two strains is below \(4 \cdot 10^{-7}\). With a change below \(0{,}08\,\%\) it does not matter whether we measure the area before or after loading. The rubber band of section 1.1, however, we stretched from 10 cm to 15 cm, and its cross section becomes noticeably smaller. To which area the stress should refer when deformations are large is the question of the next section.
